legal_basis: Section 302 IPC [now BNS 103(1)] — punishment for murder: death, or imprisonment for life, and fine (PDF 334)

Section 304 IPC [now BNS 105] — punishment for culpable homicide not amounting to murder: imprisonment for life or up to ten years where the act is done with intention to cause death or such bodily injury as is likely to cause death; up to ten years, or fine, or both, where done only with knowledge that it is likely to cause death (PDF 334-335)

Section 307 IPC [now BNS 109] — attempt to murder: up to ten years and fine; imprisonment for life if hurt is caused; and where a life convict offending under this section causes hurt, he may be punished with death (PDF 335)
Section 308 IPC [now BNS 110] — attempt to commit culpable homicide: up to three years, or fine, or both; up to seven years if hurt is caused (PDF 335)
Section 336 IPC [now BNS 125] — act so rashly or negligently as to endanger human life or the personal safety of others: up to three months, or fine up to Rs. 250, or both (PDF 335)
Section 337 IPC [now BNS 125(a)] — causing hurt by an act endangering life or personal safety of others: up to six months, or fine up to Rs. 500, or both (PDF 335)

Section 25 Arms Act 1959 — punishment for contravention of ss.3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 17, 24A, 24B (acquiring, possession, carrying, manufacture, sale, transfer, conversion, repair, testing, proving, import, export, shortening of barrel, etc.). The Arms Act is a separate central statute and is unaffected by the 2023 codes — no BNS equivalent applies (PDF 336)

Section 27 Arms Act 1959 — punishment for using arms: use of arms/ammunition in contravention of s.5 — not less than three years and up to seven years and fine; use of prohibited arms/ammunition in contravention of s.7 — not less than seven years up to imprisonment for life and fine; and where such use or act results in the death of any other person — punishable with death (PDF 336)

Section 157 CrPC [now BNSS 176] — officer in charge of the police station, having recorded the information and forwarded the report to the Magistrate, shall proceed in person (or send a subordinate) to the spot to investigate the facts (PDF 336)
Arms Act 1959 — statutory definitions of 'arms' and 'ammunition' relied on when framing queries to the ballistic expert about fired ammunition and live ammunition (PDF 373, PDF 375)

State of Orissa vs. Ramachandra, AIR 1965 Orissa 175 — cited in the guide (printed as 'state of Orissa vs. Ramachandra AIR, 1965 Orissa 175') and described by the guide as 'a ruling of the Supreme Court of India' that an IO can ask the medical officer to take an x-ray of the body and recover the projectiles; note that the citation as printed is to an Orissa High Court report, so the 'Supreme Court' attribution is the guide's own and should be checked before being relied on in court (PDF 371)

NHRC D.O. No. 4/7/2008 PRPNP dated 12 May 2010, 'Revised Guidelines/Procedures to be Followed in Cases of Death Caused by Police Action', Para G(b)3(iii) — 'Results of forensic examination of "hand wash" of the deceased to ascertain the presence of residue of gunpowder to justify exercise of right to self-defense' (PDF 381)
steps.triage_why: Proper labeling is sound practice for organization and clarity in court, but not a statutory mandate that would invalidate the evidence.

steps.title: Secure the Evidentiary Basis of Scene Photographs
steps.text: Secure the evidentiary basis of the photographs/video: when a photograph/videograph is to be submitted as evidence, the electronic-record certificate is mandatory (s.65B Evidence Act [now BSA s.63]); in grave crimes/important cases record the photographer's statement u/s 161 CrPC [now BNSS 180]; and if photography was done by a digital camera, collect the memory chip containing the clips along with the developed prints to prove genuineness in Court.
legal_basis: BSA 63 (printed as s.65B Evidence Act)
BNSS 180 (printed as s.161 CrPC)
steps.triage_why: BSA s.63 (formerly 65B) certification is a mandatory statutory requirement for the admissibility of electronic evidence; without it, the photos/videos are inadmissible.

ticks.do: Obtain the electronic-record certificate whenever a photograph or videograph is to be submitted as evidence (s.65B Evidence Act [now BSA s.63]).
notes: The certificate is mandatory.

ticks.do: Record the photographer's statement u/s 161 CrPC [now BNSS 180] in grave crimes and important cases.
Collect the memory chip containing the clips along with the developed prints to prove genuineness in Court, where photography was done by a digital camera.

steps.title: Deposit Seized Property and Report to Court
steps.text: After completion of the search proceedings, deposit the seized items/documents/properties/material objects into the Malkhana of the nearest police station by making a proper entry in the Malkhana Register, to maintain the chain of custody; report the seizure to the court having jurisdiction just after the search and obtain the permission of the competent jurisdictional court, where required, for retention of the seized properties.
steps.stage: Handling, seizure documentation and packaging at the scene
steps.deadline: Report the seizure to the jurisdictional court just after the search (BPRD SOP p.60)
steps.triage_why: Failure to maintain the chain of custody via the Malkhana register and failure to report seizures to the court can lead to evidence being declared inadmissible due to tampering risks.

steps.title: Prepare and Attest the Seizure Memo
steps.text: After completion of the search, the IO decides which recovered articles/objects/documents/movable properties to seize, keeping in view their evidentiary value, and prepares the seizure memo in the NCRB Integrated Investigation Form-IV (Annexure-C; IIF-2 in CCTNS parlance): list every seized article with brief description and colour; for serial-numbered items (mobile phones, electronic devices, computers, pen drives, laptops) clearly indicate the make with serial/model number; state the composition of the team and the date and time of commencement and completion of the search; have officials and witnesses attest it; serve a copy on the owner/occupant of the premises and obtain their signature; and have the witnesses and the IO append their signatures on the seized documents/articles. Videograph the preparation and signing of the seizure memo, and mention in it the recording-device details, date/time, description of the storage media and the hash value of each individual image/video footage (the hash value also being entered in the panchnama and the case diary).
steps.stage: Handling, seizure documentation and packaging at the scene
legal_basis: BNSS 105
steps.triage_why: The seizure memo is the primary legal document proving the recovery of evidence (like the mobile phone); without it, the recovery cannot be legally established.

Draw the sample seal in triplicate and hand over the seal used to a witness, with instructions to produce it before the court at the appropriate time and to maintain the integrity of the chain of custody.

steps.title: Complete the checks before leaving the crime scene
steps.text: Before leaving the crime scene the IO shall ensure that the crime scene has been photographed properly; that the crime scene search has been done thoroughly; that all the evidence collected at the scene is properly packed, labelled and sealed; and that all memos are duly filled in and all other formalities in respect of the procedures mandated by the law are completed. Take detailed photographs of the scene, of all the evidences and of the surrounding areas from different angles, including a final photograph of the scene and close photographs of the evidences.
steps.stage: Handling, seizure documentation and packaging at the scene
steps.applies_when: Conclusion of scene work at any crime scene, before the IO leaves the spot
steps.triage_why: This is a final quality check. While critical for a thorough investigation, it is a summary of other MUST_DO steps rather than a separate statutory duty.

ticks.do: Ensure the following before leaving the crime scene.
sub: The crime scene has been photographed properly.
The crime scene search has been done thoroughly.

All memos are duly filled in and all other formalities in respect of the procedures mandated by the law are completed.
notes: The IO shall ensure each of these.

steps.title: Handle and Lift Objects to Preserve Traces
steps.text: Lift objects without destroying latent evidence: flat objects only by holding at the edges; bottles and glass tumblers only by the rim of top and bottom (the rim may carry salivary stains usable for DNA profiling); daggers/knives by the tips, securing the cutting edges with jute or cotton; never handle anything bare-handed, as it can destroy latent fingerprints. Properly preserve and lift fingerprint evidence and send the prints to the Fingerprint Bureau via Court immediately after the scene examination.
steps.stage: Handling, seizure documentation and packaging at the scene
steps.deadline: Lifted fingerprints to the Fingerprint Bureau via Court immediately after the scene examination (Kerala SOP p.54)
steps.triage_why: In a sexual offence case, DNA and fingerprints are critical. Improper handling (bare hands) destroys this fragile evidence, which cannot be recovered.

sub: Hold flat objects only by the edges.
Hold bottles and glass tumblers only by the rim of top and bottom.
Hold daggers and knives by the tips, securing the cutting edges with jute or cotton.
notes: The rim of a bottle or glass tumbler may carry salivary stains usable for DNA profiling.

steps.title: Pack, Label and Seal Scene Exhibits
steps.text: Protect all evidence against loss, contamination, cross-transfer (suspect to victim, victim to suspect, scene to scene, item to item) and deterioration, and take care while picking and packing that no article is inadvertently contaminated with extraneous material. Pack each article separately with a label indicating the serial number of the item; never pack more than one type of item together; label each exhibit with FIR number and date, section of law, IO's name, police station, district and state, duly signed and sealed by the IO; number labels consecutively with the forwarding officer's signature; enclose all packets belonging to one case in one box or outer covering; never forward articles of different cases under the same cover; and seal all parcels so they cannot be opened without destroying the seals.
steps.stage: Handling, seizure documentation and packaging at the scene
steps.triage_why: Cross-contamination in sexual assault cases (victim to suspect) can lead to the collapse of the forensic case during cross-examination.

steps.title: Apply the Fallback Safeguards Outside e-SAKSHYA
steps.text: ONLY where recording in e-SAKSHYA is technically not possible, record with a mobile or other recorder and then: (a) note the reasons for not using e-SAKSHYA in the Station Diary and case diary; (b) obtain a certificate under s.63 Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam for the recording; (c) store at least three copies on other storage media (pen drive/DVD/CD/memory card/hard disk) kept safely in the IO's own custody; (d) place the storage device in an envelope, obtain the signatures of both panchas and of the person concerned (accused/victim), sign as the person present (rubaru), paste the signature slip on the envelope and seal it; (e) maintain the chain of custody - record the handling, packing and transportation of seized articles from seizure of the muddamal to handover of custody and from dispatch for examination to retrieval (description, date/time of transfer, name of the handler, changes in custody) in the case diary and Station Diary, make a detailed entry of the sealed articles/documents in the muddamal register, and deposit the muddamal at the police station, noting this in the Station Diary and case diary; (f) send a copy of the recording to the concerned Court within 48 hours.
legal_basis: BSA 63
steps.deadline: Copy of the recording to the concerned Court within 48 hours (Gujarat SOP 9, p.39)
steps.applies_when: Audio-video recording in the e-SAKSHYA application is not possible for technical reasons
steps.triage_why: Compliance with e-SAKSHYA/BSA s.63 is now a statutory requirement for the integrity of digital recordings in Indian criminal law.

conflicts.description: guj_cid_29_sops_2024 SOP 9 (p.38) requires at least three copies of the fallback recording to be stored on separate media and kept safely in the IO's OWN custody; bprd_av_recording_sop (bprd-av-recording-procedures pp.41-43 and p.60) requires exactly one WORM 'master negative' plus one 'negative duplicate' held by the evidence specialist in secured departmental custody, expressly outside the investigative case files, with the recording deleted from the officer's own phone/recorder after download.
conflicts.resolution: For Gujarat the binding SOP 9 custody regime governs the e-SAKSHYA-failure branch: three sealed copies in the IO's custody with the muddamal-register and diary entries. The BPRD master-negative/mirror regime is retained as the national-advisory best practice for the normal (e-SAKSHYA or departmental-device) stream and is not to be read as authorising deletion of the fallback recording from the IO's custody.

steps.title: Document custody from seizure through to court
steps.text: Maintain a written chain of custody for every recording and every sealed evidence package from creation/seizure until handover to the forensic laboratory and to the court: once packed and sealed in front of the witnesses, keep a clear written chain of custody record for each package, documenting the name and signature of every person (including internal staff) who takes possession of or transports the evidence, the date of transfer, and the evidence's label or serial number, using the Chain of Custody Form (Case Details; Device Details; transfer-by-transfer Chain of Custody Documentation). Keep the record in a secure and reliable system with appropriate access controls and audit trails so it remains in 'proper custody' (BSA Explanation to ss.80 and 81, and s.93); send the sealed package for forensic examination without undue delay; and at the time of chargesheet submit the chain of custody with the chargesheet u/s 193 BNSS.
legal_basis: BNSS 193(3)
BSA 80
BSA 81
BSA 93
steps.deadline: Send the sealed evidence package to the forensic laboratory without undue delay (BPRD SOP p.61)
steps.triage_why: A broken chain of custody for sealed evidence allows the defense to argue that the evidence was swapped or tampered with, often leading to acquittal.

steps.title: Certify electronic records under BSA section 63(4)
steps.text: Submit a certificate under BSA s.63(4) with the electronic record at EACH instance it is produced for admission: it must identify the electronic record containing the statement and describe the manner in which it was produced, give particulars of any device involved in its production, and deal with the s.63(2) conditions; it is signed BOTH by the person in charge of the computer or communication device or of the management of the relevant activities (Schedule Part A) AND by an expert (Part B), matters being stated to the best of knowledge and belief in the format specified in the Schedule. Certification does not require the OWNER of the device but the person who actually manages the device regularly at the relevant time. Never submit digital evidence to court without this certificate.
steps.triage_why: Statutory requirement under BSA s.63(4); the certificate is the legal bridge that allows electronic records to be admitted as evidence.

ticks.do: Submit a certificate under BSA s.63(4) with the electronic record at EACH instance it is produced for admission.
Include in the certificate each of the following.
sub: Identification of the electronic record containing the statement
A description of the manner in which the record was produced
Particulars of any device involved in its production
Treatment of the s.63(2) conditions

ticks.do: Obtain both signatures on the certificate.
sub: The person in charge of the computer or communication device, or of the management of the relevant activities (Schedule Part A)
An expert (Part B)

ticks.do: State the matters to the best of knowledge and belief in the format specified in the Schedule.
Take the certificate from the person who actually manages the device regularly at the relevant time rather than from the OWNER of the device.
Never submit digital evidence to court without this certificate.

details.text: Certification is required for BOTH categories: (1) digital recordings made under the new laws - AV recording of statements of victim and witnesses u/s 180 BNSS (preferable), AV recording of search and seizure (mandatory), and other procedural compliances such as identification parade and property disposal (preferable); and (2) digital devices routinely seized during investigation (mobiles, social media accounts, emails, computers, CCTV cameras) - each certified doubly, by the handler (or manager) and by an expert.
details.citation: BPR&D - SOP on Audio-Video Recording under the New Criminal Laws (BNSS/BSA)

details.text: Part A ('to be given by party') is signed by the owner/handler or operator/first responder/manager. Where videography by the first-responder police team was actually done by a constable, the Part A certificate may be given by the head constable of that same first-responder team which routinely manages the police station's AV recording, or by the records head-mohrir under whom the record is downloaded and archived - but the chain of custody form must clearly mention the change of hands and the reasons. For seizure of digital evidence the Part A giver is the owner/operator/handler or manager or person in charge of the device in contention. Part B is signed by an 'expert' - a person occupying a responsible official position who is witness to the chain of events (e.g. the SHO; where the first responder recorded the video, the forensic team in-charge may give Part B).
details.citation: BPR&D - SOP on Audio-Video Recording under the New Criminal Laws (BNSS/BSA)

details.text: The s.63(4) expert is NOT the Examiner of Electronic Evidence (s.79A IT Act 2000; BSA s.39(2)): the first responder/SHO submits the mirror copy with the chain of custody and proper certifications; the burden lies on the defence to challenge and prove violation of authenticity, whereupon the court may seek the Examiner's opinion and check the hashing and chain of custody.
details.citation: BPR&D - SOP on Audio-Video Recording under the New Criminal Laws (BNSS/BSA)

details.text: Certification u/s 63(4) BSA is by the operator (Form A) and the forensic expert (Form B) - Form A by the first responder and Form B by the forensic expert respectively, in any of the recording scenarios.

details.text: Certification does not necessarily require the owner of the device but the person who manages the device regularly at relevant times, in the prescribed format laid down in the BSA Schedule Part-A.

details.text: Annexure-A to the SOP is the Schedule certificate: Part A (to be filled by the Party) identifies the device/digital record source (computer/storage media, DVR, mobile, flash drive, CD/DVD, server, cloud); Part B (to be filled by the Expert) records the device source, make and model, colour, serial number, IMEI/UIN/UID/MAC/Cloud ID particulars and the hash value(s) with the algorithm used, with the hash report enclosed.

details.text: Ensure admissibility by following the procedures demanded by law including the BSA s.63(4)(c) certificate, and maintain authenticity and data integrity through hash values at the different points of transmission and storage.

steps.title: Create the Master Negative and Mirror Copy
steps.text: Create the permanent record: the evidence specialist (or designated officer) copies the files, WITHOUT opening them, onto a write-once-read-many (WORM) 'master negative' storage device which is the permanent record, is kept in a secured location or designated desktop, does not become part of the investigative case files and is never removed from departmental custody; copy the master negative (again without opening) onto a 'negative duplicate / mirror image' working device, one per criminal case, confirming the images were correctly transferred; any copy for review by the IO, prosecutor or defence is made afresh from the negative duplicate; any enhancement of digital image files is documented by the evidence specialist and recorded on a separate device; and keep all originals in a designated/partitioned drive in a separate file which is not touched by anyone once it is hashed, with working copies kept separately.
steps.triage_why: Creating a WORM master negative is an excellent technical safeguard for data integrity, but not a statutory requirement for prosecution.

ticks.do: Have the evidence specialist or designated officer copy the files, WITHOUT opening them, onto a write-once-read-many (WORM) 'master negative' storage device.
Treat the master negative as the permanent record and keep it on the following terms.
sub: Keep it in a secured location or designated desktop.
Keep it out of the investigative case files.
Never remove it from departmental custody.

ticks.do: Copy the master negative, again without opening, onto a 'negative duplicate / mirror image' working device, one per criminal case, confirming the images were correctly transferred.
Make any copy for review by the IO, prosecutor or defence afresh from the negative duplicate.
Document any enhancement of digital image files through the evidence specialist and record it on a separate device.
Keep all originals in a designated or partitioned drive in a separate file which is not touched by anyone once it is hashed.
Keep the working copies separately.

details.text: Under BSA s.57 Explanation 6, where a video recording is simultaneously stored in electronic form and transmitted, broadcast or transferred to another, each of the stored recordings is primary evidence - hence the mirror image made while transferring from the phone/AV recorder to the destination computer can be submitted to court with sufficient credibility.

details.text: Giving a matching hash value of the original record as proof of evidence is admissible as secondary evidence; the importance attaches to the integrity of the specific file, not to the entire storage medium.

steps.title: Transfer and Hash the Recorded Evidence
steps.text: On completion of the operation, bring the recording device to the police station and transfer the AV recording to the local designated desktop (directly through device insertion, or by cable or Bluetooth) WITHOUT opening the files; mention this transfer in the chain of custody form and do the hashing. Hash BOTH the primary evidence (original media) and the mirrored copy and match the hash values to prove they contain the same data, and document the hashing; depict all transfers in chain of custody forms duly signed by the responder and the evidence expert. When seizing digital evidence/devices, do the hashing through write-blocking devices to make it alter-proof. Algorithms: MD5 is less secure with collision risk and SHA-1 is being phased out; the SHA-2 family (SHA-256/384/512) is recommended.
steps.triage_why: Hashing is the only technical way to prove that digital evidence has not been altered. Without matching hash values, the integrity of the electronic evidence is compromised.

ticks.do: Bring the recording device to the police station on completion of the operation.
Transfer the AV recording to the local designated desktop WITHOUT opening the files.
sub: Direct device insertion.
Cable.
Bluetooth.

ticks.do: Mention this transfer in the chain of custody form and do the hashing.
Hash BOTH the primary evidence (original media) and the mirrored copy, match the hash values to prove they contain the same data, and document the hashing.
Depict all transfers in chain of custody forms duly signed by the responder and the evidence expert.
Do the hashing through write-blocking devices when seizing digital evidence or devices, to make it alter-proof.
Use the recommended SHA-2 family of algorithms (SHA-256/384/512).
notes: MD5 is less secure with collision risk and SHA-1 is being phased out.

details.text: At the conclusion of the tour of duty, turn in the camera's memory card by placing it in an evidence envelope with identifying case information, sealed, and deliver the sealed envelope to the evidence specialist; download the unaltered images into a limited-access computer file using departmentally approved writing software that does not permit re-writing or alteration of recorded images.

details.text: First-responder workflow: for a mobile device, activate the app/tool, record the essence of the place plus the preparation of the list of seized items plus the signing by witnesses, connect to the destination computer, archive the record file and generate a mirror image for producing in court; for an audio-video recorder, remove the flash drive and insert it into the destination computer WITHOUT opening it, then archive the record file.

details.text: Name the downloaded file in the standard format FIR No_ddmmyy_SNo so the FIR number, police station, date and video serial number are captured; make a general diary entry linking the file name to the FIR number, police officer ID, date and time of recording, latitude-longitude and remarks; scan the recording for viruses; only then delete the recording from the officer's smartphone or audio-video recorder.

steps.title: Wear protective equipment and control scene access
steps.text: Wear gloves and protective clothing (PPE: gown, cap, shoe covers, mask, goggles) to avoid contaminating evidence; sanitize hands before touching the kit; never touch biological evidence with bare hands; avoid sneezing or coughing over evidence items; limit scene access to people directly involved in scene processing; strictly follow the established entry/exit routes; use disposable devices for the collection of biological evidence materials.
steps.triage_why: In cases involving physical relations (POCSO/BNS 64), biological evidence is paramount. Contamination by the IO's own DNA/skin cells can render forensic results useless.

ticks.do: Wear gloves and protective clothing to avoid contaminating evidence.
sub: gown
cap
shoe covers
mask
goggles

details.text: Crime scene investigation kit for biological evidence (part 1): high resolution digital camera; disposable gown, cap, shoe covers, gloves, mask, goggles, hand-towels; bio-hazard polythene bag for biological waste; sterile gauze, filter paper and desiccant; alcohol swabs, tissue and hand sanitizer; evidence marking letters and direction indicators; hand torch and magnifier lens.

details.text: Crime scene investigation kit for biological evidence (part 2): surgical blades, forceps, scissors, dropper and syringe; sterile water, saline and phosphate buffer; EDTA vials and FTA cards; surface swabs, cotton swabs and plastic containers; evidence collecting envelopes and cardboards.

steps.title: Set tasks and time frames for forensic personnel
steps.text: Lay down the manner and the time frame in which the photographers and the other specialised forensic personnel of the different fields are to carry out their tasks at the scene — dog squad, finger-print and foot-print collection, and collection of hair, vomit, excreta, blood or seminal stains and other items for DNA or other testing.
steps.triage_why: While forensic coordination is good practice, the lack of a pre-defined 'time frame' for personnel does not inherently defeat the prosecution if evidence is collected.

steps.title: Keep the scene unaltered until recording finishes
steps.text: Never alter the position of any potential object or evidence, including the dead body, before the complete recording of the scene by photography, videography, sketching or panchnama is done; keep all doors, windows, locks, staircases, lightings, fans and routes of entry and exit in their original condition till the examination of the scene is over; never use the utilities (bathroom, toilet, washbasin, telephone) belonging to the crime scene premises.
steps.triage_why: Altering the scene before recording (photography/panchnama) destroys the integrity of the crime scene and can lead to the exclusion of evidence in court.

steps.title: Collect every trace material at the scene
steps.text: Never overlook stains of blood, semen, urine, smears, paint, fibres or hair — preserve the bits of objects affected; never omit to collect suspicious pieces of cloth, fibre, hair, paper or documents; always note the presence of bottles, containers, glasses and utensils and their condition (filled, half filled, empty, stained) where a poisonous substance or alcohol is expected or suspected; never hesitate to preserve objects which look useless at the time unless absolutely sure about them, as they could be vital at later stages; do not exclude details about furniture, doors, windows, curtains, tapestry, carpet, upholstery, flooring, fixtures and fittings.
steps.triage_why: In a sexual assault case (POCSO/BNS 64), biological stains (semen, hair) are primary evidence. Overlooking them results in the permanent loss of DNA evidence.

steps.title: Photograph footprints and fingerprints at the scene
steps.text: At the scene of the offence, footprints and fingerprints — whether or not visible to the naked eye — may be present on any article; photographs thereof shall be taken by a qualified police photographer in the presence of the police officer and with the assistance of the forensic team.
steps.triage_why: Fingerprints are supportive evidence; however, the case relies heavily on the victim's testimony and biological evidence.

steps.title: Photograph the body, evidence and blood patterns
steps.text: Use photography as part of the documentation for all physical crime scenes: photograph the dead body (if present) to show its location, injuries and condition; photograph each piece of evidence to illustrate where it was found and to establish its relationship to the victim; take photographs from straight above to eliminate potential distance distortions; photograph blood patterns along with a scale from different angles — the bloodstain pattern can indicate the type of weapon of offence.
steps.triage_why: Documentation of the scene and the relationship of evidence to the victim is essential to prove the location of the offence (Moje Jaldeep Flat).

ticks.do: Use photography as part of the documentation for all physical crime scenes.
Photograph the dead body, if present, to show its location, injuries and condition.
Photograph each piece of evidence to illustrate where it was found and to establish its relationship to the victim.
Take photographs from straight above to eliminate potential distance distortions.
Photograph blood patterns along with a scale from different angles.
notes: The bloodstain pattern can indicate the type of weapon of offence

details.text: Record the scene of all important and heinous crimes by black and white as well as colour photography; never fail to photograph the entry and exit points; always include the relative positions of building, road, boundary wall, fence, shrubbery, doors, windows, pole and trees; take close-up photographs of injuries, ligature marks, traces of resistance, scratches, tears, contusion and abrasion on the victim's body; always use a scale when photographing tool marks, tyre marks, skid marks, footprints and shoeprints; the photograph must be a truthful representation of a material and relevant object, showing the relationship of objects to one another against a recognizable background; maintain a record of photographs including time, date, case number, police station, place and name of photographer.

details.text: Never fail to photograph the dead body in homicides, suspicious deaths, strangulation, burning, hanging, drowning and road accident cases, and always take a sufficient number of photographs of the dead body from all possible angles covering injuries and marks.

steps.title: Dry and pack wet biological exhibits safely
steps.text: Air dry articles bearing wet or damp biological material at room temperature before final packaging; under no circumstances should wet or moist items remain in plastic or paper containers for more than two hours; never dry stained material by heating, by a hot air blower or heater, or by placing the article in bright/direct sunlight — hang clothing and similar items in a room with adequate air circulation; never pack clothing or objects carrying wet bloodstains (and clothes whether dry or wet) in airtight containers or polythene/plastic bags.
steps.deadline: Wet/moist items: not more than 2 hours in a plastic or paper container before drying (dna_guidelines p.6)
steps.triage_why: Biological evidence (semen/blood) degrades rapidly or molds if left wet in plastic, rendering DNA testing impossible.

ticks.do: Air dry articles bearing wet or damp biological material at room temperature before final packaging.
Do not leave wet or moist items in plastic or paper containers for more than two hours under any circumstances.
Never dry stained material by heating, by a hot air blower or heater, or by placing the article in bright or direct sunlight.
Hang clothing and similar items in a room with adequate air circulation.
Never pack clothing or objects carrying wet bloodstains, and clothes whether dry or wet, in airtight containers or polythene or plastic bags.

conflicts.description: dna_guidelines p.6 allows a wet or moist item to remain in a container for no more than 2 hours; the up_pictorial_forensic_sop short-term storage table (p.20) allows 'wet bloody items (if they cannot be dried)' to be held at temperature-controlled conditions (15.5-24 degrees C) for less than 24 hours.
conflicts.resolution: The national 2-hour rule governs wherever the item can be dried — drying is the primary obligation. The state matrix's window applies only to the residual class of wet bloody items that CANNOT be dried, for which the same table marks frozen as best and refrigerated as acceptable; it does not license leaving a dryable item wet for 24 hours.

steps.title: Secure, package and label crime scene exhibits
steps.text: Identify and secure each item of evidence in a container at the crime scene and avoid excessive handling of evidence after it is collected; use paper bags / paper sheets / paper envelopes for biological evidence and never use printed paper, as the ink may contaminate the exhibits; pack and label each article separately and never pack more than one item together; label each exhibit with FIR number and date, section of law, name of IO, police station, district and state, duly signed and sealed by the IO; number the labels consecutively with the signature of the forwarding officer, doing the labelling on the cover and not on the evidence itself; enclose all packets belonging to one case in one box or an outer covering.
steps.triage_why: Cross-contamination of biological evidence or improper labeling (chain of custody) can lead to the evidence being dismissed as unreliable.

conflicts.description: dna_guidelines p.6 forbids the use of any printed paper for packaging because the ink may contaminate the exhibit; up_crime_inv_tips repeatedly directs that the paper packet be placed 'in a printed envelope' which is then sealed and marked (hair p.4, glass p.6, paint p.9, fibres p.22).
conflicts.resolution: The national DNA guideline governs for biological evidence: no printed paper in contact with the exhibit. The state tips' printed/pre-printed envelope is retained only as the OUTER marked container for non-biological trace evidence (glass, paint, fibres), the exhibit itself always being wrapped first in a clean unprinted paper packet.

steps.title: Collect and transport liquid blood samples
steps.text: Collect liquid blood at the scene in an EDTA tube using a disposable syringe or dropper (from a pool of blood: lift into an EDTA vial and simultaneously lift the sample on sterile-tipped foam surface swabs), OR transfer onto a gauze piece / FTA card, air dry and keep in a paper packet/envelope; submit to the laboratory within 24 hours of collection, keeping liquid blood samples in a thermos flask or thermocol box stuffed with ice or a coolant pack during transport; collect a fresh/wet blood clot in a sterile tube with an equal volume of normal saline or PBS (PBS is preferred for DNA evidence samples).
steps.deadline: Submit liquid blood within 24 hours of collection (dna_guidelines p.10); the state tips warn that beyond 48 hours the sample may become useless (up_crime_inv_tips p.1)
steps.triage_why: While blood collection is important, the summary emphasizes physical relations (semen) over blood; this is sound practice but less critical than semen collection here.

ticks.do: Collect liquid blood at the scene in an EDTA tube using a disposable syringe or dropper.
Lift blood from a pool into an EDTA vial and simultaneously lift the sample on sterile-tipped foam surface swabs.
Transfer the blood onto a gauze piece or FTA card, air dry it and keep it in a paper packet or envelope as the alternative method.
Submit the liquid blood to the laboratory within 24 hours of collection.
notes: Beyond 48 hours the sample may become useless

ticks.do: Keep liquid blood samples in a thermos flask or thermocol box stuffed with ice or a coolant pack during transport.
Collect a fresh or wet blood clot in a sterile tube with an equal volume of normal saline or PBS.
notes: PBS is preferred for DNA evidence samples

details.text: Lift liquid blood onto a gauze pad or other sterile cotton cloth and let it air-dry at room temperature; cool or freeze the dried gauze sample as soon as possible and deliver it to the laboratory as quickly as possible — if the delay exceeds 48 hours the sample may become useless; if the laboratory is nearby, send the stain-bearing object immediately.

details.text: If the victim is so badly injured that a transfusion is necessary, try to obtain — or initiate the necessary procedure to obtain — the pre-transfusion specimen collected by the hospital; hospitals do not keep these specimens long, so act promptly.
details.citation: UP Police - Crime Investigation Tips/Guidance for Investigating Officers - TRANSLATED FROM HINDI

details.text: Ensure that blood-stained clothing worn by the person is air-dried and refrigerated so that it remains available as a secondary standard; refrigerate — do not freeze — liquid blood standards, collect the standard on a sterile gauze pad or swab, air dry it and pack it in paper (never a plastic container), and send liquid standards to the laboratory as quickly as possible.

conflicts.description: Anticoagulant/container: dna_guidelines (pp.6, 10, 16) and up_pictorial_forensic_sop p.19 prescribe EDTA vials for blood; up_crime_inv_tips p.2 prescribes a yellow-stoppered (ACD) or purple-stoppered vacutainer for the standard specimen drawn by the pathologist from the heart.
conflicts.resolution: EDTA vials govern (national DNA guideline, corroborated by the UP discipline matrix, which additionally requires the donor's name and date of collection on the vial and an ice container). The ACD vacutainer is recorded as the older state-tips practice. Grey-stoppered BA (blood-alcohol) tubes remain a distinct container for blood-alcohol work.

conflicts.description: Freezing: up_crime_inv_tips p.1 says to cool or freeze the sample as soon as possible, while the up_pictorial_forensic_sop storage tables (p.20) mark 'Never' against Liquid Blood in the Frozen column in BOTH the short-term and long-term tables, and up_crime_inv_tips p.3 itself says to refrigerate and not freeze blood standards.
conflicts.resolution: Never freeze liquid blood (matrix tables p.20, corroborated by tips p.3). The tips' p.1 'cool or freeze' applies only to the air-dried gauze-lifted sample, not to liquid blood.

conflicts.description: Transport temperature: dna_guidelines p.10 prescribes a thermos flask or thermocol box with ice/coolant pack, while dna_guidelines p.16 prescribes a 'dry ice storage box maintaining the temperature at least 4 degrees C'; the state matrix (p.20) bars freezing liquid blood outright.
conflicts.resolution: The 4 degrees C floor printed in the national guideline governs: transport chilled at refrigeration temperature (2-8 degrees C per the matrix) and never allow liquid blood to freeze; the printed phrase 'dry ice storage box' is retained as printed but is subordinate to the 4 degrees C requirement and the matrix's 'Never' entry.

steps.title: Obtain authenticated reference samples from victim and accused
steps.text: All liquid blood of victims and accused should be in EDTA vials with the details written and signed by the doctor on each vial and separate packaging for each; only liquid blood in EDTA vials should be transported in a dry ice storage box, maintaining the temperature at least 4 degrees C until submission in the laboratory; evidence samples of the victim for DNA examination are vaginal swabs, a slide of vaginal smear and undergarments, along with the victim's reference blood sample in an EDTA vial / gauze / FTA card; evidence samples of the accused are blood samples in EDTA vials / gauze / FTA card and any other swabs such as a penile swab taken by the doctor during medical examination.
steps.responsible: Medical officer (collection and authentication); IO (obtaining and forwarding)
steps.triage_why: Vaginal swabs are the primary statutory evidence for proving sexual intercourse in POCSO/BNS cases. Failure to collect/preserve them defeats the prosecution.

ticks.do: Keep all liquid blood of victims and accused in EDTA vials, with the details written and signed by the doctor on each vial and separate packaging for each.
notes: Collection and authentication rest with the medical officer; obtaining and forwarding rest with the IO

ticks.do: Transport only liquid blood in EDTA vials in a dry ice storage box, maintaining the temperature at least 4 degrees C until submission in the laboratory.
Obtain the evidence samples of the victim for DNA examination.
sub: vaginal swabs
a slide of vaginal smear
undergarments
the victim's reference blood sample in an EDTA vial, gauze or FTA card

ticks.do: Obtain the evidence samples of the accused for DNA examination.
sub: blood samples in EDTA vials, gauze or FTA card
any other swabs such as a penile swab taken by the doctor during medical examination

details.text: Biological materials from a dead body or a living person should always be collected by the medical officer only; remember the tiniest part of a biological material could be vital for DNA profiling, and never omit to preserve the integrity of the biological specimen during packaging and transportation.

details.text: Never forget to ask the medical officer about collection of seminal evidence such as a vaginal slide and pubic hairs from the victim of sexual assault, and to ask the autopsy surgeon about the collection of postmortem samples for DNA profiling if required for the investigation.

details.text: In sexual offence cases always have the victim examined by a physician, using a Sexual Assault Evidence Collection Kit to collect evidence from the victim and following the kit's instructions carefully so that maximum benefit is obtained from the evidence collected.

steps.title: Recover hair evidence and reference samples
steps.text: Collect hair with root (dry, or wet with blood/semen/saliva) from the crime scene, weapon or clothing with tweezers/forceps into white or butter paper and pack in a paper envelope; if hair is found attached in dry blood or on a weapon, do NOT remove the hair — pack the entire substrate intact, and if the object is small, mark it, wrap it in clean brown paper and pack it in cotton cloth; if recovered hairs are wet, allow them to dry in shade and never wash them; collect reference hair samples of 50-100 hairs from the victim and suspects and forward them; submit without any delay.
steps.triage_why: Hair collection is supportive forensic evidence but not the primary means of proving the offence in this specific case.

ticks.do: Collect hair with root from the crime scene, weapon or clothing with tweezers or forceps into white or butter paper, and pack it in a paper envelope.
notes: Applies to hair that is dry, or wet with blood, semen or saliva

ticks.do: Pack the entire substrate intact where hair is found attached in dry blood or on a weapon, and do NOT remove the hair.
Mark a small substrate object, wrap it in clean brown paper and pack it in cotton cloth.
Allow recovered wet hairs to dry in shade and never wash them.
Collect reference hair samples of 50-100 hairs from the victim and suspects and forward them.
Submit the hair evidence without any delay.

details.text: Collect plucked, pulled-out or fallen hairs for DNA profiling — cut hairs, being dead material, are useless for the purpose; collect each group of hairs, with respect to their origin, in separate packaging; hairs mixed with blood, tissue or semen must always be allowed to air dry before packaging.
details.citation: Director, Forensic Science Laboratory, UP Police - Crime Scene (Protocol) Management (English section)

details.text: Recover all hair present; where possible pick up hairs with the fingers or small forceps, wrap them in paper, place that in a larger envelope, seal it and mark the outer envelope; if hair is stuck in dried blood or adhering to metal or a piece of glass, do not attempt to remove it — if the object is small, mark it, wrap it and seal it in an envelope, and if the object is large, wrap the area bearing the hair thoroughly in paper so hairs are not dislodged and lost in transit.
details.citation: UP Police - Crime Investigation Tips/Guidance for Investigating Officers - TRANSLATED FROM HINDI

details.text: Known-sample method: have the person bend over a large clean sheet of paper and rub or massage the hair/scalp so that loose hairs fall onto the paper, and use the same method for other body areas; 50-100 hairs are desired for a head-hair sample and 30-60 from the pubic region; do not cut the hairs; if the person is a suspect, take samples from all parts of the body; in rape cases also obtain a combed hair sample from the victim's pubic region.

conflicts.description: Reference quantity: dna_guidelines p.12 requires 50-100 reference hairs (up_crime_inv_tips p.5 specifies 50-100 head hairs and 30-60 pubic hairs); up_crime_scene_protocol p.29 says to collect at least 10 to 20 hairs with root for successful results.
conflicts.resolution: The national guideline's 50-100 governs reference-sample collection; the state protocol's 10-20 rooted hairs is recorded as the minimum workable quantity where more cannot be obtained.

steps.title: Collect dried body-fluid stains from unmovable surfaces
steps.text: For dried blood, semen, vomit, sputum or other body-fluid stains (crust/stain/spatter) on unmovable surfaces such as a floor or concrete wall: moisten the dry stain for 5-10 minutes with PBS or distilled water, collect the moistened stain with a foam tipped swab / FTA card / gauze piece, air dry the swab and pack it in a paper envelope; use a separate swab for each spot, dry in shade and pack each spot separately in its own packet/envelope — never swab stains at different places with a single cloth; never use direct sunlight, a hot air blower or a heater to dry swabs; submit without any delay.
steps.triage_why: Proper recovery of dried biological stains from the room (floor/walls) is necessary to link the accused to the specific location of the crime.

ticks.do: Moisten the dry stain for 5-10 minutes with PBS or distilled water, for dried blood, semen, vomit, sputum or other body-fluid stains on unmovable surfaces such as a floor or concrete wall.
Collect the moistened stain with a foam tipped swab, FTA card or gauze piece.
Air dry the swab and pack it in a paper envelope.
Use a separate swab for each spot, dry in shade and pack each spot separately in its own packet or envelope.
notes: Never swab stains at different places with a single cloth.

ticks.do: Never use direct sunlight, a hot air blower or a heater to dry swabs.

details.text: Moisten dry/old stains with PBS buffer and leave for 5 minutes, then collect the stain with an FTA card or tipped foam surface swab; use only swabs / FTA card / gauze piece to collect semi-dry or liquid body fluids; air dry the stain/swab before packaging.

details.text: If a dried stain is on a small solid object, send the entire labelled and packaged object; if on a large solid object, cover the stained area with clean paper and seal the edges down with tape; if sending the whole object is impractical, scrape the stain onto a clean piece of paper which is folded and placed in an envelope (never scrape directly into the envelope), using a clean washed and dried knife washed again before each separate stain; do not mix dried stains — one stain per envelope; never attempt to wipe or wash dried stains off an object with a moistened cloth or paper; if the stain is on clothing, wrap the item in clean paper, place it in a box or brown paper bag, seal and label it, and do not attempt to remove the stain from the cloth.

steps.title: Dry, roll and pack bloodstained clothing
steps.text: Thoroughly air dry wet/damp bloodstained clothing and fabrics of the victim, the deceased and the suspect at room temperature, roll each in clean or brown paper and pack in a paper bag/envelope or cotton bag; keep the clothes of the victim/deceased and of the accused separate; handle the clothing as little as possible; always document the stain pattern by sketching, photography or videography before removing the items; submit to the laboratory without any delay.
steps.triage_why: Clothing of the victim and accused often contains the only available DNA evidence of the assault; improper drying/storage destroys this evidence.

ticks.do: Air dry wet or damp bloodstained clothing and fabrics of the victim, the deceased and the suspect thoroughly at room temperature.
Roll each item in clean or brown paper and pack it in a paper bag or envelope or a cotton bag.
Keep the clothes of the victim or deceased and of the accused separate.
Handle the clothing as little as possible.
Always document the stain pattern by sketching, photography or videography before removing the items.
Submit the clothing to the laboratory without any delay.

details.text: Never use direct sunlight, a hot air blower or a heater to dry stains on clothing and fabrics, and never pack clothes (dry or wet) in airtight containers or polythene bags.

steps.title: Dry, cut and pack stained objects
steps.text: For a wet stained movable object: thoroughly air dry at room temperature, collect the item as it is, and pack it in a paper bag/envelope or a cardboard/shipping box depending on its size. For stains on a weapon, firearm, bullet or small object (household utensils, stones, bricks): allow the stains to dry, collect the item directly, and pack and seal it in a cardboard/shipping box sealed with evidence tape. For stains on vehicle upholstery, carpet, wallpaper or wood: cut out the stained area, allow it to dry in shade, package each cutting separately, and also collect an unstained cutting from the adjacent area as a control. Submit without any delay.
steps.triage_why: General procedure for movable objects; less critical here as no specific weapon was mentioned in the summary.

steps.title: Collect blood and buccal samples on FTA cards
steps.text: FTA (Flinders Technology Associates) cards may be used for DNA sample collection, allowing collection, room-temperature storage, shipping and processing, with simple collection, convenient room-temperature storage/transport and safe handling. Blood: place the kit contents on a clean dry surface, wear gloves, unfold the protective flap to expose the printed circle, clean the finger with an alcohol wipe, prick it with the lancet, press the finger to deposit a drop of blood in the printed circle without touching the card, never oversaturate (DNA cannot be recovered from an FTA card saturated with too much blood), dry fully for 1-2 hours at room temperature, then close the cover and insert the card with a desiccant packet into the multi-barrier pouch and the pouch into the mailing envelope. Buccal: soak the sterile foam tipped applicator by running it on the inside cheek for 30 seconds and repeat with the opposite side, then lift the paper cover of the indicating FTA card, apply pressure and rock the applicator side to side three times within the sample circle and repeat with the other side (the pink area turns white indicating transfer), dry the card completely at room temperature and pouch it with desiccant.
steps.triage_why: This describes a specific tool (FTA cards) and how to use them; it is a technical reference for the officer.

Never oversaturate the card

Close the cover and insert the card with a desiccant packet into the multi-barrier pouch, and the pouch into the mailing envelope

steps.title: Preserve stains, controls and non-absorbent exhibits
steps.text: Process every stain and control sample in the sequence (1) air-dry, (2) pack in paper, (3) refrigerate; take special care with non-absorbent objects such as metal or plastic, where moisture and caking from softening can spoil or destroy the evidence — keep such objects at low temperature and send them to the laboratory as quickly as possible; handle and store physiological fluid evidence with reasonable, good-faith efforts to preserve items of evidentiary value and any concealed latent fingerprints on them.
steps.triage_why: The sequence of air-dry, pack, and refrigerate is the standard for preventing biological degradation. Failure to follow this spoils the evidence.

steps.title: Collect blood, semen, hair and nail evidence
steps.text: In rape cases, exhibits carrying blood and seminal stains must invariably be collected and preserved for further examination; always look for the presence of hair, especially from the pubic area, at the crime scene; never omit to collect control samples of pubic hairs from the victim as well as from the culprit; always look for traces of blood, tissue and skin from the culprit beneath the nails of the victim; never forget to look for the presence of dust, soil, mud and vegetation belonging to the crime scene on the clothing of both the victim and the culprit; and have the culprit examined for marks of violence on his person or his clothing being torn.
steps.applies_when: Rape / sexual assault cases
steps.triage_why: In sexual assault cases (POCSO/BNS 64), biological evidence like semen and blood is transient and critical for DNA profiling to prove the act and identity of the accused.

ticks.do: Collect and preserve invariably, in rape cases, the exhibits carrying blood and seminal stains for further examination.

Collect control samples of pubic hairs from the victim as well as from the culprit, never omitting them.
Look always for traces of blood, tissue and skin from the culprit beneath the nails of the victim.
Look for the presence of dust, soil, mud and vegetation belonging to the crime scene on the clothing of both the victim and the culprit.
Have the culprit examined for marks of violence on his person or for his clothing being torn.

steps.title: Preserve tool marks and despatch marked objects
steps.text: Do not attempt to fit a recovered tool into the questioned mark or to make test marks before the laboratory examination — doing so can alter the questioned mark or the tool, destroy the lines of transferred paint or other stains on the tool, transfer additional material onto it, and render the laboratory examination worthless; wrap the entire contaminated or edged portion of the tool in paper so that fine or sharp edges are protected from contact; as far as possible send the whole object bearing the tool mark, and if that is not possible sketch or photograph the marked area (the photograph will not substitute for comparison but helps the laboratory determine how the mark was made) and, if possible, cut out and send the marked portion; a cast should be made only by a person with adequate experience, since a poor cast is useless and improper technique can destroy the mark; pack small marked objects wrapped in clean paper inside envelopes or boxes, protect the important area of larger objects by wrapping it in paper, and crate large objects against transit damage.
steps.triage_why: No tools or tool marks are mentioned in the case summary; this is a general rule for different types of crime scenes.

steps.title: Protect, mark and transport latent print evidence
steps.text: The primary precaution in all cases is to prevent adding fingerprints to the evidence and to prevent destroying those already present: touch the object as little as possible and then only in areas where identifiable latent prints are unlikely, such as rough surfaces; gloves or a handkerchief may be used to pick up exhibits but unnecessary contact must be avoided, since careless use of cloth may wipe off or smudge the prints actually present; mark all latent-print evidence in a distinctive manner, exercising care so that the prints are not damaged; mark lifted developed latents or seal/mount them in marked envelopes, and photograph developed latents both with and without a scale and identification markings; place large objects bearing latents (glass, metal articles, firearms) on wood or cardboard fastened tightly, or on a pegboard, so they cannot shift or contact other objects in transport; stand bottles and glasses upright on a board in the bottom of a box, held by nails or through a hole in a piece of cardboard; place papers and documents bearing latents individually in cellophane or manila envelopes sandwiched between two pieces of cardboard, wrapped and boxed for despatch.
steps.triage_why: Standard forensic practice to preserve latent prints, though not the primary evidence in this specific sexual assault/coercion case.

steps.title: Seize and preserve electronic evidence at the scene
steps.text: Always adopt general forensic and procedural principles while dealing with electronic evidence and never omit to take the assistance of a trained person while conducting the search, collection and preservation; ensure that no change takes place in the status of the evidence and avoid touching the keyboard or clicking the mouse to recover data or explore the contents; obtain information about the purpose of the system from the person concerned, ascertain the names of the owner and users along with the passwords required to access the system, and get information about any off-site data storage, any unique security scheme or destructive device, and documentation explaining the hardware or software installed; record all actions taken at the scene regarding the monitor, computer, printer and other peripherals; photograph the monitor screen and record the information displayed; remove the power source cable from the computer end instead of from the wall outlet; record the make, model and serial numbers of all devices; mark and label all connectors and cable ends before packaging to allow exact reassembly; package magnetic media in an antistatic container and package multiple computer systems separately so that they can be reassembled as found; pack the collected digital exhibits in a cardboard box with thermocol support inside a Faraday bag.
steps.applies_when: Cases involving computers / digital devices
steps.triage_why: The case relies heavily on electronic evidence (Instagram, call recordings, photos). Improper handling can lead to inadmissibility in court under electronic evidence laws.

steps.title: Collect and separate threads and fibres for comparison
steps.text: Pick up threads and long fibres with the fingers, place them in a paper packet and then in an envelope which is sealed and marked — never place loose fibres directly into a mailing envelope, where they can be lost or destroyed; if the fibres are short or few in number, wrap the area or the entire bearing object in paper and send the whole exhibit; pick up fibres on tape only if the laboratory in your jurisdiction authorises it and advises that it is necessary; if threads or fibres are recovered, send all clothing of the persons from which they might have originated for comparison; for person-to-person or person-to-object contact comparisons keep each item of each person's clothing strictly separate — spread each garment on a clean sheet of paper, mark the exhibit and wrap it in separate paper — because if one person's garment touches another's or is laid on a surface in contact with the other suspect's clothing the comparison may become meaningless, the examination having value only where it is known that no contact occurred before or after the crime.
steps.triage_why: Trace evidence (fibres) can strengthen the link between the victim and the room/accused, but is secondary to DNA and electronic evidence.

steps.title: Apply the short-term and long-term storage tables
steps.text: Store biological evidence by the temperature tables — short term is up to 72 hours, long term is more than 72 hours. Liquid blood: frozen = NEVER (both tables); refrigerated (2-8 degrees C) = best short and long term; temperature controlled (15.5-24 degrees C) = less than 24 hours short term only. Urine: frozen (at or below -10 degrees C) = best; refrigerated = less than 24 hours. Dry biological stained items: temperature controlled = best; room temperature = acceptable short term. Wet bloody items that cannot be dried (short term only): frozen = best, refrigerated = acceptable, temperature controlled = less than 24 hours. Bones: short term frozen, temperature controlled and room temperature all acceptable; long term temperature controlled = best. Hair: temperature controlled = best, room temperature = acceptable. Swab with biological material: refrigerated = best when wet, temperature controlled = best when dried. Vaginal smears: temperature controlled = best. Buccal swabs: temperature controlled = best, room temperature = less than 24 hours short term. Feces: frozen = best. DNA extracts (long term): frozen = best (liquid), refrigerated = acceptable (liquid), temperature controlled = acceptable (dried).
steps.deadline: Short-term storage is defined as up to 72 hours and long-term as more than 72 hours (up_pictorial_forensic_sop p.20)
steps.triage_why: Biological evidence degrades rapidly. Failure to follow temperature protocols can destroy DNA evidence, defeating the prosecution.

ticks.do: Store biological evidence by the temperature tables, short term being up to 72 hours and long term more than 72 hours.
Store liquid blood and urine as follows:
sub: Liquid blood: frozen = NEVER (both tables); refrigerated (2-8 degrees C) = best short and long term; temperature controlled (15.5-24 degrees C) = less than 24 hours short term only
Urine: frozen (at or below -10 degrees C) = best; refrigerated = less than 24 hours

ticks.do: Store stained and wet items as follows:
sub: Dry biological stained items: temperature controlled = best; room temperature = acceptable short term
Wet bloody items that cannot be dried (short term only): frozen = best, refrigerated = acceptable, temperature controlled = less than 24 hours

ticks.do: Store bones and hair as follows:
sub: Bones: short term frozen, temperature controlled and room temperature all acceptable; long term temperature controlled = best
Hair: temperature controlled = best, room temperature = acceptable

ticks.do: Store swabs and smears as follows:
sub: Swab with biological material: refrigerated = best when wet, temperature controlled = best when dried
Vaginal smears: temperature controlled = best
Buccal swabs: temperature controlled = best, room temperature = less than 24 hours short term

ticks.do: Store feces frozen, which is best.
Store DNA extracts long term as follows:
sub: Frozen = best (liquid)
Refrigerated = acceptable (liquid)
Temperature controlled = acceptable (dried)

details.text: Keep wet biological material refrigerated at 4 degrees Celsius and submit it to the laboratory at the earliest; wet blood samples must be preserved in a suitable anticoagulant such as EDTA.

steps.title: Direct exhibits to the examining FSL division
steps.text: Route each exhibit to the correct FSL discipline: Physics (glass, paint, rags/cloth shreds, marks of feet, shoes, tools and tyres, numbers erased on a vehicle, valuable gadgets); Questioned Documents (erasure, loss or alteration of handwriting, over-writing, secret writing, typewriting and printed matter, ink and paper, stamp impressions, fax, carbon and xerox copies, rubber stamps and seals); Firearms/Ballistics (firearms and their parts, cartridges, bullets, pellets, clothing and other material affected by firing); Computer Forensics (software, hardware, computer peripherals, communication equipment, and material relating to crypto currency, pornography and software piracy); Forensic Engineering (material from substandard construction of buildings, roads and dams, train or air accidents, failed machines and structures — each item wrapped and sealed separately, grease stains kept from contact with other material, important stains MAY be protected with aluminium foil); Narcotics (narcotic drugs and psychotropic substances, adulterated liquor and toddy); Chemistry (adulterated petrol, HSD, oil, detergent, cosmetics and cement, explosive material, arson and fire residues, unknown chemicals); Toxicology (poisons, medicines and intoxicants); Serology (blood, saliva, other body fluids and skin tissue — fluids converted into stains and packed separately in sterile paper envelopes or cardboard boxes; the page banner lists the common biological evidence as blood, semen, saliva, teeth, bone, urine, soft tissue and hair with root and shaft); Biomedical (skull, skeletal remains, skin, tissue); DNA (blood, blood stains and swabs, semen and semen stains, medical slides and swabs, bones, tissue, hair, teeth, saliva, skeletal remains); Biology (hair, fibre, semen and semen stains, medical slides and swabs, diatom, tobacco products and other plant material, pollen, leaves, wood, seeds, fruits, flowers, insects, faeces — dried in shade and packed separately); Forensic Psychology (the person of the suspect, witness or complainant, referred with the consent of the Court, a medical certificate if there is any medical problem, the FIR, and the crime scene sketch or photographs).
legal_basis: NDPS Act, Excise Act and central excise duty matters, Copyright Act, Patent Act and 'Piracy Act' as printed in the source discipline table
Consent of the Court is printed as a mandatory accompanying document for any forensic psychological examination
steps.triage_why: This is a general routing guide for FSL disciplines rather than a case-specific investigative step.

steps.title: Secure evidence storage and record every movement
steps.text: Limit access to the evidence storage facility or location so as to assure that items of evidence cannot be switched or tampered with throughout the chain of custody; provide a safe facility that limits access to vulnerable evidence; secure firearms and narcotics and controlled substances in a separate space from other evidence and strictly enforce and supervise access to that space; keep inventory records of the location where the evidence is stored (e.g. shelf number or bin), the date/time and identity of the person who stored it, and every removal and return of evidence from storage; classify any location where evidence may be stored for 72 hours or less as temporary storage and any location where it may be stored for more than 72 hours as long term or more permanent storage.
steps.deadline: Temporary storage = 72 hours or less; long term / more permanent storage = more than 72 hours (up_pictorial_forensic_sop p.36)
steps.triage_why: Tampering with evidence in a high-stakes POCSO case will lead to the collapse of the prosecution during cross-examination.

Keep inventory records of the storage particulars.

steps.title: Maintain the chain of custody document
steps.text: Maintain a chain of custody document recording the chronological history of every item of evidence: the name or initials of the individual collecting the evidence, each person or entity subsequently having custody of it, the dates the items were collected or transferred, the agency and case number, the victim's or suspect's name, and a brief description of the item.
steps.triage_why: A broken chain of custody for biological and electronic evidence is a primary ground for the court to reject evidence.

details.text: The chain of custody is the identification of the person or agency having custody of evidence and of the place where it is kept, in chronological order, from the time of collection to destruction, in a formal WRITTEN process; the record must also reflect the dates on which and a brief reason for which evidence is transferred from one location or person to another (e.g. delivery to laboratory, viewing of evidence by court, viewing of evidence by IO), and access to the storage facility must be limited so that items cannot be switched or tampered with.
details.citation: State Forensic Science Laboratory UP / Technical Services HQ, Lucknow - A Collection of Standard Operating Procedures for Crime Scene Investigation (pictorial, BNSS/BSA era) - TRANSLATED FROM HINDI

details.text: 'Evidence' means property that may be related to a crime and/or that may implicate or clear a person of a crime — an object, a biological sample found on such an item or at a scene, a latent print on an item, or a cell phone or computer. The record identifies three roles: the Evidence Collector (who initially took possession, custody or control for evidentiary purposes), the Evidence Custodian (responsible for evidence processing at a given location — property and evidence room, hospital, court, crime laboratory) and every Evidence Handler (any person who has had the evidence in his possession at any point of time). The documentation must include a description of the evidence, the unique case identifier (e.g. FIR number, PS), where the evidence was collected (location, address), where it was stored (location, address), the person having possession and for what purpose, what was done to it (e.g. analysis or re-packaging), and the date and time of both incident and collection; also record the manner in which each item was wrapped, bagged or boxed.

steps.title: Track evidence through fifteen custody stages
steps.text: Follow the fifteen-stage custody flow: (1) identification, collection and preservation of evidence at the crime scene by the forensic experts and the investigation officer; (2) handover of evidence by the forensic experts to the IO; (3) documentation of the evidences by the IO with the help of the forensic experts; (4) deposition in the Maalkhana (police property store room) by the IO; (5) submission to the FSL for analysis via special messenger by the forwarding officer; (6) receiving of the evidences by the receipt section of the FSL; (7) receiving in the concerned division by its laboratory assistant; (8) handover to the expert/scientist by the laboratory assistant; (9) analysis by the expert/scientist; (10) handover back to the laboratory assistant after analysis; (11) collection by the special messenger from the laboratory assistant/dispatch; (12) handover to the IO by the special messenger; (13) submission in the Maalkhana by the IO; (14) production in the Court during hearing by the IO; (15) deposition in the Maalkhana till further order of the Court.
steps.responsible: IO, forwarding officer, special messenger, FSL receipt section, divisional laboratory assistant and expert/scientist
steps.triage_why: Strict adherence to the custody flow is required to ensure the legal integrity of the evidence from scene to court.

steps.title: Assemble the full DNA case with all forms
steps.text: For DNA cases submit the COMPLETE case — a partial case is not acceptable for DNA examination where the laboratory has no DNA database facility for crime evidence or unidentified dead bodies: standard reference blood samples of BOTH accused and victim are required in sexual assault cases, and of both alleged parents in paternity / criminal paternity cases; prepare all case documents in the language(s) accepted by the receiving laboratory; forward a letter from the SSP addressed to the Director of the laboratory containing a brief history of the case (5-10 lines), details of each parcel with impressions and number of seals affixed, and the type of examination required, enclosing the copy of FIR, vernacular report, MLR/PMR of the victim, MLR of the accused, autopsy specimen submission form (if applicable), clearly visible attested sample seals on a piece of cloth corresponding to each parcel, blood sample authentication forms of victim and accused with attested photograph duly filled by the doctor, sexual assault form duly filled by the doctor with attested photograph, evidence submission form duly filled by the SSP, chain of custody form duly filled by the IO, aborted foetus identification sheet duly filled by the doctor (in criminal paternity cases) and a copy of the road certificate; have the medical officer complete the Blood Sample Authentication, Autopsy Specimen(s) Submission, Sexual Assault Victim Information and Abortus Identification forms as applicable.
steps.responsible: SSP (forwarding letter and evidence submission form), IO (chain of custody form), medical officer (authentication and medical forms)
steps.applies_when: Cases submitted to the FSL DNA division
steps.triage_why: DNA examination is useless without reference samples from both the victim and the accused to establish a match.

details.text: Abortus collection, storage and packing: wear gloves; the physician selects tissue from the abortus and places approximately a 2 sq. cm portion into a sterile plastic tube labelled with the mother's name and the date of collection and the physician's initials; do not preserve the tissue in formalin — freeze it and transport it on ice; collect the mother's blood sample in sterile EDTA tubes and do NOT freeze it; complete and sign all forms; package each sample separately and affix a tamper proof seal.

steps.title: Forward the sealed exhibits to the Forensic Science Laboratory
steps.text: Send the exhibits requiring forensic examination and expert opinion to the Forensic Science Laboratory in strong and sturdy packaging and in sealed condition, along with the duly filled in Performa (FSL/CFSL form), the transcription, the specimen seal impression, and other relevant documents useful to the laboratory examination.

steps.title: Retain evidence after trial for the required periods
steps.text: Evidence may be retained long term in a variety of circumstances: regardless of whether it was admitted as an exhibit at trial, it must be retained for the duration of a convicted person's sentence and the parole and/or probation term; in serious crimes that are not solved in the immediate aftermath of the crime the evidence must be retained; and exhibits must be retained post-conviction unless a judge orders otherwise.
steps.deadline: Duration of the convicted person's sentence plus the parole and/or probation term; post-conviction retention unless a judge orders otherwise (up_pictorial_forensic_sop p.39)
steps.triage_why: This is a policy on long-term evidence retention, not an active investigative step for the current triage of the case.

In serious crimes that are not solved in the immediate aftermath of the crime

steps.title: Issue a Production Order Under Section 94 BNSS
steps.text: Where any document, electronic communication (including a communication device likely to contain digital evidence) or other thing is necessary or desirable for the investigation, the officer in charge of the police station may issue a written production order under Section 94 BNSS, in physical or electronic form, to the person in whose possession or power the item is believed to be, requiring him to attend and produce it, or to produce it, at the time and place stated in the order; a Court compels production by summons under the same section. A person required merely to produce may comply by causing the item to be produced rather than attending personally. This is the principal tool for calling for CDRs, CCTV footage, devices, and bank or company records, and may be used instead of a search.
steps.stage: Obtaining documents and things by production order (Section 94 BNSS)
legal_basis: BNSS 94
steps.deadline: Production at the time and place stated in the summons or order; no fixed statutory period (Section 94 BNSS)
steps.responsible: Officer in charge of the police station (SHO) / Investigating Officer
steps.triage_why: The case relies on electronic evidence (Instagram, call recordings). A legal production order under Section 94 BNSS is required to lawfully obtain this data from the accused or service providers.

ticks.do: Issue a written production order under Section 94 BNSS, in physical or electronic form, where any document, electronic communication or other thing is necessary or desirable for the investigation.
notes: The power lies with the officer in charge of the police station.

A Court compels production by summons under the same section.

steps.title: Forward search grounds and deputation order to the Magistrate
steps.text: Send copies of the record made before the search — the written grounds of belief and any written order deputing a subordinate — to the nearest Magistrate empowered to take cognizance of the offence forthwith, and in no case later than forty-eight hours, and keep copies available in the case diary. The owner or occupier of the place searched is entitled, on application, to be furnished by the Magistrate with a copy of the record free of cost.
legal_basis: BNSS 185
steps.deadline: Forthwith, and not later than 48 hours (Section 185 BNSS)
steps.responsible: Officer in charge of the police station / Investigating Officer
steps.triage_why: Statutory requirement under BNSS to notify the Magistrate within 48 hours of a search; failure to do so can lead to the search being declared illegal.

steps.title: Record the Grounds Before a Warrantless Search
steps.text: Search without warrant under Section 185 BNSS only where there are reasonable grounds to believe that a thing necessary for the investigation cannot otherwise be obtained without undue delay. Before the search, record the grounds of that belief in writing in the case diary, specifying the thing for which the search is to be made, and confine the search to places within the limits of your own police station (for other stations see the out-of-jurisdiction step).
legal_basis: BNSS 185
steps.responsible: Officer in charge of the police station / Investigating Officer
steps.triage_why: Searching without a warrant under Section 185 BNSS requires written grounds of belief in the case diary. Without this, the search is unauthorized and evidence may be suppressed.

steps.title: Route out-of-jurisdiction searches through the local station
