steps.title: Restrict handcuffs to the listed categories of arrestee
steps.text: Use handcuffs only, having regard to the nature and gravity of the offence, on a habitual or repeat offender, a person who escaped from custody, or a person accused of organised crime, terrorist act, drug-related crime, illegal possession of arms and ammunition, murder, rape, acid attack, counterfeiting of coins and currency notes, human trafficking, sexual offences against children, or offences against the State (BNSS 43(3)).
legal_basis: BNSS 43(3)
steps.triage_why: Provides guidelines on the use of handcuffs; while applicable to sexual offences against children, it is a discretionary power, not a mandatory step for every arrest.

ticks.do: Use handcuffs only, having regard to the nature and gravity of the offence, on a person in one of the following categories [BNSS 43(3)]:
sub: A habitual or repeat offender.
A person who escaped from custody.
A person accused of organised crime, terrorist act or drug-related crime.
A person accused of illegal possession of arms and ammunition.
A person accused of murder, rape or acid attack.
A person accused of counterfeiting of coins and currency notes.
A person accused of human trafficking or sexual offences against children.
A person accused of offences against the State.

details.text: Gujarat maps the categories to BNS/special-Act sections (escape from custody s.253; organised crime s.111; terrorist act s.113; adulteration of drugs ss.123, 276, 277, 278; rape ss.63, 67, 68, 69, 70; murder s.101; acid attack s.124; counterfeiting of coins and currency notes under BNS Chapter 10; human trafficking s.111(1) as tabulated; offences against the State ss.147 to 157; Arms Act; POCSO Act) and includes habitual or repeat offenders.
details.citation: Twenty-Nine Standard Operating Procedures - C.I.D. Crime & Railways, Gujarat Police, circular PRC/Circular-SOP-1/656/2024 dated 29/10/2024

details.text: Even for these categories, use handcuffs only in two circumstances: at the time of arresting the person, and when he is produced in Court.
details.citation: Twenty-Nine Standard Operating Procedures - C.I.D. Crime & Railways, Gujarat Police, circular PRC/Circular-SOP-1/656/2024 dated 29/10/2024

details.text: When the accused is taken for medical examination, for recovery of the weapon used or of stolen property, or for re-creation of the scene of occurrence, apply handcuffs only after obtaining an order of the Court.
details.citation: Twenty-Nine Standard Operating Procedures - C.I.D. Crime & Railways, Gujarat Police, circular PRC/Circular-SOP-1/656/2024 dated 29/10/2024

details.text: Do not use handcuffs in ordinary circumstances.
details.citation: Twenty-Nine Standard Operating Procedures - C.I.D. Crime & Railways, Gujarat Police, circular PRC/Circular-SOP-1/656/2024 dated 29/10/2024

details.text: Do not use handcuffs as a form of punishment or to damage the person's reputation, or in a manner causing unnecessary pain or injury; avoid handcuffing for long periods without proper and necessary reason, on persons who are not a danger to themselves or others, or on ill persons for whom handcuffing is hazardous; ensure Article 21 is not violated in any manner and human dignity is not harmed. Make a clear Station Diary entry of the justifiable reasons for handcuffing and of any Court order obtained.
details.citation: Twenty-Nine Standard Operating Procedures - C.I.D. Crime & Railways, Gujarat Police, circular PRC/Circular-SOP-1/656/2024 dated 29/10/2024

details.text: Clearly mention the reasons why handcuffs have been used in the Case Diary; they must also be shown to the court if so required.
details.citation: Kerala Police - Standard Operating Procedure: Investigation & Prosecution in General (SOP Series), State Police Chief, 01.11.2020

details.text: A person arrested in execution of an arrest warrant issued by a magistrate must not be handcuffed unless prior permission has been taken from the magistrate; once produced before the court, the escorting officer must take the court's permission before handcuffing him to and from the court.
details.citation: Kerala Police - Standard Operating Procedure: Investigation & Prosecution in General (SOP Series), State Police Chief, 01.11.2020

details.text: In an arrest without warrant, handcuff only on concrete proof that the person is prone to violence, has a tendency to escape, or is so dangerous and desperate that there is no other practical way to restrain him, and then only till he is taken to the police station and thereafter to the magistrate's court; ideally do not use handcuffs on women, the infirm, bailable-offence accused, juvenile offenders or arrested witnesses (Prem Shanker Shukla; Citizen for Democracy).
details.citation: Kerala Police - Standard Operating Procedure: Investigation & Prosecution in General (SOP Series), State Police Chief, 01.11.2020

conflicts.resolution: Canonical text follows the BNSS 43(3) category list (law); the Kerala conduct criteria survive only as additional cautions restraining use within the permitted categories.

steps.title: Effect the arrest and limit force used
steps.text: In making the arrest, actually touch or confine the body of the person unless there is submission to custody by word or action. If the person forcibly resists or attempts to evade arrest, use all means necessary to effect the arrest — but there is no right to cause the death of a person who is not accused of an offence punishable with death or imprisonment for life.
legal_basis: BNSS 43(1)
BNSS 43(2)
steps.triage_why: Guidance on the physical act of arrest and use of force; failure does not typically defeat the prosecution unless it results in excessive violence.

ticks.do: Actually touch or confine the body of the person in making the arrest, unless there is submission to custody by word or action [BNSS 43(1)].
Use all means necessary to effect the arrest if the person forcibly resists or attempts to evade arrest [BNSS 43(2)].
Do not cause the death of a person who is not accused of an offence punishable with death or imprisonment for life.
notes: There is no right to cause such death.

steps.text: Forthwith give information of the arrest and the place where the arrestee is held to his relatives, friends or persons nominated by him, and to the designated police officer of the district (BNSS 37). legal_basis: BNSS 48
steps.deadline: Forthwith; arrestee informed of his rights as soon as brought to the police station
steps.triage_why: Statutory duty under BNSS 37 to inform relatives and the designated officer; failure is a breach of mandatory arrest procedure.

Inform the arrestee of these rights as soon as he is brought to the police station.
Record in a book kept at the police station who was informed of the arrest.

details.text: Note the intimation to the relative/friend of the arrested person's choice in the arrest memo.

details.text: Make an entry in the diary at the place of detention regarding the arrest, disclosing the name of the next friend informed and the names and particulars of the police officials in whose custody the arrestee is (D.K. Basu).

steps.title: Arrange medical examination of every arrested person
steps.text: Have every arrested person examined by a medical officer in Central/State Government service — or, if a medical officer is not available, by a registered medical practitioner — soon after the arrest is made; a further examination may follow if the examiner thinks one more is necessary. A female arrestee shall be examined only by, or under the supervision of, a female medical officer or female registered medical practitioner. The examiner records any injuries or marks of violence and the approximate time of their infliction, and a copy of the report is furnished to the arrested person or the person nominated by him.
legal_basis: BNSS 53
steps.deadline: Soon after the arrest is made
steps.triage_why: Mandatory medical examination of the arrested person is required to prevent allegations of custodial torture and to document the state of the accused.

ticks.do: Have every arrested person examined by a medical officer in Central or State Government service soon after the arrest is made [BNSS 53].
notes: Where a medical officer is not available, a registered medical practitioner examines him.

ticks.do: Arrange a further examination if the examiner thinks one more is necessary.
notes: A further examination may follow - permissive.

ticks.do: Have a female arrestee examined only by, or under the supervision of, a female medical officer or female registered medical practitioner.
notes: This shall be so in every case.

ticks.do: Ensure the examiner records any injuries or marks of violence and the approximate time of their infliction.
Furnish a copy of the report to the arrested person or to the person nominated by him.

steps.title: Seize offensive weapons from the arrested person
steps.text: Immediately after the arrest, take from the arrested person any offensive weapons he has about his person, and deliver all weapons so seized to the Court or officer before whom the arrestee is required by the Sanhita to be produced.
legal_basis: BNSS 50
steps.deadline: Immediately after the arrest
steps.triage_why: While standard procedure, there is no indication of weapons in this specific case of sexual coercion and rape.

ticks.do: Take from the arrested person any offensive weapons he has about his person, immediately after the arrest [BNSS 50].
Deliver all weapons so seized to the Court or officer before whom the arrestee is required by the Sanhita to be produced.

conflicts.description: bnss_2023 (BNSS 50) permits the officer or other person making an arrest to take offensive weapons from the arrested person ('may take'), while making delivery of all weapons so taken to the Court or officer mandatory; guj_cid_29_sops_2024 SOP 23 (p.102) renders the same provision as a duty - 'the police officer or other person making an arrest shall, immediately after the arrest, take from the person apprehended the offensive weapons upon his person, and hand over all weapons so taken...'.
conflicts.resolution: BNSS 50 governs as the law layer: taking the offensive weapons is a power ('may take') and only the delivery of the weapons so taken to the Court or officer is mandatory. The Gujarat SOP's mandatory phrasing is recorded here as the binding_gujarat restatement and does not change the canonical requirement.

steps.title: Obtain medical examination affording evidence of the offence
steps.text: Where the nature and circumstances of the offence give reasonable grounds to believe that a medical examination of the arrested person will afford evidence of its commission, have a registered medical practitioner examine him at the request of any police officer, using such force as is reasonably necessary. 'Examination' includes blood, blood stains, semen, swabs in sexual offences, sputum, sweat, hair samples and finger-nail clippings, using modern and scientific techniques including DNA profiling. A female is examined only by or under the supervision of a female registered medical practitioner. The practitioner forwards the report to the investigating officer without any delay.
legal_basis: BNSS 51
steps.deadline: Examination report to the IO without any delay
steps.triage_why: In sexual offences, biological evidence (semen, DNA) on the accused is volatile and critical for corroboration; failure to collect it promptly degrades the evidence.

ticks.do: Have a registered medical practitioner examine the arrested person where there are reasonable grounds to believe the examination will afford evidence of the offence's commission [BNSS 51].
notes: The grounds arise from the nature and circumstances of the offence.
The examination is made at the request of any police officer, using such force as is reasonably necessary.

ticks.do: Cover in the examination blood, blood stains, semen, swabs in sexual offences, sputum, sweat, hair samples and finger-nail clippings.
notes: Modern and scientific techniques including DNA profiling are included.

ticks.do: Have a female examined only by, or under the supervision of, a female registered medical practitioner.
Obtain the practitioner's report forwarded to the investigating officer without any delay.

steps.title: Get the arrested rape accused medically examined
steps.text: Where a person is arrested on a charge of rape or attempt to commit rape and there are reasonable grounds to believe that an examination of his person will afford evidence, it is lawful for a registered medical practitioner employed in a Government or local-authority hospital (or, if none is available within a 16 km radius of the place of offence, any other registered medical practitioner), acting at the request of any police officer, to examine him and to use reasonably necessary force for that purpose. The practitioner must without delay prepare a report recording his name/address and who brought him, his age, marks of injury, the description of material taken for DNA profiling and other particulars, the precise reasons for each conclusion, and the exact times of commencement and completion of the examination; the report is forwarded without delay to the investigating officer, who forwards it to the Magistrate with the s.193 charge-sheet documents.
legal_basis: BNSS 52
steps.deadline: Examination, report preparation and forwarding without any delay
steps.applies_when: Arrest on a charge of rape or attempt to commit rape
steps.note: Section 52 BNSS is an ENABLING provision: it authorises the medical examination of the arrested accused and the use of reasonably necessary force, at the request of a police officer. It does not impose a statutory duty on the investigating officer to procure the examination. Render this as an available power, not as a compulsory action item. The reporting duties in the second sentence ARE mandatory on the practitioner once an examination is made.
steps.triage_why: Statutory requirement for medical examination of the accused in rape cases to establish physical evidence of the crime.

ticks.do: Have a person arrested on a charge of rape or attempt to commit rape examined by a registered medical practitioner
notes: The examination is lawful when made at the request of any police officer, and the practitioner may use force reasonably necessary for that purpose.
sub: reasonable grounds exist to believe that examination of his person will afford evidence
[BNSS 52]

ticks.do: Use a registered medical practitioner based on availability and location.
sub: a registered medical practitioner employed in a Government or local-authority hospital
any other registered medical practitioner if none such is available within a 16 km radius of the place of offence

ticks.do: Require the practitioner to prepare a report without delay recording:
sub: his name and address and the name and address of the person by whom the arrested person was brought
the age of the arrested person
marks of injury on his person
the description of material taken from his person for DNA profiling
other particulars
the precise reasons for each conclusion arrived at
the exact time of commencement and completion of the examination

ticks.do: Obtain the report forwarded without delay to the investigating officer.
Forward the report to the Magistrate along with the documents filed with the charge-sheet under Section 193.

steps.title: Search the arrested person and secure his articles
steps.text: Where the arrested person is held under a warrant that makes no provision for bail, or is arrested without warrant or by a private person and cannot be admitted to bail or cannot furnish bail, the arresting officer may search him and place in safe custody all articles found upon him, other than necessary wearing apparel; where any article is seized, a receipt shall be given to the arrested person. Any search of a woman shall be made only by another woman with strict regard to decency (BNSS 49).
legal_basis: BNSS 49(1)
BNSS 49(2)
steps.triage_why: Standard administrative procedure for seizure of property during arrest; missing it is a procedural lapse but rarely defeats the prosecution of the main offence.

ticks.do: Search the arrested person and place in safe custody all articles found upon him, other than necessary wearing apparel [BNSS 49(1)].
notes: The arresting officer may do so - permissive.
Applies where the person is held under a warrant that makes no provision for bail, or is arrested without warrant or by a private person and cannot be admitted to bail or cannot furnish bail.

ticks.do: Give a receipt to the arrested person where any article is seized.
Have any search of a woman made only by another woman, with strict regard to decency [BNSS 49(2)].

details.text: Search the arrested person forthwith and, after taking proper action, seize all articles found and keep them in safe custody, giving him a receipt (seizure list) of the seized articles.

conflicts.description: The statute and the binding Gujarat SOP differ on whether the search of an arrested person is a power or a duty. BNSS 49(1) is permissive as to the search itself: the officer making the arrest may search such person and place in safe custody all articles other than necessary wearing apparel found upon him, and where any article is seized a receipt shall be given — only the receipt limb (and, under s.49(2), the rule that a woman is searched only by another woman with strict regard to decency) is mandatory. guj_cid_29_sops_2024 SOP 11 p.24-49 (binding_gujarat) instead directs that the officer 'shall search the arrested person forthwith and, after taking proper action, seize all articles found and keep them in safe custody (Section 49(1) BNSS); give a receipt (seizure list) of the seized articles to the arrested person'.
conflicts.resolution: The statute sets the floor and is stated permissively in the canonical text, because a lower-authority source cannot strengthen a higher one. The Gujarat direction is not discarded: within Gujarat, the binding CID SOP requires the search to be made forthwith, so a Gujarat officer must search — but that mandate is a binding_gujarat administrative direction layered on top of BNSS 49, not a requirement of the section itself, and it must not be cited as though the statute compelled it. The mandatory receipt and the woman-searched-by-woman rule are mandatory under the statute in either reading.

steps.title: Notify the designated officer and display arrest records
steps.text: A police control room shall exist in every district and at State level, and a designated police officer not below the rank of Assistant Sub-Inspector in every district and every police station shall maintain the names and addresses of arrested persons and the nature of the offences charged, prominently displayed/published at every police station and at District Headquarters in any form, including digital mode. Route arrest information to this designated officer.
legal_basis: BNSS 37
steps.responsible: State Government / designated police officer (not below ASI)
steps.triage_why: This is an administrative duty of the Police Control Room and Station House Officer, not a specific investigative step for the IO to execute for this case.

ticks.do: Ensure a police control room exists in every district and at State level [BNSS 37].
Designate in every district and every police station a police officer not below the rank of Assistant Sub-Inspector for this purpose.
notes: The State Government is the responsible authority for the control room and the designation.

ticks.do: Maintain through that designated officer the names and addresses of arrested persons and the nature of the offences charged.
Display or publish those particulars prominently at every police station and at District Headquarters in any form, including digital mode.
Route arrest information to this designated officer.

details.text: Display the names and addresses of the persons arrested and the names and designations of the police officers who made the arrests on the notice board kept outside the district control room.

steps.title: Report searches made outside your local jurisdiction
steps.text: If a search connected with the arrest is to be carried out in the area of another police station outside the local jurisdiction, or of another State, make a written report to the officer in charge of that police station and comply with Sections 103, 104, 105, 185 and 186 BNSS. If a personal search was made and a seizure list prepared, deposit a copy immediately with the local police station having jurisdiction, send a copy of the papers at the earliest to the nearest Magistrate having local jurisdiction, and record this in the case diary.

BNSS 104

steps.applies_when: Search outside the arresting officer's local jurisdiction
steps.triage_why: Only applicable if the search occurs outside the local jurisdiction; the case facts do not currently necessitate this.

steps.title: Safeguard the health and safety of the accused
steps.text: The person having custody of an accused must take reasonable care of the health and safety of the accused at all times, from arrest through detention.
legal_basis: BNSS 56
steps.triage_why: Essential for human rights and avoiding litigation/complaints, but not a step that directly proves or disproves the elements of the crime.

ticks.do: Take reasonable care of the health and safety of the accused at all times, from arrest through detention [BNSS 56].
notes: The duty lies on the person having custody of an accused.

details.text: If the person is suffering from illness or injury at the time of arrest, or becomes ill or sustains injury while in custody, subject him to medical examination at the earliest opportunity, give proper treatment, and record the treatment in the General Diary of the place where he is confined.

steps.title: Seek police custody within the statutory window
steps.text: Police custody may be authorized by the Magistrate for up to 15 days in total, in whole or in parts, at any time during the initial 40 days (for 60-day cases) or 60 days (for 90-day cases) of the detention period. Every police-custody authorization requires physical production of the accused before the Magistrate and the Magistrate's written reasons; after the period of custody is over, duly produce the accused before the Magistrate within time.
legal_basis: BNSS 187
steps.deadline: Police custody max 15 days total, available in whole or in parts within the first 40/60 days of detention
steps.triage_why: Statutory duty regarding the legality of detention; failure to follow remand procedures leads to illegal detention and can result in the case being thrown out.

ticks.do: Seek authorization of police custody from the Magistrate for up to 15 days in total, in whole or in parts [BNSS 187].
notes: Police custody may be authorized - permissive.

ticks.do: Seek that custody at any time during the initial 40 days of the detention period for 60-day cases, or the initial 60 days for 90-day cases.
Produce the accused physically before the Magistrate for every police-custody authorization, and obtain the Magistrate's written reasons.
Produce the accused duly before the Magistrate within time after the period of custody is over.

details.text: Ensure the police-custody requisition has satisfactory reasons and (per Kerala Rule 20 practice) accompany it with an affidavit setting out briefly the prior history of the investigation and the likelihood of further clues expected from having the accused in custody, sworn by the investigating or other police officer not below the rank of Sub Inspector of Police.

details.text: Recognised reasons for granting police custody include: identification of the accused by persons residing at a distant place; the accused offering during interrogation to show stolen property, weapons or other articles connected with the crime; and the accused being able to show places where he procured the weapons used and where he disposed of the proceeds of the offence.

details.text: When the accused is given to police custody, medically examine him at the start and end of the remand period and in addition every 48 hours; daily examination is advisable if the situation permits.

conflicts.description: kerala_police_sop_2020 (pp.162, 164, per CrPC 167 as it stood) states the initial remand shall be to judicial custody and police custody can be granted only within the FIRST 15 days of remand; BNSS 187 (2023) allows the 15 days of police custody to be taken in whole or in parts at any time during the initial 40 days (60-day cases) or 60 days (90-day cases).
conflicts.resolution: Canonical text follows BNSS 187 (law); the Kerala first-15-days rule is superseded and retained only inside this conflict record.

conflicts.description: delhi_compendium_2024 (Scenario 11 pp.104 and 108, Scenario 12 p.115) states that under Sec 187 BNSS the IO can take a total of 15 days of Police Custody Remand in parts 'up to 40 days from the date of arrest of the accused'. BNSS 187 makes the 15-day police custody available during the initial forty days only where the total detention period is sixty days; where the offence is punishable with death, imprisonment for life or imprisonment for ten years or more, the window is the initial sixty days of a ninety-day period.
conflicts.resolution: The law layer prevails. The canonical text carries the statutory 40/60-day windows and the 60/90-day outer caps, and the Delhi formulation is retained in details[] and in the source stack as an incomplete statement of the same provision; the two figures have not been averaged. Which window applies in a given case turns on the punishment prescribed for the BNS section invoked, so the IO must check the punishment prescribed for the section actually invoked rather than assume a window.

conflicts.description: delhi_compendium_2024 Scenario 17 p.161 states the IO can take 15 days of Police Custody Remand, in parts, 'up to 60 days from the date of arrest'. BNSS 187 allows the 15 days in whole or in parts only within the initial 40 days (60-day cases) or 60 days (90-day cases) of the detention period.
conflicts.resolution: Canonical text follows BNSS 187 (law). The Delhi 'up to 60 days from the date of arrest' window is superseded and retained only in this conflict record.

steps.title: Produce the arrestee before a Magistrate without delay
steps.text: Take or send the arrested person, without unnecessary delay and subject to the bail provisions, before a Magistrate having jurisdiction in the case or before the officer in charge of a police station. Do not detain him beyond what is reasonable in the circumstances, and in no case beyond 24 hours exclusive of the time necessary for the journey from the place of arrest to the Magistrate's Court, unless a Magistrate's special remand order under BNSS 187 is obtained.
legal_basis: BNSS 57
BNSS 58
steps.deadline: Within 24 hours of arrest, excluding journey time
steps.triage_why: Constitutional and statutory mandate to produce the accused before a Magistrate within 24 hours; failure is a gross violation of law.

ticks.do: Take or send the arrested person without unnecessary delay before a Magistrate having jurisdiction in the case, or before the officer in charge of a police station [BNSS 57].
notes: Subject to the provisions as to bail.

ticks.do: Do not detain him beyond what is reasonable in the circumstances [BNSS 58].
Do not detain him in any case beyond 24 hours, exclusive of the time necessary for the journey from the place of arrest to the Magistrate's Court.
notes: Longer detention requires a Magistrate's special remand order under BNSS 187.

details.text: If it is not possible to produce the arrested accused before the competent court within 24 hours as per Section 58 BNSS, produce him before the competent court and obtain a transit warrant.

details.text: Where it is not possible to produce the accused before the Magistrate before nightfall and it is necessary to retain him, he may be lodged in the lock-up — always subject to the 24-hour limit from the time of arrest; if he is not released on bail, produce him at the earliest with a remand application.

steps.title: Forward the accused for remand and track detention caps
steps.text: When the investigation cannot be completed within the 24 hours allowed by BNSS 58 and the accusation appears well-founded, the officer (not below the rank of Sub-Inspector) transmits the case-diary entries to, and forwards the accused before, the nearest Magistrate with a remand application. Total detention pending investigation cannot exceed 90 days for offences punishable with death, life imprisonment or 10 years or more, and 60 days for other offences; on expiry the accused has a right to default bail if he furnishes it. Where no Judicial Magistrate is available, an empowered Executive Magistrate may authorize detention up to 7 days (counted within the overall period). A woman under 18 is placed only in a remand home or recognized social institution.
legal_basis: BNSS 187
steps.deadline: Detention caps: 60/90 days pending investigation (default bail on expiry); Executive Magistrate remand max 7 days
steps.triage_why: Statutory requirement for legal detention beyond 24 hours; essential for the legality of the custody.

ticks.do: Obtain authorization of detention up to 7 days from an empowered Executive Magistrate where no Judicial Magistrate is available.

steps.title: Produce the accused when seeking extension of custody
steps.text: Extension of judicial custody may be authorized with the accused produced physically or through audio-video electronic means; every police-custody authorization always requires physical production (BNSS 187). Do not seek extension without production except for special and extraordinary reasons specifically recorded by the Magistrate in the extension order; if proper reasons for non-production cannot be furnished, the competent Court may order release of the accused on bail.
legal_basis: BNSS 187
steps.triage_why: Statutory requirement for the extension of custody; failure to produce the accused physically for PC remand is a legal error.

ticks.do: Produce the accused physically or through audio-video electronic means when seeking extension of judicial custody [BNSS 187].

details.text: Absence of physical production may be condoned where it is physically impossible to produce the accused — for instance if he is mortally injured or grievously ill in hospital, or must be produced on the same date at two different places.

steps.title: Attach the property of a proclaimed person
steps.text: After issuing the proclamation, the Court may, for reasons recorded in writing, at any time order attachment of any movable or immovable property (or both) of the proclaimed person; an order made simultaneously with the proclamation requires the Court's satisfaction, by affidavit or otherwise, that he is about to dispose of his property or remove it from the Court's jurisdiction. Before applying, the IO identifies the movable and immovable property of the accused's independent ownership, prepares a detailed list and produces it in Court with the grounds. Attachment modes: movable property and debts by seizure, appointment of a receiver, a written prohibitory order, or any combination; revenue-paying land through the Collector of the district in which it is situated; other immovable property by taking possession, a receiver, or a prohibitory order on rent or delivery. Property outside the ordering Court's district is attached when the order is endorsed by the District Magistrate of the district where the property is situated. Livestock and perishables may be ordered sold at once, the proceeds abiding the Court's order; the attached property is finally disposed of as directed in the final judgment.
legal_basis: BNSS 85
steps.deadline: Attachment order at any time after the proclamation, or simultaneously with it where disposal/removal of property is imminent
steps.triage_why: Only applicable if the accused absconds and becomes a proclaimed offender; not relevant to the immediate investigation of the arrest.

ticks.do: Identify the movable and immovable property of the accused's independent ownership, prepare a detailed list and produce it in Court with the grounds, before applying.
Apply for an order of attachment of any movable or immovable property, or both, of the proclaimed person after the proclamation has been issued [BNSS 85].
notes: The Court may so order at any time, for reasons recorded in writing.

An order made simultaneously with the proclamation requires the Court's satisfaction, by affidavit or otherwise, that he is about to dispose of his property or remove it from the Court's jurisdiction.

Attach other immovable property by taking possession, by a receiver, or by a prohibitory order on rent or delivery.

Seek an order for immediate sale of livestock and perishables, the proceeds abiding the Court's order.

ticks.do: Dispose of the attached property finally as directed in the final judgment.

details.text: Move the absconding order and the demand for attachment of the absconder's property together, along with reasonable grounds — for instance showing the likelihood of property being disposed of in haste by the accused; the Court may pass the attachment order after obtaining the IO's report, and by that order the IO obtains authority to attach property situated within or outside the district.

steps.title: Publish the Court's proclamation in the prescribed manner
steps.text: The Court publishes a written proclamation requiring the person to appear at a specified place and time not less than 30 days from the date of publication. Publication is made by: (a) public reading in a conspicuous place of the town or village where he ordinarily resides; (b) affixture to a conspicuous part of his house or homestead, or of such town or village; and (c) affixture to a conspicuous part of the Court-house; the Court may also direct publication in a daily newspaper circulating in the place where he ordinarily resides. The Court's written statement that publication was duly made is conclusive evidence of compliance. The IO carries out the execution/publication of the proclamation.
legal_basis: BNSS 84
steps.deadline: Appearance date in the proclamation not less than 30 days from the date of publication
steps.triage_why: duty of another authority, not the IO

ticks.do: Obtain from the Court a written proclamation requiring the person to appear at a specified place and time not less than 30 days from the date of publication [BNSS 84].
Carry out the execution and publication of the proclamation as the investigating officer.
Publish the proclamation by each of the following means:
sub: (a) Public reading in a conspicuous place of the town or village where he ordinarily resides.
(b) Affixture to a conspicuous part of his house or homestead, or of such town or village.
(c) Affixture to a conspicuous part of the Court-house.
notes: The Court may also direct publication in a daily newspaper circulating in the place where he ordinarily resides.

ticks.do: Obtain the Court's written statement that publication was duly made.
notes: That written statement is conclusive evidence of compliance.

details.text: Gujarat practice: also execute the proclamation personally on the accused or upon any one adult person in his family, obtaining proper acknowledgement where a copy is so given; and affix or paste it, in the presence of at least two independent witnesses, upon the entrance door of the house/dwelling where he resides and at an easily visible place in public buildings such as the Court building and the Panchayat office.

conflicts.description: guj_cid_29_sops_2024 SOP 15 (p.70) lists the modes as personal service on the accused, service on an adult family member, two-witness affixture at the dwelling entrance and public buildings, and optional newspaper publication; BNSS 84 prescribes as mandatory public reading in the town/village, affixture at the house/homestead and affixture at the Court-house, with newspaper publication optional.
conflicts.resolution: Canonical text follows the BNSS 84 mandatory publication modes (law); the SOP 15 personal-service-with-acknowledgement and public-building affixture practice is retained as additional Gujarat procedure in details.

steps.title: Apply for a proclamation after an unexecuted warrant
steps.text: If, despite necessary and sufficient efforts, the arrest warrant could not be executed for a period exceeding one month (30 days), apply before the Magistrate for issuing a proclamation of absconding under Section 84 BNSS (precondition: the Court has reason to believe the person against whom the warrant was issued has absconded or is concealing himself so that the warrant cannot be executed).
legal_basis: BNSS 84
steps.deadline: Apply once the warrant has remained unexecuted for a period exceeding one month (30 days) despite necessary and sufficient efforts
steps.triage_why: Standard procedure for absconding accused; while important for trial, it does not inherently defeat the prosecution of the underlying POCSO/BNS crimes if the accused is eventually caught.

ticks.do: Apply before the Magistrate for issuing a proclamation of absconding under Section 84 BNSS once the arrest warrant has remained unexecuted for a period exceeding one month (30 days).
notes: Applies despite necessary and sufficient efforts to execute the warrant.
Precondition: the Court has reason to believe the person against whom the warrant was issued has absconded or is concealing himself so that the warrant cannot be executed.

steps.title: Request foreign-State assistance against a proclaimed person's property
steps.text: For property of a proclaimed person located in a contracting State (a foreign country with reciprocal arrangements), a police officer not below the rank of Superintendent of Police or Commissioner of Police makes a written request to the Court, which may initiate the process of requesting assistance from a Court or authority in that contracting State for identification, attachment and forfeiture of the property, following the Chapter VIII BNSS procedure.
legal_basis: BNSS 86
steps.responsible: Police officer not below SP/Commissioner of Police, through the Court
steps.applies_when: Proclaimed person's property is located abroad in a contracting State
steps.triage_why: Specific to foreign contracting states; no evidence in the case summary suggests the accused is abroad or has foreign assets.

ticks.do: Make a written request to the Court for property of a proclaimed person located in a contracting State [BNSS 86].
notes: A contracting State is a foreign country with reciprocal arrangements.
The request is made by a police officer not below the rank of Superintendent of Police or Commissioner of Police.

ticks.do: Seek initiation by the Court of the process of requesting assistance from a Court or authority in that contracting State for identification, attachment and forfeiture of the property.
notes: The Court may initiate that process, following the Chapter VIII BNSS procedure.

steps.title: Obtain a declaration of proclaimed offender status
steps.text: Where the proclamation relates to a person accused of an offence punishable with 10 years' imprisonment or more, life imprisonment or death, and he fails to appear at the specified place and time, the Court may, after making such inquiry as it thinks fit, pronounce him a proclaimed offender and make a declaration to that effect. The publication and conclusive-evidence rules of BNSS 84 apply to that declaration also.
legal_basis: BNSS 84
steps.triage_why: This is a judicial function (Court pronouncing the offender), not a direct investigative duty of the IO.

ticks.do: Establish that the proclamation relates to a person accused of an offence punishable with 10 years' imprisonment or more, life imprisonment or death [BNSS 84].
Establish that he has failed to appear at the specified place and time.
Move the Court to pronounce him a proclaimed offender and make a declaration to that effect.
notes: The Court may do so after making such inquiry as it thinks fit.

ticks.do: Apply the publication and conclusive-evidence rules of BNSS 84 to that declaration also.

details.text: If, despite publication/execution of the proclamation, the accused does not appear, the IO shall apply in Court for declaring the proclamation of absconding against him, producing at that time the papers relating to the publication/execution and a copy of the Case Diary; if the Court is satisfied it shall pass the order.

conflicts.resolution: Canonical text follows the discretionary wording of BNSS 84 (law); the SOP is read as instructing the IO to seek the declaration, not as compelling the Court.

steps.title: Seek a Look Out Circular against a travelling accused
steps.text: If the accused is suspected to have travelled, or is likely to travel, abroad, seek a Look Out Circular: the IO makes a written request with details and reasons to the officer notified by the MHA circular, who alone gives directions for opening the LOC by passing an order; the request goes in the prescribed proforma to the Deputy Director, Bureau of Immigration, and must carry the approval of an officer not below the notified ranks (District Magistrate or SP of the district concerned, Joint Secretary in the State Government, Deputy Secretary to the Government of India, or the specified equivalents in CBI, NCB, DRI/CBDT/CBEC, IB/BoI, R&AW, NIA, Enforcement Directorate, Protector of Emigrants or the designated Interpol officer); LOCs may also issue as per the directions of any Criminal Court in India. Recourse to an LOC lies in cognizable offences under penal law where the accused deliberately evades arrest or does not appear despite non-bailable warrants and is likely to leave the country (Sumer Singh Salkan v. Asstt. Director, Delhi HC, 11.8.2010).
legal_basis: MHA Office Memorandum No. 25016/31/2010-Imm dated 27.10.2010
steps.deadline: LOC valid one year from the date of issue; renewal must be requested before expiry or the name is automatically removed (exceptions: ban-entry, loss-of-passport, impounding-of-passport, and Court/Interpol LOCs)
steps.applies_when: Accused evading arrest/NBWs with likelihood of leaving or having left India
steps.triage_why: Preventative measure to stop flight; useful but not a statutory duty that invalidates the case if omitted.

ticks.do: Seek a Look Out Circular if the accused is suspected to have travelled, or is likely to travel, abroad.
Make a written request with details and reasons to the officer notified by the MHA circular (MHA Office Memorandum No. 25016/31/2010-Imm dated 27.10.2010).
notes: That officer alone gives directions for opening the LOC by passing an order.

ticks.do: Send the request in the prescribed proforma to the Deputy Director, Bureau of Immigration.
Obtain the approval of an officer not below one of the notified ranks:
sub: District Magistrate or SP of the district concerned.
Joint Secretary in the State Government.
Deputy Secretary to the Government of India.
The specified equivalents in CBI, NCB, DRI/CBDT/CBEC, IB/BoI, R&AW, NIA, Enforcement Directorate, Protector of Emigrants or the designated Interpol officer.
notes: LOCs may also issue as per the directions of any Criminal Court in India.

ticks.do: Confine recourse to an LOC to cognizable offences under penal law where the accused deliberately evades arrest or does not appear despite non-bailable warrants and is likely to leave the country.
notes: Sumer Singh Salkan v. Asstt. Director, Delhi HC, 11.8.2010.

ticks.do: Request renewal of the LOC before expiry, the LOC being valid one year from the date of issue.
notes: The name is automatically removed if renewal is not requested before expiry.
Exceptions: ban-entry, loss-of-passport, impounding-of-passport, and Court/Interpol LOCs.

details.text: An LOC is valid for one year and can be extended before expiry of the one-year period, failing which it is automatically closed by the Immigration Officer concerned; requests must come from the Central or State Government in the prescribed form and only from officers of the specified rank, though criminal courts dealing with criminal law enforcement can issue directions resulting in an LOC (Vikram Sharma v. Union of India, Delhi HC, 26.7.2010).

details.text: The subject of an LOC must join the investigation by appearing before the IO, surrender before the court concerned, or satisfy the court that the LOC was wrongly issued; he may also approach the officer who ordered its issuance. The LOC can be withdrawn by the authority that issued it and can also be rescinded by the trial court where the case is pending, on an application by the person concerned.
details.citation: Kerala Police - Standard Operating Procedure: Investigation & Prosecution in General (SOP Series), State Police Chief, 01.11.2020

details.text: The name and designation of the officer signing the LOC proforma must invariably be mentioned, without which the request will not be entertained.

details.text: Provide the originator's contact details in column VI of the proforma and the contact telephone/mobile number of the respective control room to ensure proper communication and effective follow-up action.

details.text: An LOC cannot be opened unless a minimum of three identifying parameters, apart from sex and nationality, are available — though it can also be issued if the name and passport particulars are available; constantly review LOC requests and proactively provide additional parameters to minimise harassment to genuine passengers.
details.citation: Kerala Police - Standard Operating Procedure: Investigation & Prosecution in General (SOP Series), State Police Chief, 01.11.2020

details.text: The details in column IV regarding 'reason for opening LOC' must invariably be provided, without which the subject will not be arrested/detained; where there is no cognizable offence the subject cannot be detained, arrested or prevented from leaving the country and the agency can only request to be informed about his arrival/departure. The legal liability for action taken by the immigration authorities under the LOC rests with the originating agency.

details.text: Requests cannot emanate from statutory bodies such as the NCW, NHRC and the National Commission for Protection of Children's Rights; such requests with full facts are first brought to the notice of the police, and the SP concerned then makes the LOC request upon an assessment of the situation and strictly per the prescribed procedure.
details.citation: Kerala Police - Standard Operating Procedure: Investigation & Prosecution in General (SOP Series), State Police Chief, 01.11.2020

details.text: In exceptional cases LOCs can be issued without complete parameters and/or case details against CI suspects, terrorists and anti-national elements in the larger national interest.
details.citation: Kerala Police - Standard Operating Procedure: Investigation & Prosecution in General (SOP Series), State Police Chief, 01.11.2020

details.text: The LOC proforma specifies the action expected from the Immigration Check Point: inform of arrival/departure; seize travel documents; prevent entry; prevent departure; or detain and hand over to the local police — alongside personal particulars, physical description, passport details, the reason for opening the LOC (FIR number, sections, police station, district or wanted-by-court details) and the originator's particulars.
details.citation: Kerala Police - Standard Operating Procedure: Investigation & Prosecution in General (SOP Series), State Police Chief, 01.11.2020

details.text: The period of retention specified in the proforma cannot exceed 12 months; renewal requests are made by the competent authority from time to time or yearly.
details.citation: Kerala Police - Standard Operating Procedure: Investigation & Prosecution in General (SOP Series), State Police Chief, 01.11.2020

steps.title: Proceed under BNS 209 against a non-appearing absconder
steps.text: Where intimation of the proclamation order has been given to the accused and the absconding accused still does not remain present in Court by the appointed date: if the investigation is in progress, add Section 209 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita 2023 against the accused in the charge-sheet; if the investigation against him has been completed, register a fresh complaint under BNS Section 209 against the person declared an absconder.

steps.triage_why: Procedural step for adding a secondary charge of absconding; does not affect the primary POCSO/BNS charges.

Register a fresh complaint under BNS Section 209 against the person declared an absconder where the investigation against him has been completed.

steps.title: Obtain and execute a warrant against an evading accused
steps.text: Investigate the cognizable offence and take steps for effecting the arrest of the accused. If, during the investigation, the accused evades arrest or moves about in concealment and does not cooperate, apply to the Court for the issue of an arrest warrant; the IO shall remain personally present in Court and state to the Magistrate the reasonable grounds for issuing it. After obtaining the warrant, the IO may give it to any police officer for execution, and shall mention in the Case Diary the action taken for its execution.
steps.triage_why: Fundamental duty to investigate a cognizable offence and secure the accused for trial.

ticks.do: Investigate the cognizable offence and take steps for effecting the arrest of the accused.
Apply to the Court for the issue of an arrest warrant if, during the investigation, the accused evades arrest or moves about in concealment and does not cooperate.
Remain personally present in Court and state to the Magistrate the reasonable grounds for issuing the warrant.
notes: The IO shall remain personally present.

ticks.do: Give the warrant to any police officer for execution after obtaining it.

ticks.do: Mention in the Case Diary the action taken for execution of the warrant.

details.text: Where sufficient evidence justifying arrest is collected but the accused is found evading arrest, first issue notices/summons to secure his presence to join the investigation and document all efforts taken; make enquiries with his relatives, friends and other persons likely to be aware of his movements and warn them all against harbouring him; if his presence is still not secured, report the facts and apply to the Court for bailable and non-bailable warrants and take all efforts to trace and arrest him.

details.text: The details of all wanted persons may be uploaded on the State Police website (through the State Crime Records Bureau) and circulated amongst other law-enforcement agencies to compel the person to join the investigation.

steps.title: Seek an Interpol Red Notice for a fugitive abroad
steps.text: For a fugitive suspected to be, or likely to go, abroad, additionally seek an Interpol Red Notice through the National Central Bureau using the prescribed Red Notice form (identity particulars; caution indicators such as armed, dangerous, escape risk, suicidal or violent; aliases and nicknames; family details; occupation; languages; regions/countries likely to be visited; identity documents, of which nationality, type and number are mandatory; identification material including photographs, fingerprints, DNA and dental information; physical description; and facts of the case with date, town, country, offence codes and a summary limited to 1000 characters/200 words). For a fugitive wanted for prosecution all fields are mandatory, the arrest warrant should be open dated, and the conduct must be punishable by a maximum deprivation of liberty of at least two years or a more serious penalty; for a fugitive wanted to serve a sentence the person must have at least six months of imprisonment imposed and/or at least six months remaining to be served. A Blue Notice may also be used to collect additional information about a person's identity, location or activities in relation to a crime.
steps.applies_when: Absconder suspected to be, or likely to go, outside India
steps.triage_why: Extreme measure for international fugitives; not applicable based on current case facts.

steps.title: Obtain a Magistrate's order for specimens and samples
steps.text: Where specimen signatures, finger impressions, handwriting or voice samples are required from any person, including the accused, obtain an order of a Magistrate of the first class who is satisfied that it is expedient for the investigation or proceeding; the person must attend at the specified time and place and furnish the specimen or sample. Ordinarily the person must at some time have been arrested in connection with the investigation or proceeding, but the Magistrate may, for reasons recorded in writing, order specimens or samples from a person who has not been arrested.

steps.triage_why: Statutory requirement to obtain a Magistrate's order for specimen samples; failure to do so makes the evidence inadmissible.

conflicts.description: The Delhi compendium prints the provision for taking specimen signatures, finger prints and voice samples as 'section 349 of BNS, 2023' (Scenario 20, p.191). The extraction of that source itself flags the citation, listing it as '349 (specimen signatures, finger prints and voice samples - printed as BNS in source; see notes)'.
conflicts.resolution: Resolved in favour of the law layer. bnss_2023 BNSS 349 ('Power of Magistrate to order person to give specimen signatures or handwriting, etc.') is the provision that empowers a Magistrate of the first class to order any person, including an accused, to give specimen signatures, finger impressions, handwriting or a voice sample, so the compendium's 'BNS' is a misprint for BNSS and the canonical text follows BNSS 349. The compendium's substantive additions - that arrest is not required and that 'any person' covers the complainant and witnesses - agree with BNSS 349, which records the same expansion, and are retained as detail.

conflicts.description: delhi_compendium_2024 states that 'as per Section 349 BNSS, the IO can take samples of handwriting, specimen signatures, finger impressions and voice impressions of any person, including the accused person, without effecting his/their arrest' (Scenario 17 p.160; same statement at Scenario 4 p.42 and Scenario 13 p.128), which reads as a police power and omits the Magistrate entirely; bnss_2023 BNSS 349 vests the power in a Magistrate of the first class who is satisfied that it is expedient, and permits an order against an unarrested person only for reasons recorded in writing.
conflicts.resolution: The law layer prevails: the canonical text keeps the first-class Magistrate's order as mandatory. The two are not blended. The point the compendium was correctly making - that BNSS 349 extends to persons who have not been arrested - survives, but only with the statutory condition that the Magistrate records his reasons in writing.

conflicts.description: delhi_compendium_2024 Scenario 17 p.160 states that 'As per Section 349 BNSS, the IO can take samples of handwriting, specimen signatures, finger impressions and voice impressions of any person, including the accused person, without effecting his/their arrest', omitting the requirement of an order of a Magistrate of the first class. Section 349 BNSS in fact requires such an order, and permits it in respect of a person who has not been arrested only for reasons recorded in writing by the Magistrate.
conflicts.resolution: Law prevails: specimens or samples under Section 349 BNSS may be taken only on the order of a Magistrate of the first class. The Delhi wording is read as making the point that arrest is not a precondition, not as dispensing with the Magistrate's order.

steps.title: Enter and search premises to effect arrest
steps.text: Search of place entered by person sought to be arrested [BNSS 44]: If any person acting under a warrant of arrest, or any police officer having authority to arrest, has reason to believe that the person to be arrested has entered into, or is within, any place, any person residing in or being in charge of such place SHALL, on demand of such person acting as aforesaid or such police officer, allow him free ingress thereto and afford all reasonable facilities for a search therein. If ingress cannot be obtained under sub-section (1), the statute says it SHALL BE LAWFUL - an enabling permission, not a command - in any case for a person acting under a warrant, and in any case in which a warrant may issue but cannot be obtained without affording the person to be arrested an opportunity of escape, for a police officer to enter such place and search therein, and, in order to effect an entrance, to break open any outer or inner door or window of any house or place, if after notification of his authority and purpose and demand of admittance duly made he cannot otherwise obtain admittance. Where the place is an apartment in the actual occupancy of a female (not being the person to be arrested) who according to custom does not appear in public, such person or police officer SHALL before entering give her notice that she is at liberty to withdraw and SHALL afford her every reasonable facility for withdrawing, and MAY then break open the apartment and enter it. Any police officer or other person authorised to make an arrest MAY also break open any outer or inner door or window of any house or place in order to liberate himself or any other person who, having lawfully entered for the purpose of making an arrest, is detained therein.
steps.stage: Statutory basis of arrest and identification
legal_basis: Section 44 BNSS 2023
steps.triage_why: This is a procedural rule regarding the power to search a premises during arrest; it is a reference for the officer's authority, not a case-specific mandatory step.

ticks.do: Demand free ingress and all reasonable facilities for a search from the person residing in or in charge of any place the person to be arrested has entered or is within [BNSS 44].
notes: Such person SHALL allow ingress on demand of the person acting under a warrant of arrest, or of the police officer having authority to arrest, who has reason to believe the person to be arrested is there.

ticks.do: Enter such place and search therein where ingress cannot be obtained under sub-section (1).

ticks.do: Break open the apartment and enter it thereafter.

ticks.do: Break open any outer or inner door or window of any house or place to liberate himself or any other person
notes: Any police officer or other person authorised to make an arrest MAY do this.

steps.title: Request court-directed identification of the arrested person
steps.text: Identification of person arrested [BNSS 54]: Where a person is arrested on a charge of committing an offence and his identification by any other person or persons is considered necessary for the purpose of investigation of such offence, the Court having jurisdiction MAY, on the request of the officer in charge of a police station, direct the person so arrested to subject himself to identification by any person or persons in such manner as the Court may deem fit. The power is the Court's and is discretionary; the officer in charge of a police station does not order the identification himself, he requests it. Where the person identifying the person arrested is mentally or physically disabled, such process of identification SHALL take place under the supervision of a Magistrate, who shall take appropriate steps to ensure that such person identifies the person arrested using methods that person is comfortable with, and the identification process SHALL be recorded by any audio-video electronic means. The section has no sub-sections; it is a single provision with one proviso.
steps.stage: Statutory basis of arrest and identification
legal_basis: Section 54 BNSS 2023
steps.triage_why: This describes a discretionary power of the Court (MAY) for identification parades, not a statutory duty of the IO.

ticks.do: Request the Court having jurisdiction to direct the arrested person to subject himself to identification where it is considered necessary for the investigation of the offence [BNSS 54].
notes: The request is made by the officer in charge of a police station; the power is the Court's and is discretionary - the Court MAY so direct, in such manner as it may deem fit.
The officer in charge of a police station does not order the identification himself, he requests it.
Section 54 has no sub-sections; it is a single provision with one proviso.

Record the identification process by any audio-video electronic means.

steps.title: Examine witnesses early but only after scene work
steps.text: Examine witnesses as early as possible — memory fades with lapse of time, and belated examination risks witnesses enriching their account from what they hear from others or filling gaps from imagination — but do not begin interrogation of witnesses until the place of occurrence has been carefully inspected, the scene-of-crime map prepared, searches made and exhibits preserved.
steps.stage: Planning and timing of witness examination
steps.deadline: As early as possible, but only after scene inspection, scene map, searches and exhibit preservation (kerala_police_sop_2020 para 3.9, p. 111)
steps.triage_why: In POCSO and sexual offence cases, prompt examination of the victim and preservation of the scene are critical to prevent evidence degradation and allegations of tutoring.

Belated examination risks witnesses enriching their account from what they hear from others or filling gaps from imagination.

preparation of the scene-of-crime map

steps.title: Establish the motive and sequence of the crime
steps.text: Find out the motive of the crime, and examine the injured, the witnesses, the relatives (to find out about previous quarrels) and the CCTVs to establish the exact sequence of events, the role of each accused person, and the motive.
steps.stage: Planning and timing of witness examination
steps.triage_why: Establishing motive and sequence via CCTV strengthens the case, but the primary evidence in POCSO is the victim's testimony and medical evidence.

the witnesses
the relatives, to find out about previous quarrels

details.text: In a road accident, find out whether the accused and the victim are acquainted with each other, so as to assess or eliminate any ill mens rea behind the act and be sure that the act was the result of only an accident and not an attempt on the victim's life; analyse the CDR of the accused and the victim for the same purpose if the situation so dictates.

steps.title: Revive a witness's lost memory without suggestion
steps.text: Where witnesses could not be contacted within reasonable time and have forgotten all or a substantial part of the occurrence, revive lost memory in two ways: (i) the association method — link the occurrence to a memorable event of about the same date (a sensational political event for an educated witness, a village festival for a rustic villager); (ii) place the witness amidst the surroundings in which he first made his observations — it is advantageous to examine all important witnesses on the spot. Never suggest anything to make the witness testify to matters outside his personal knowledge: trustworthy testimony must come spontaneously, not from suggestions or feelers thrown at him.
steps.stage: Planning and timing of witness examination
steps.triage_why: This is a technique for memory revival to be used only if witnesses have forgotten facts; it is not a standard requirement.

ticks.do: Revive lost memory in the two ways below where witnesses could not be contacted within reasonable time and have forgotten all or a substantial part of the occurrence.
sub: (i) the association method, linking the occurrence to a memorable event of about the same date, such as a sensational political event for an educated witness or a village festival for a rustic villager
(ii) placing the witness amidst the surroundings in which he first made his observations
notes: It is advantageous to examine all important witnesses on the spot.

steps.title: Compel witness attendance by written order
steps.text: To secure a witness's attendance, issue a written order requiring any person who appears acquainted with the facts and circumstances of the case — within the limits of the Investigating Officer's own or any adjoining police station — to attend before him so that questioning relating to the offence may be carried out and his statement recorded; the person so ordered is legally bound to attend.
legal_basis: BNSS 179
steps.triage_why: Using formal written orders ensures witness attendance, but is a tool of convenience/practice rather than a statutory requirement that defeats the case if omitted.

steps.title: Spare listed witnesses from attending the police station
steps.text: Do not call to the police station, or require to attend at any place other than the place where such person resides: (1) a male under 15 years or above 60 years of age; (2) any woman; (3) a mentally or physically disabled person; (4) a person suffering from acute (serious) illness. Question such protected persons at their place of residence; if such a person is voluntarily willing to attend at the police station, permission may be granted.
legal_basis: BNSS 179 proviso
steps.triage_why: Statutory protection for women and minors; failing to question the 17-year-old victim at her residence (unless she volunteers) violates legal safeguards.

(4) a person suffering from acute (serious) illness

steps.title: Examine persons orally and respect the self-incrimination exception
steps.text: Orally examine any person supposed to be acquainted with the facts and circumstances of the case (the examination may also be done by an officer not below the prescribed rank acting on the Investigating Officer's requisition). The person examined is bound to answer truly all questions relating to the case, except questions the answers to which would tend to expose him to a criminal charge, penalty or forfeiture — never compel a witness to give a statement of a kind by which he would incriminate himself.
steps.triage_why: Recording statements of persons acquainted with the facts is a fundamental statutory duty of the investigating officer.

The source's illustration is a crime of molestation in which the accused, who was in a position of authority in government, took the alibi that he was never at home on that day as it was a holiday and that he would always move to his own home during weekends, so he was not at all present in the soc during the alleged crime; the investigators obtained the landline telephone print-outs of all those days, which showed several national and international calls received and made by the accused on the official telephone that nobody else would have access to, and he cooled down only when confronted with the print-out.
legal_basis: Sections 180 and 183 BNSS [= 161 and 164 CrPC] — statements of victim/witness, printed by the source as 'statements u/s 180 and 183 BNSS' (p.117) and 'The 180 and 183 statements' (p.127), to be recorded as per the procedure in the ITPA and POCSO Acts

ITPA — the 180 statement of a rescued woman, irrespective of age, shall be recorded by a female police officer; if a female is not available, by a male police officer in the presence of a female social worker (p.127)

POCSO Act — mandatory to have a female official interview and record statements of children, both male and female; if a female police officer is not available, a female government official, and if that is not possible, a woman from an NGO (p.127); the law does not exclude male police officers from interviewing, it only requires that the statement be recorded by a female person

section 192 BNSS [= 172 CrPC] — operational part of the Case Diary, in which the interview challenges, emotional outbursts, trauma and related responses of the victim are to be captured without editing (p.120)

Indian Evidence Act — admission of the accused before a police officer is not admissible unless it leads to discovery or recovery (p.124) [the source cites the IEA as such; under the new era s.25 IEA is now s.23(1) BSA 2023, s.26 IEA is now s.23(2) BSA, and the discovery/recovery exception in s.27 IEA is now the proviso to s.23(2) BSA]

Provision in law for turning a co-accused into an 'approver' and treating that person as a witness (the source refers to the provision without citing a section, p.125) — the admission must be inculpatory and not exculpatory, the role must be of a minor nature and not that of the mastermind, and the prosecutor must agree and place it before the court and the court must finally agree
Rights-based interrogation: torture and 'third degree' are not permitted at all and shall be shunned completely; even fear and threat constitute torture (p.123)
steps.triage_why: Provides an illustrative example/case study for the IO's guidance.

steps.title: Keep witness statements free of pressure or suppression
steps.text: Offer or make no inducement, threat or promise of the kind mentioned in Section 24 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872 to any person during the investigation; equally, do not prevent, by caution or otherwise, any person from making of his own free will any statement in the course of the investigation.

steps.triage_why: Inducements or threats render statements inadmissible and violate the law of evidence.

steps.title: Match the technique to the class of witness
steps.text: Identify the class of witness and apply the matching handling technique: (i) interested witnesses (stand to gain from a successful investigation) — tap them fully but do not repose implicit faith without preliminary verification; they are prone to exaggerate, so guard against half-truths lest a false charge be unwittingly brought before a court; (ii) hostile witnesses (stand to lose; generally drawn from the suspect's friends, relatives, associates, receivers or well-wishers) — deal with them tactfully, courteously and firmly, give no advance intimation, take them by surprise and examine them at a place away from friends, associates, lawyers and relations; (iii) disinterested witnesses — devoid of personal motive, their evidence deserves the highest credence but they rarely come forward of their own accord; fix a time convenient to them, develop a common ground of conversation, and approach with utmost civility and politeness without provoking their apathy; (iv) lying witnesses — find the motive for the false information (lack of or incorrect observation, self-interest, interest in the suspect) and shape questions accordingly; let an intentional liar talk as much as he likes until he contradicts himself on material points; (v) unwilling witnesses — discover the cause of the aversion in each case and take steps to remove it; (vi) nervous witnesses — pick up information slowly and gradually, point by point in a systematic fashion, in a conversational manner and in their own surroundings, never with a volley of interrogatories; (vii) child witnesses — use a friendly, almost fatherly tone, ask for their own experiences and not what they heard, keep it a brief and simple conversation, and never put leading or suggestive questions (children tend to answer them affirmatively without understanding their implications); (viii) female witnesses — examine at their residence in the presence of a relation or guardian, with a high standard of decorum and courtesy, requisitioning the services of women police.
steps.triage_why: Guidance on witness credibility assessment; sound practice but not a statutory mandate.

steps.title: Examine witnesses separately and in the right order
steps.text: Examine each witness separately — none of the suspects or witnesses may be allowed to hear the examination of another — and, as far as possible, hear the important, favourable and trustworthy witnesses first, so that the investigator is sufficiently conversant with the facts of the case before taking up the interrogation of the suspect or of unfavourable witnesses.
steps.triage_why: Prevents witness contamination; sound practice but not a statutory duty that defeats the case if missed.

steps.title: Adapt questioning technique to the witness
steps.text: Frame questions that are clear and unambiguous, neither suggestive nor leading; as a rule allow the witness first to give an account of his experience in his own way, and only thereafter begin the real interrogation. See that the witness omits no important detail while guarding against being misled by any false or inaccurate statement. Vary the method of interrogation according to the psychology of the person interrogated — his age, sex, education and social status — and prefer patient and sympathetic treatment: make the complainant and the inmates of the house feel they are narrating their tale of woes to their own kith and kin; a word of sympathy brings witnesses much nearer to the investigator than a thousand harsh words.
steps.triage_why: Best practice for questioning to avoid 'leading' the witness; failure is a tactical error, not a statutory breach.

steps.text: Do not take the signature or thumb impression of the witness upon a statement recorded by the police.
legal_basis: Section 162(1) CrPC [now BNSS 181]
steps.applies_when: Statements recorded by the police in the course of investigation (BNSS 180). The bar does not extend to a dying declaration, on which the declarant's signature or thumb impression must invariably be taken, nor to a confession or statement recorded by a Magistrate under BNSS 183, which is signed by its maker.
steps.triage_why: Police statements are generally not signed by the witness; taking a signature can lead to the statement being challenged as coerced or converted into a different legal instrument.

details.text: The statutory bar: no statement made to a police officer in the course of an investigation shall, if reduced to writing, be signed by the person making it (Section 162(1) CrPC, printed pre-2023 citation).

steps.title: Cover every witness holding special case information
steps.text: Question as many witnesses as needed, but ensure that the statements of the important witnesses who possess special and complete information relating to the incident are recorded; it is not compulsory to mention in the charge-sheet the witnesses of all the statements recorded during the investigation.
steps.triage_why: Sound investigative practice to build a strong case, but not a statutory duty that would invalidate the proceedings if some witnesses are omitted from the charge-sheet.

steps.title: Certify statements and supply copies to the accused
steps.text: Have the recording police officer certify each statement as truly recorded and attach it to the case diary at the relevant dates; before commencement of the trial, copies of the statements of all persons whom the prosecution proposes to examine as its witnesses must be supplied to the accused free of cost — sternly comply with Section 207 CrPC [now BNSS 230].

steps.title: Safeguard silence and counsel while questioning the accused
steps.text: During any questioning of an accused or suspect, honour the right to remain silent and the right against self-incrimination (Section 161(2) CrPC [now BNSS 180(2)]; Article 20(3), Constitution of India): never coerce or influence him into giving a statement pointing to his guilt; inform him of these rights; and inform him of his right to consult a lawyer at the time of questioning — with the lawyer by his side if desired — irrespective of whether he is under arrest or in detention.

steps.title: Examine the suspect to fix defence and charges
steps.text: Examine the suspect/accused thoroughly with a view to ascertaining his defence as well as proving the charges against him: inform him of the details of the charge and seek his explanation; record his statement according to the provisions of Section 161(3) CrPC [now BNSS 180(3)] (Nandini Satpathi v. P. L. Dani 1978 Crl. J 968 SC). In important cases prepare a questionnaire for the examination with the guidance of senior officers and record the statements in narrative form; read over to the accused the answers recorded. If any material objects or information relevant to the commission of the offence are disclosed, record the accused's statement in the presence of witnesses mentioning the recovery of the articles, weapons etc. disclosed by him, and thoroughly verify all points so that the prosecution is fully prepared to counter the defence.
steps.stage: Examination of the suspect or accused
steps.triage_why: Important for the investigation's thoroughness, but the specific method of questioning (questionnaires) is a matter of practice, not a statutory requirement.

steps.title: Apply forthwith for Magistrate to record victim's statement
steps.text: In cases punishable under BNS Sections 64 to 71, 74 to 79 and 124, apply forthwith — upon the offence coming to the knowledge of the police — for the victim's statement to be recorded by the Magistrate; the Magistrate must record the statement immediately after the police application, as soon as the commission of the offence is brought to the notice of the police, as far as practicable by a woman Magistrate.

The Delhi Police guidelines record a 24-hour outer limit from registration of the FIR, resting on the Supreme Court in Attorney General v. Shiv Kumar Yadav and State of Karnataka v. Shivanna, 2014(8) SCC 816 (delhi-sexual-offence-response p.7; delhi_compendium_2024 Scenario 1 p.10); any delay exceeding 24 hours in taking the victim to the Magistrate must be recorded with reasons in the case diary and a copy handed to the Magistrate.
steps.applies_when: Cases punishable under BNS Sections 64-71, 74-79 or 124
steps.triage_why: Statutory duty for sexual offences (BNS 64). Failure to apply for the victim's statement to be recorded by a Magistrate is a breach of mandatory legal procedure in these specific offences.

steps.title: Route the Section 183 application to the right Magistrate
steps.text: Make the application for recording a confession or statement under Section 183 BNSS to the Judicial Magistrate having jurisdiction where the case has been registered, or to any Judicial Magistrate of that district; when a Judicial Magistrate other than the jurisdictional Magistrate is approached, record the reasons for this in the application. Keep along with every such application a copy of the statement recorded before the police under Section 180 BNSS. Where the statement is recorded by a Magistrate other than the jurisdictional Magistrate, ensure it is sent immediately to the Magistrate who will inquire into or try the case.
legal_basis: BNSS 183(1)
steps.deadline: A statement recorded by a non-jurisdictional Magistrate must be sent to the jurisdictional Magistrate immediately (Gujarat SOP 5, p.20)
steps.triage_why: Ensures the legal validity of the statement under Section 183 BNSS; improper jurisdiction or lack of reasoning for non-jurisdictional applications can be challenged.
