conflicts.description: kerala_police_sop_2020 (p. 98), printed under Section 164(1) CrPC, allows any Metropolitan Magistrate or Judicial Magistrate to record the confession or statement whether or not he has jurisdiction in the case, with no district restriction; bnss_2023 BNSS 183(1) and guj_cid_29_sops_2024 SOP 5 (p. 19) confine recording to a Magistrate of the district in which the information about the offence has been registered.
conflicts.resolution: BNSS 183(1) (law) prevails: apply to a Magistrate of the district of registration — the jurisdictional Judicial Magistrate first, or any Judicial Magistrate of that district with reasons recorded in the application. The Kerala text reflects the superseded CrPC 164(1) position.

steps.title: Confine Section 183 requests to the permitted window
steps.text: Seek recording under Section 183 BNSS only within its window: during the police investigation, or after submission of the final report (charge-sheet) but before the Court commences inquiry or trial proceedings. Do not seek recording in a preliminary inquiry under Section 173(3) BNSS — the Section applies only to cases under investigation — and do not seek it after the inquiry or trial proceedings have been commenced by the Court.

steps.title: Arrange interpreter and video for a disabled maker
steps.text: Where the maker of a Section 183 BNSS statement is mentally or physically disabled, is deaf or dumb, or is not able to understand the local language, ensure the Magistrate takes the assistance of an interpreter or a special educator. Where the maker is mentally or physically disabled, ensure in addition that the statement is recorded by audio-video electronic means (desirably by mobile phone); such a statement is deemed to have been taken as the person's examination-in-chief under Section 142 of the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023, and cross-examination may be conducted only upon that statement — it need not be recorded again at the time of trial.
legal_basis: BNSS 183(6)

steps.triage_why: This is a conditional rule that applies only if the witness is disabled or has a language barrier; not applicable to all cases.

steps.title: Secure the statutory safeguards for a judicial confession
steps.text: Ensure the statutory safeguards attend every judicial confession: the confession is recorded forthwith; before recording, the Magistrate must explain to the accused that he is not bound to make any confession and that, if he does so, it may be used as evidence against him, and must ascertain that the confession is being made voluntarily before recording it; no police officer on whom any power of a Magistrate has been conferred may record a confession; the confession is recorded in the manner provided by Section 316 BNSS, signed by its maker, with the Magistrate's memorandum at the foot of the record.

steps.deadline: Recording of the confession forthwith (guj_cid_29_sops_2024 SOP 5, p. 20)

steps.text: If an accused person, on being arrested, expresses his desire to make a confession before a Magistrate, send him immediately to a competent Magistrate under proper escort, with a memorandum containing the request. steps.title: Prove a Section 27 disclosure leading to discovery
steps.text: To prove a disclosure leading to discovery (Section 27, Indian Evidence Act, 1872): obtain the accused's name and other particulars for proper identification; indicate the date, time and venue of recording; the statement may be recorded in the presence of two witnesses, who then accompany the Investigating Officer and the accused to the place of discovery. Record only the relevant portion of the statement leading to the discovery of the articles or physical evidence, signed by the accused (who cannot be compelled to give his signature); pack and seal the recovered articles in the presence of those witnesses; have the seizure memo signed by the Investigating Officer, the witnesses and the accused (again, not compellable); a photograph of the witnesses along with the IO, the accused and the seized articles may be taken.
legal_basis: Section 27 Indian Evidence Act, 1872

steps.title: Weigh and record extra-judicial confessions correctly
steps.text: Handle extra-judicial confessions for what they are worth: (i) a confession before members of the public is not given much weight in court — the courts require the exact words used by the accused as nearly as possible and some other supporting evidence, so never remain satisfied with this sort of evidence alone, though in conjunction with other evidence it has great value in fixing guilt; (ii) if an accused on being arrested is willing to confess to a police officer, record it in the case diary, as far as practicable in the accused's same words and in the first person, with the officer's certificate at the end that it was correctly recorded — such a confession is not admissible except under Section 27 of the Evidence Act, and only so much of the statement as leads to the discovery is reproduced in the recovery mahazar, which is attested by witnesses; (iii) record the accused's version even if the statement does not amount to a confession, since it may help further investigation and collection of evidence.
legal_basis: Section 27 Indian Evidence Act, 1872
steps.triage_why: Extra-judicial confessions are weak evidence; the IO should seek corroboration to ensure the case doesn't rely on unreliable testimony.

steps.title: Treat a co-accused's confession as weak and corroborate it
steps.text: Never build the case on the confession of a co-accused: it is very weak evidence requiring corroboration, is not substantive evidence against the other accused, and no conviction of the other accused can be based on it even where it led to the discovery of a material fact under Section 27 of the Evidence Act. It may be considered under Section 30 of the Evidence Act only by the court trying the case, and only when: (i) the statement is a confession of the person who makes it; (ii) it affects the confessing prisoner and his fellow prisoner; (iii) the confessor is tried jointly with the others; (iv) the trial is for the same offence (an offence under the same section of law); (v) the joint trial is a legal one; and (vi) the confession is proved. The Investigating Officer must be able to show that the maker implicated himself in all the offences in which he implicates the co-accused, and must make all efforts to collect other collateral and corroborative evidence to support the case.
legal_basis: Section 30 Indian Evidence Act, 1872
steps.triage_why: This is a legal principle regarding the weight of evidence for the court's consideration, not a field action.

steps.title: Record the accused's narration for investigative use
steps.text: When the accused narrates his involvement to the police (for investigative use), recording of the confession can be done in one of three ways — sentence by sentence, stage by stage, or heard completely and then drawn up as a comprehensive statement — keeping in mind: (i) name, parentage, residence etc. of the suspect and associates; (ii) acts showing motive and preparation for the crime; (iii) actual commission of the crime with details of time and manner; (iv) subsequent conduct — details of retreat, division and disposal of property; (v) information on the same lines regarding previous offences; (vi) names and activities of receivers, accomplices and harbourers. The IO may record just the relevant information, which may give further clues to the crime; the exercise may become infructuous if the accused, once produced in court, decides not to confess, but details obtained from him earlier may still be useful in further unfolding the truth.
steps.triage_why: Detailed recording of the accused's narrative helps in identifying contradictions and building the investigative theory.

steps.title: Observe the evidentiary limits of police statements
steps.text: Treat statements recorded by police under Section 161 CrPC [now BNSS 180] as non-substantive evidence: they are not evidence for the prosecution, cannot be used against the accused, and shall not be used for any purpose except to contradict a prosecution witness in the manner provided by Section 145 of the Evidence Act under the proviso to Section 162(1) CrPC [now BNSS 181] — the defence may so use them, and the Public Prosecutor may with the court's permission, including to cross-examine a prosecution witness who turns hostile; a part so used may also be used in re-examination, but only to explain matters referred to in cross-examination. An omission to state a fact may amount to a contradiction if it appears significant and otherwise relevant in the context (a question of fact). The bar does not apply to statements falling within Section 32(1) of the Evidence Act [now BSA 2023 s.26(a)] (dying declarations) or to Section 27 discoveries, which the prosecution can use as evidence; and the relevant portions of a hostile witness's evidence remain usable in appropriate situations, at least to corroborate the evidence of other independent witnesses in material particulars.
legal_basis: Section 162 CrPC [now BNSS 181]
Sections 27 and 32(1) Indian Evidence Act, 1872
Section 145 Indian Evidence Act, 1872

steps.title: Select panch witnesses and complete the panchnama properly
steps.text: Select two or more independent and respectable persons as panch witnesses. After preparation of the panchnama, have the panchas read its contents; if a panch is illiterate, read the panchnama over to him and make an endorsement on it that the contents were read over to him. Where there was no source of light at the time of making the panchnama, mention how the source of light was managed to prepare it (guidance may be taken from Section 100(4) and (5) CrPC [now BNSS 103]). Where there is no eye witness to the offence and the case rests wholly on circumstantial evidence, the panchnama carries immense value.
legal_basis: Section 100(4)-(5) CrPC [now BNSS 103]
steps.triage_why: Panchnamas for the crime scene (Moje Jaldeep Flat) and recoveries are essential; failure to follow proper panch witness procedure can lead to the evidence being discarded as fabricated.

steps.title: Apply settled credibility principles when citing witnesses
steps.text: Apply the settled credibility principles when selecting and citing witnesses: a related witness is not equivalent to an interested witness — a witness is 'interested' only where he derives some benefit from the litigation or from seeing the accused punished — and relationship alone does not affect credibility or justify rejection of the testimony as a matter of rule; an injured witness has a special status in law with a built-in guarantee of his presence at the scene (probe what he was doing there at that hour, his relation to the parties, and how he came to be injured) and his testimony can be acted upon even without corroboration absent grounds for rejection based on major contradictions and discrepancies; an eye-witness must have been capable of adequate vision with light adequate enough to see and identify, and must not be a stock witness — appreciation of his evidence depends on the accuracy of his original observation, the correctness and extent of what he remembers, and his veracity; the evidence of police officials cannot be discarded merely because it is not corroborated by an independent witness or because they belong to the police force (Kripal Singh v. The State of Rajasthan 2019 All SCR (Online) 145), though the rule of prudence requires a greater degree of scrutiny and, as a precaution, corroboration by some independent witness; courts insist on the testimony of an independent witness only where some doubt exists — non-examination of an independent witness is not a serious lacuna where the prosecution evidence inspires confidence (independent witnesses are often unwilling to come forward, leaving the prosecution to fall back on friends and family of the victim); the evidence of interested and of trap witnesses is not discarded but scrutinized with utmost care and caution; and chance-witness evidence may be reliable or unreliable depending on the circumstances.
steps.triage_why: Proper witness selection ensures the prosecution's case is resilient against defense claims of bias.

steps.title: Reconcile eyewitness account with divergent medical evidence
steps.text: Where the eyewitness account and the medical evidence diverge, remember that medical evidence does not itself establish the guilt or innocence of the accused — it provides expert opinion based upon objective, indisputable facts which helps evaluate the reliability and credibility of other witnesses — and that conviction cannot be based solely on medical evidence, which must be corroborated by other evidence. On a conflict of opinion between experts, obtain further opinion from senior experts. Where the eyewitness account is found credible and trustworthy, medical evidence pointing to alternative possibilities is not accepted as conclusive; where the two are not of exactly similar opinion yet both lead to the same story there is no contradiction (Jheena v. State of M.P. 1986 Cri LJ 1375 (MP)); the Court first examines the discrepancies carefully and makes every effort at a harmonious construction of the medical and eyewitness evidence — but on a contradiction between ocular testimony and medical evidence, ocular testimony is neither accepted nor rejected at the instance of the medical evidence and the accused gets the benefit of doubt (Mahar Singh v. State of Punjab AIR 1981 SC 1578).
steps.triage_why: Given the victim is 'injured', reconciling medical reports with the victim's account is vital for credibility.

steps.title: Apply the bar on police statements under BNSS 181
steps.text: Statements to police and use thereof [BNSS 181]: Sub-section (1) is prohibitory: no statement made by any person to a police officer in the course of an investigation under this Chapter shall, if reduced to writing, be signed by the person making it; nor shall any such statement or any record thereof, whether in a police diary or otherwise, or any part of such statement or record, be used for any purpose, save as hereinafter provided, at any inquiry or trial in respect of any offence under investigation at the time when such statement was made. The proviso creates a narrow permissive exception: when any witness is called for the prosecution in such inquiry or trial whose statement has been reduced into writing as aforesaid, any part of his statement, if duly proved, "may be used by the accused, and with the permission of the Court, by the prosecution, to contradict such witness" in the manner provided by section 148 of the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 - this is an option, not an obligation, and the prosecution's use additionally needs the Court's permission. And when any part of such statement is so used, any part thereof may also be used in the re-examination of such witness, but for the purpose only of explaining any matter referred to in his cross-examination. Sub-section (2) provides that nothing in the section shall be deemed to apply to any statement falling within the provisions of clause (a) of section 26 of the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023, or to affect the provisions of the proviso to sub-section (2) of section 23 of that Adhiniyam. The Explanation states that an omission to state a fact or circumstance in the statement referred to in sub-section (1) "may amount to contradiction" if the same appears to be significant and otherwise relevant having regard to the context in which such omission occurs, and whether any omission amounts to a contradiction in the particular context shall be a question of fact.

steps.title: Bar inducement and never block a voluntary statement
steps.text: No inducement to be offered [BNSS 182]: Sub-section (1) is an absolute prohibition: no police officer or other person in authority shall offer or make, or cause to be offered or made, any such inducement, threat or promise as is mentioned in section 22 of the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023. Sub-section (2) imposes the mirror-image prohibition on suppression, and widens the class of persons bound by dropping the words "in authority": "But no police officer or other person shall prevent, by any caution or otherwise, any person from making in the course of any investigation under this Chapter any statement which he may be disposed to make of his own free will". The section therefore bars the officer both from procuring a statement by inducement, threat or promise and from discouraging or cautioning a willing person out of making one. The single proviso qualifies only sub-section (2): "Provided that nothing in this sub-section shall affect the provisions of sub-section (4) of section 183" - that is, the requirement that a confession be recorded in the manner provided in section 316, be signed by the person making it, and carry the Magistrate's memorandum at the foot of the record (verified against section 183(4) as printed on PDF page 71).

legal_basis: Section 182 BNSS 2023
steps.triage_why: Any inducement or threat used to obtain a statement renders that statement inadmissible and can defeat the entire prosecution.

steps.title: Send the FIR report and proceed to the spot
steps.text: On reason to suspect the commission of a cognizable offence the officer in charge shall forthwith send the report (FIR) to the Magistrate empowered to take cognizance of the offence upon a police report, and proceed in person to the spot to investigate the facts and circumstances and, if necessary, take steps for the discovery and arrest of the offender, or depute a subordinate officer not below the rank prescribed by the State Government.

steps.title: Record and intimate a decision not to investigate
steps.text: Where it appears there is no sufficient ground for entering upon a police investigation, the officer in charge shall not investigate the case; the SHO shall record the particulars and reasons in the prescribed register (Gujarat Annexure-2) and shall intimate the complainant, if any, of the decision not to investigate, recording the date, time and medium of that intimation in the register.

steps.triage_why: This governs the decision NOT to investigate; the case has already been registered and requires investigation.

ticks.do: Do not investigate the case where it appears there is no sufficient ground for entering upon a police investigation (BNSS 176(1)(b)).

Intimate the complainant, if any, of the decision not to investigate.
Record the date, time and medium of that intimation in the register.

steps.title: Fix and observe the investigation completion period
steps.text: The district SSP/SP shall personally fix the time period for completing each investigation keeping in view the gravity and sensitivity of the case; investigation work must compulsorily be completed within that period, and only the SSP/SP may extend it where a justified reason exists.
steps.deadline: Within the period prescribed by the district SSP/SP; extension only by the SSP/SP for justified reasons

steps.text: Classify serious/heinous offences and entrust their investigation only to selected, trained, experienced and professionally competent investigators; do not burden such investigators with other duties (VIP security, maintenance of law and order etc.); ensure they are fully equipped with modern scientific tools of investigation.

steps.title: Keep the diary current and never alter it
steps.text: Every police officer making an investigation shall day by day enter his proceedings in the case diary in the prescribed form, setting forth the time the information reached him, the times he began and closed investigation, the places visited, and a statement of the circumstances ascertained. Write the diary promptly, on the very day of investigation, and dispatch it without delay: failure to write day-by-day the facts discovered gives rise to the suspicion that those circumstances did not exist, and delay leads to suspicion by the Court and adversely affects the IO and the prosecution, while day-to-day writing attaches sanctity and credibility to the evidence collected. Changing or delaying case diaries is strictly prohibited.
steps.stage: Case diary: writing, format and contents
legal_basis: Section 172(1) CrPC [now BNSS 192]
steps.deadline: Day by day - on the very day of investigation, dispatched without delay
steps.triage_why: Daily entry in the case diary is a statutory requirement; failure to do so can lead to the evidence being viewed as fabricated or the investigation being questioned in court.

steps.text: Maintain the case diary as a bound volume, duly paginated. steps.title: Write the case diary in full detail
steps.text: Fill every column of the case diary (FIR number, sections, CD serial number and date, times of commencement/conclusion, FIR date, complainant, accused, property lost/recovered with value and nature, deceased, places visited, persons examined and their total number, day's investigation details) and record in it: the time information reached the IO and its gist; the scene visit with description, sketch map, index and photographs; a true record of scene observations with a statement and reasons for the circumstances ascertained; places visited chronologically with date and time; the daily proceedings of investigation; consultation of police-station records and its outcome; details of inquests, searches, seizures, arrests and witness examinations with their places; witness particulars with the complete s.161 CrPC [now BNSS 180] statements inserted; every step including dispatch of the accused, reports, documents and seized articles to experts with dates and times of dispatch and receipt and their opinions; and every addition or alteration of sections of law or of accused brought to the notice of the competent Court by petition. Record witness-statement gists in the third person, clearly mention the grounds of warrantless searches and of arrests, describe scene objects by reference to objects having a fixed position, note the fact of photography/videography, draw the map or plan on a separate sheet with distances as accurate as possible, maintain a correct record of time throughout, mention every clue (even if it appears of no value at the time) and the methods adopted by the suspects, and end each day's diary with a note of further actions yet to be taken and of the dispatch and means of dispatch of copies to superior officers.
steps.stage: Case diary: writing, format and contents
steps.triage_why: Ensures completeness of the record, though missing a specific column is less likely to defeat the prosecution than missing the evidence itself.

steps.title: Document and notify any change of accused
steps.text: For removing, adding or bringing to light the name of any accused during the investigation, the IO records the action and its evidential basis in the case diary (no prior written approval of a designated supervisory officer is required) and the diaries are sent without delay to the supervisory officers for monitoring; if the supervisory officer finds the action wrong or unsupported by sufficient evidence he records his objection with reasons and issues clear directions to the IO. Any addition or alteration of sections of law or of accused must also be brought to the notice of the competent Court by filing a petition.
steps.stage: Case diary: writing, format and contents
steps.triage_why: Provides a transparent audit trail for changes in the accused list, strengthening the case against challenges of malice.

conflicts.description: DG Circular 66/2015 (up_major_crimes_handbook, up-handbook-circulars-p46-p65 p.48) abolishes the earlier requirement of prior written approval for adding, removing or bringing to light an accused's name (SP for murder/rape, Addl SP for dacoity/loot/dowry death, Circle Officer for other crimes), whereas DG Circular 03/2013 (up-handbook-circulars-p106-p116 p.107) requires the SP in charge to record his clear opinion on deleting or adding accused names before the charge sheet/final report in murder and rape cases.
conflicts.resolution: Both are same-tier state_advisory circulars from one document, so the ladder cannot separate them; they are separated by stage and by recency. The later DG 66/2015 governs mid-investigation name changes - no prior approval, supervisory control operating through case-diary monitoring - and is the canonical text here. DG 03/2013's SP opinion survives only as the concluding-report vetting step in murder and rape (canonical step core-documentation-supervision-sp-opinion-final-report), not as a prior approval for changes made during investigation.

steps.title: Take statements promptly and accept affidavit evidence
steps.text: Record the statements of the informant, victim/injured and other important witnesses of fact at the earliest, as far as possible within 24 hours of FIR registration; if that is not possible, furnish a separate written explanation for the late recording of each witness's statement along with that statement. The same discipline applies to statements of the accused and defence witnesses. Also inform the informant and all witnesses that they may submit their evidence on affidavit (sworn before an Oath Commissioner or Public Notary) by e-mail, speed post or registered post; such affidavits must be received and taken into consideration, with liberty to the IO to make further queries.
steps.deadline: Within 24 hours of FIR registration; otherwise a separate written explanation per witness
steps.triage_why: In POCSO and sexual assault cases, early statements of the victim are critical to prevent allegations of tutoring and to capture fresh details of the assault.

steps.text: Provide copies of s.161 CrPC [now BNSS 180] statements simultaneously to the informant and witnesses, with intimation that any objection to the statement or discrepancy found in it should be brought to the IO's notice at the earliest, preferably within a week, along with supporting evidence; make an endorsement to this effect in the case diary.
steps.deadline: Objections preferably within a week of supply of copies
steps.triage_why: While transparency is good practice, providing statements to witnesses during the investigation is not a statutory mandate that, if missed, defeats the prosecution.

ticks.do: Provide copies of s.161 CrPC [now BNSS 180] statements simultaneously to the informant and witnesses.
Intimate that any objection to the statement or discrepancy found in it should be brought to the IO's notice at the earliest, preferably within a week, along with supporting evidence.
Make an endorsement to this effect in the case diary.

steps.title: Collect scene evidence early and map the site
steps.text: Collect each and every material and piece of evidence available at the place of incident at the earliest; if this is not done within 24 hours, furnish a written explanation to that effect. Prepare a site plan of each and every place connected with the crime, showing all the necessary details such as the distance of the witness, injured and aggressor.
steps.deadline: Within 24 hours; otherwise a recorded explanation
steps.triage_why: The victim is injured and the crime occurred in a specific room; forensic evidence (DNA, biological traces) is volatile and will be lost or degraded if not collected promptly.

ticks.do: Collect each and every material and piece of evidence available at the place of incident at the earliest.
Furnish a written explanation to that effect if this is not done within 24 hours.
Prepare a site plan of each and every place connected with the crime, showing all the necessary details such as the distance of the witness, injured and aggressor.

steps.title: Record and preserve witness statement recordings
steps.text: Make an audio/video recording of the statement of every witness as provided by s.161(3) CrPC [now BNSS 180(3)]; write one copy of all audio/video recordings collected during the investigation onto a CD/DVD in the presence of two witnesses and keep it with the case diary, and keep the second CD/DVD on the Special Report (supervision) file.
legal_basis: Section 161(3) CrPC [now BNSS 180(3)]
steps.triage_why: BNSS 180(3) mandates audio-video recording of statements in certain cases; failure to comply with this statutory requirement can jeopardize the admissibility or weight of the evidence.

ticks.do: Make an audio/video recording of the statement of every witness as provided by s.161(3) CrPC [now BNSS 180(3)].
Write one copy of all audio/video recordings collected during the investigation onto a CD/DVD in the presence of two witnesses and keep it with the case diary.
Keep the second CD/DVD on the Special Report (supervision) file.

details.text: For recording statements, issue notice under s.160(1) CrPC [now BNSS 179] in the prescribed format and have it served on the witnesses to call them to the police station; women and children shall in no circumstances be called to the police station for recording of statements - their statements shall be recorded at their place of residence.

steps.title: Secure expert opinion before filing the charge sheet
steps.text: Never close an investigation without having collected the substantive/material evidence, and never send a charge sheet to court without the expert opinion the case requires. Send all relevant material and evidence collected from the site to the appropriate experts (handwriting, ballistic, FSL, fingerprint, DNA etc.) for opinion; have all recovered materials, including viscera in death cases, forensically examined; and investigate the culpability of all connected persons rather than only the person most conveniently available (lapses censured by the Supreme Court in Dayal Singh v. State of Uttaranchal, Crl. Appeal 529/2010). Do not base the investigation only on oral evidence - collect physical evidence (body secretions such as blood, sweat, spit, saliva for DNA sampling, and thumb/foot prints) and send the samples to the FSL without delay in the initial stage of the investigation.
steps.triage_why: In POCSO and rape cases, expert medical/forensic opinion (DNA/FSL) is substantive evidence. Filing a charge sheet without it can lead to acquittal.

ticks.do: Never close an investigation without having collected the substantive or material evidence.
Never send a charge sheet to court without the expert opinion the case requires.
Send all relevant material and evidence collected from the site for opinion to the appropriate experts, such as the following.
sub: handwriting
ballistic
FSL
fingerprint
DNA

ticks.do: Have all recovered materials, including viscera in death cases, forensically examined.
Investigate the culpability of all connected persons rather than only the person most conveniently available.
notes: Such lapses were censured by the Supreme Court in Dayal Singh v. State of Uttaranchal, Crl. Appeal 529/2010.

ticks.do: Do not base the investigation only on oral evidence.

steps.title: Keep FIR and statement records true throughout
steps.text: Record the FIR and witness statements under s.161 CrPC [now BNSS 180] without interpolations or alterations, recording the real facts as explained by the complainant and witnesses, and insert those facts in the case diary maintained under s.172 CrPC [now BNSS 192]; explain any delay in recording the FIR. The written report sent from the spot for lodging the FIR must bear the time, place and date from where it was sent, and must carry an endorsement of the FIR signed by the concerned official.
steps.triage_why: Integrity of the FIR and statements is a statutory requirement. Interpolations or unexplained delays in the FIR are primary targets for defense counsel to impeach the prosecution.

ticks.do: Record the FIR and witness statements under s.161 CrPC [now BNSS 180] without interpolations or alterations, setting down the real facts as explained by the complainant and witnesses.
Insert those facts in the case diary maintained under s.172 CrPC [now BNSS 192].
Explain any delay in recording the FIR.
Ensure the written report sent from the spot for lodging the FIR bears the time, place and date from where it was sent.
Ensure that report carries an endorsement of the FIR signed by the concerned official.

steps.title: Protect the scene, record statements and involve supervisors
steps.text: Apply the three key quality points in every investigation in principle (implementing them first in murder and rape, and extending them to other heinous crimes once the working methods have stabilised): (1) protect the scene of crime, have it photographed and have evidence collected from it by the field unit; (2) serve notice on witnesses under s.160 CrPC [now BNSS 179] and record their statements under s.161 CrPC [now BNSS 180] with an audio/video recording under s.161(3); and (3) ensure active participation of supervisory officers in the investigation. The first responder to reach the spot shall put yellow tape around the scene and prevent any unauthorised person from entering it; the field unit collects the necessary evidence in the IO's presence; keep one copy of the scene photographs with the case diary and the second with the Special Report file. Police officers of other stations or units who reach the scene and obtain information about the incident must transmit it by report to the police station concerned so that it is incorporated in the investigation.
steps.applies_when: All investigations in principle; implement first in murder and rape, then other heinous crimes
steps.triage_why: Protecting the scene and collecting evidence is critical in sexual offence cases to prevent contamination of biological evidence.

sub: (1) Protect the scene of crime, have it photographed and have evidence collected from it by the field unit
(2) Serve notice on witnesses under s.160 CrPC [now BNSS 179] and record their statements under s.161 CrPC [now BNSS 180] with an audio/video recording under s.161(3)
(3) Ensure active participation of supervisory officers in the investigation
notes: Implement them first in murder and rape, and extend them to other heinous crimes once the working methods have stabilised.

steps.title: Apply the correct sections after consulting seniors
steps.text: Apply the right and relevant sections of the IPC [now BNS] and of the applicable local and special Acts; consult the seniors and the legal expert before applying sections, and follow the direction of law as prescribed.
steps.triage_why: Incorrect application of sections (especially mixing BNS and POCSO) can lead to the case being quashed or the accused being released due to faulty charging.

Consult the seniors and the legal expert before applying sections.

steps.title: Verify a birth certificate claiming juvenility
steps.text: Whenever the accused produces a birth certificate for declaring him a juvenile / child in conflict with law, verify it during the investigation from the concerned issuing authority.
steps.triage_why: The victim is 17 (a child under POCSO). If the accused is also a juvenile, the entire trial jurisdiction shifts to the Juvenile Justice Board; failure to verify this is a fundamental legal error.

steps.title: Avoid deferring the doctor's injury opinion in grievous cases
steps.text: Do not follow the practice of deliberately not taking the doctor's opinion on injury in grievous-injury cases, producing the accused in Court for a bailable offence, and thereafter adding a grave offence without re-arresting the accused - the SOP records that such practice puts the credibility of police working in doubt.
steps.triage_why: Failure to obtain a medical opinion on injuries in a rape/assault case undermines the 'force' element of the crime and damages the credibility of the investigation.

Producing the accused in Court for a bailable offence
Thereafter adding a grave offence without re-arresting the accused

steps.title: Secure witnesses and record statements before the Magistrate
steps.text: Ensure the security of the complainant, his family members and the witnesses; if it comes to light that a witness is being obstructed from disclosing the facts of the crime by any kind of threat, promise or inducement, provide immediate protection and ensure other prompt legal action; take effective measures to strengthen the confidence of the victim and the public in the investigation so that the complainant and witnesses can present their evidence free of fear. Where even a possibility appears of the complainant or witnesses being influenced, have their statements recorded before the Magistrate under s.164 CrPC [now BNSS 183].
steps.triage_why: In POCSO cases, witness/victim intimidation is common. Failure to protect the victim can lead to her turning hostile, which effectively defeats the prosecution.

Provide immediate protection and ensure other prompt legal action where a witness is being obstructed from disclosing the facts of the crime by any kind of threat, promise or inducement.

steps.title: Prepare and dispatch case diaries in duplicate
steps.text: Write case diaries promptly in the prescribed form and dispatch them without delay. Prepare each date's case diary, with the witness statements, in duplicate: the original is retained by the IO in the case file at the station and the duplicate goes to the supervisory officer (SDPO), who scrutinises it, gives the IO the necessary instructions and retains it in the office file; where the investigating Sub-Inspector is himself the SHO of the police station, forward the case diaries directly to the SDPO concerned.

steps.deadline: Dispatch without delay; officers of supervisory rank forward copies on the day of the case diary itself
steps.triage_why: Maintaining the case diary is a statutory duty under BNSS 192. Gaps in the diary can be used to argue that the investigation was fabricated or delayed.

ticks.do: Write case diaries promptly in the prescribed form and dispatch them without delay.
notes: Officers of supervisory rank forward copies on the day of the case diary itself.

steps.title: Maintain and enclose Supplementary Case Diaries
steps.text: Every investigating officer entrusted with part investigation of a case shall maintain a case diary for the investigation made by him, called a Supplementary Case Diary (SCD), and shall submit it without any delay; the Chief Investigating Officer takes SCDs on record, may incorporate the gist of important facts disclosed in them in his own case diary for the date the SCD is received, and must invariably enclose the SCDs received with the copies of his diary sent to the supervisory officer.
steps.stage: Case diary: dispatch, supplementary diaries and closure
steps.deadline: SCDs submitted without any delay
steps.triage_why: This is an internal coordination procedure for multi-officer investigations; while important for management, it is not a statutory duty to the court.

Submit that Supplementary Case Diary without any delay.

Incorporate the gist of important facts disclosed in them in your own case diary for the date the SCD is received.

steps.title: Write the concluding case diary with reasons
steps.text: In the concluding diary record a summary of the reasons which have guided the final decision in the case; where the IO considers there is no case, the reasons must be more detailed and fact-based than in a case sent up for trial. Write the last case diary: (i) in charge-sheeted cases on the date of filing the charge sheet, case diaries continuing if further investigation proceeds under s.173(8) CrPC [now BNSS 193(9)] until it is completed; and (ii) where prosecution is not launched, on the date the competent Court passes the closure order on the Final Report.

steps.deadline: On the date of filing the charge sheet, or on the date of the Court's closure order on the Final Report
steps.triage_why: The concluding diary and the reasoning for the final report are essential for judicial scrutiny and the legal validity of the charge sheet.

steps.title: Guard the case diary and limit its access
steps.text: Treat every case diary as confidential until the final disposal of the case including the appeal, if any, or until the expiry of the period of appeal. The IO and his superiors shall ensure the physical safety of the case diary and its contents; permit no access to any unauthorized person, particularly the accused, their agents or their counsel (the accused cannot claim an unfettered right to inspect the case diary: Balakram v. State of Uttarakhand, 2017(5) SCALE 220). Access is limited to: the IO; the officer in charge of the police station; any police officer superior to him; the Court Officer (the senior-most prosecuting officer and his junior deputed to prosecute the case); staff specially authorised to deal with such diaries; and any other officer authorised by the Superintendent of Police.
steps.stage: Case diary: custody, confidentiality and court use
steps.deadline: Confidential until final disposal including appeal, or expiry of the appeal period
steps.triage_why: Confidentiality is standard procedure, but a leak of the diary, while problematic, does not automatically defeat the prosecution's legal standing.

steps.title: Apply the limits on court use of diaries
steps.text: Know the legal position on court use of the case diary: any Criminal Court may send for the diaries of a case under inquiry or trial and use them, not as evidence in the case, but to aid it in such inquiry or trial (s.172(2) CrPC [now BNSS 192]) - including to discover relevant evidence, put necessary questions to a witness, clear up ambiguities in evidence, see whether a witness has turned hostile, decide whether police-custody remand is necessary, decide bail (without disclosing the contents of the case diary in bail orders passed during investigation), see whether there is a case justifying framing of a charge, and summon additional persons as accused. Neither the accused nor his agents are entitled to call for or see the diaries merely because the Court refers to them; the privilege goes only if the police officer who made them uses them to refresh his memory or the Court uses them to contradict him - and then the accused may see only the particular entry referred to and so much of the diary as, in the Court's opinion, is necessary for full understanding of that entry, and no more. The prosecution cannot use the case diary as supporting evidence, and it cannot be used to refresh the memory of, or to contradict, any witness other than the police officer who made it; the prosecution may, with the Court's permission, use a recorded statement to contradict a hostile witness (s.162 CrPC).

legal_basis: Section 172(2),(3) CrPC [now BNSS 192]
Sections 145, 159, 160, 161 Indian Evidence Act, 1872
steps.triage_why: Provides legal background on how courts use case diaries; not a procedural action for the IO.

see whether a witness has turned hostile
decide whether police-custody remand is necessary

summon additional persons as accused

steps.title: Hold and track movement of case diary files
steps.text: Keep case diaries in the personal custody of the IO; he or a police officer deputed by him takes them to court on hearing dates, and the Prosecutor peruses them at the time of preparing the charge sheet or before/on the hearing date; the IO may also take the case diary in person to the Public Prosecutor to brief him on the case. In cases committed to the Court of Sessions send the diary to the Public Prosecutor under acknowledgement; on disposal he returns it to the SHO through the Court Officer. Whenever the CD file is transferred from one office to another, maintain the Movement Register of the CD File (on the lines of the Local Delivery Book), clearly giving the details and dates of transfer and taking the signature of the person receiving the file in each office without fail; supervisory officers monitor the movement of CD files from time to time.

steps.title: Oppose bail and move for its cancellation
steps.text: To oppose bail effectively, present before the court a clear written report incorporating the evidence against the accused, his role in the offence and his criminal history, together with the relevant records, and establish coordination with the concerned Public Prosecutor. A bail order passed by ignoring the relevant facts, evidence and law presented by the prosecution, or by considering irrelevant facts, evidence and law, is legally flawed; if the order is so flawed, or the accused while on bail influences prosecution evidence, intimidates or threatens the victim, the victim's family or prosecution witnesses, tampers with or vitiates evidence, violates the conditions of bail or otherwise misuses it, or creates law and order problems, ensure legal proceedings including cancellation of his bail.
steps.stage: Case diary: custody, confidentiality and court use
steps.triage_why: Strengthens the opposition to bail, but is a tactical preference rather than a statutory duty.

his role in the offence
his criminal history

Ensure legal proceedings including cancellation of the accused's bail on any of the following grounds.

the accused while on bail influences prosecution evidence
the accused intimidates or threatens the victim, the victim's family or prosecution witnesses
the accused tampers with or vitiates evidence
the accused violates the conditions of bail or otherwise misuses it
the accused creates law and order problems

details.text: Bail factors the court weighs (State of U.P. v. Amarmani Tripathi): prima facie or reasonable ground to believe the accused committed the offence; nature and gravity of the charge; severity of the punishment on conviction; danger of the accused absconding; character, behaviour, means, position and standing of the accused; likelihood of the offence being repeated; reasonable apprehension of the witnesses being tampered with; and danger of justice being thwarted.

steps.title: Attend bail arguments and record the outcome
steps.text: On receiving information that a bail application has been filed, personally visit the concerned Public Prosecutor and be present in Court at the time of the bail arguments; if unavoidably engaged, detail a responsible officer with the necessary notes to meet the Public Prosecutor and record in the CD file the reason and the name of the officer authorised to attend Court. steps.title: Submit copies for the accused and victim
steps.text: With the police report, submit to the Magistrate as many duly listed copies of the report and the accompanying documents as are necessary for furnishing to the accused (a report and documents submitted through electronic communication are deemed duly served). Where proceedings are commenced on a police report the Magistrate shall, without delay and in any case within 14 days from the date the accused is produced or appears, furnish free of cost to the accused and to the victim (if represented by an advocate) copies of the police report, the FIR recorded under BNSS 173, the BNSS 180(3) statements of all persons the prosecution proposes to examine (excluding any part whose exclusion the police officer has requested under BNSS 193(7)), the confessions and statements recorded under BNSS 183, and any other document or relevant extract forwarded with the police report under BNSS 193(6); where a document is too voluminous the Magistrate may instead order copies to be furnished electronically or allow inspection in Court personally or through an advocate.

steps.title: Open and supervise Special Report crime files
steps.text: Treat the heinous/sensational crimes designated in the State's police regulations (together with the other categories placed in the Special Report category from time to time by order or circular) as Special Report cases upon their registration at the police station: send information immediately to senior officers, open a Special Report file, and investigate the case in depth and in a time-bound manner under closer and deeper supervision by senior officers, the investigator receiving correct guidance. The Circle Officer writes the Special Report case file (supervision notes) in his own hand, and where the investigator is a gazetted officer the Dy.SP/Additional SP completes the file personally with appropriate directions; all successive progress reports are approved every month by the district SSP/SP only - not cursorily by the Additional SP - and range/zone-level supervisors open their own Special Report crime files, monitor them every month and issue directions to subordinates. Along with the quality of investigation ensure one-hundred-percent arrest of the accused; take departmental action against investigators who show laxity in investigation and against officers who take no interest in supervision work, adverse remarks in the annual confidential assessment of negligent supervising officers being considered. Zonal IGs and Range DIGs shall, at the time of district inspections or visits, also review the case files of some Special Report crimes whose monitoring is not being done by them.

conflicts.description: The circulars disagree on which paragraph of the Police Regulations designates the Special Report crimes: DG Circulars 73/2007 (up-handbook-circulars-p106-p116 p.112), 15/2008 (p.111), 44/2015 (up-handbook-circulars-p46-p65 p.55) and 40/2016 (up-handbook-circulars-p26-p45 p.35) all cite paragraph 101, while ADG Circular 12/2001 (up-handbook-circulars-p106-p116 p.114) cites paragraph 100.
conflicts.resolution: All are same-tier state_advisory sources within one document. The canonical text is worded generically ('the crimes designated in the State's police regulations'), so the paragraph-number variance does not change the requirement; the later and more numerous circulars (paragraph 101) are the operative citation and the variance is recorded here for traceability rather than resolved by the ladder.

steps.title: Run the pendency review ladder for pending investigations
steps.text: Run a standing pendency-review ladder for investigations: the SHO/Inspector-in-charge reviews at his own level all investigations, including special crime cases, pending more than 45 days and sends a weekly report showing the reasons for pendency to the Circle Officer; the Circle Officer holds at least 2 order rooms per month for his circle and sends the Additional SP a monthly list of all investigations pending more than 3 months with reasons; the Additional SP holds a monthly order room reviewing that 3-month list and forwards the list of investigations pending more than 6 months, with reasons, to the SSP/SP; the SSP/SP holds an order room at least once a month reviewing the over-6-month cases in depth, takes action against the investigators at fault, and sends the list to the Range DIG, who reviews each such investigation in depth and obtains a weekly progress report from the SSP/SP. Where pendency is due to awaited FSL or other expert reports in serious crime, the SSP/SP, Range DIG and Zonal IG shall themselves establish coordination with the FSL and expert units and have the reports obtained promptly; the Circle Officer, Additional SP and SSP/SP take action according to the rules against negligent investigators whose cases are found pending without reason, and Range DIGs and Zonal IGs review compliance during their tours and report negligence to headquarters.
steps.deadline: SHO report weekly (>45 days); CO at least 2 order rooms per month and a monthly list of cases over 3 months; Addl SP monthly order room; SSP/SP order room at least once a month (>6 months); Range DIG weekly progress reports
steps.responsible: SHO; Circle Officer; Additional SP; SSP/SP; Range DIG; Zonal IG
steps.triage_why: Administrative review process for supervisors; not a step for the Investigating Officer to execute in the case file.

notes: The SSP/SP, Range DIG and Zonal IG shall themselves establish that coordination.

notes: The Circle Officer, Additional SP and SSP/SP take this action.

steps.title: Order and supervise transfer of an investigation
steps.text: Transfer of an investigation is ordered only by the district SSP/SP - never at Circle Officer or Additional SP level and, as a rule, never on the request of the accused party - by a written speaking order, a copy of which must invariably be sent to the range-level supervisory officer, and only once within the district (from one police station to another or to the Crime Branch). The SSP/SP personally supervises transferred investigations and ensures they are completed impartially within 2 months for heinous crimes and 1 month for ordinary crimes. Transfer outside the district is done only once, by the range-level officer (with a copy of the order to the zonal officer), who likewise supervises to the same time limits. Transfer orders are not ordinarily issued from state police headquarters or zonal level and may be issued from there only where the impartiality of the investigation is in doubt; re-transfer of an investigation requires the approval of the state police chief on a reasoned proposal routed through the supervisory chain with recommendations. Higher formations compile lists of transferred investigations, obtain the explanation of the officer concerned where the time limits are exceeded, and report quarterly.
steps.deadline: Transferred investigations: heinous crimes within 2 months, ordinary crimes within 1 month; quarterly compilation to state headquarters
steps.responsible: District SSP/SP; Range DIG; Zonal IG
steps.triage_why: Administrative rule regarding the authority to transfer investigations.

conflicts.description: DG Circular 27/2014 (up_major_crimes_handbook, up-handbook-circulars-p66-p85 p.66) provides that transfer of an investigation - including to the Crime Branch - is ordered by the district SSP/SP alone, by written order with a copy to the Range DIG, whereas the earlier DG Circular 75/2013 (same file, p.69) allows the district SP to transfer investigations to the Crime Branch only after the approval of the Range DIG.
conflicts.resolution: Both are same-tier state_advisory circulars in one document, so the ladder cannot separate them; the later DG 27/2014 governs the canonical text (SSP/SP orders the transfer, copy to the Range DIG). The earlier prior-approval requirement is not carried into the canonical step and its Crime Branch entrustment scheme is listed in unmerged as UP-organisational detail.

steps.title: Review disposal and arrests at the circle orderly room
steps.text: The district police chief shall hold a monthly orderly room at the headquarters of every circle/tehsil (in proper uniform, without summoning the personnel to district headquarters) reviewing the status of disposal of investigations, part-pending investigations, disposal of applications, and the arrest of warrantees, wanted criminals and criminals carrying declared rewards. Every IO attends with his own case diary and investigation register for in-depth review; the SP obtains a written certificate from all Circle Officers who, after examining the crime registers, report the pendency of investigations, part-pending cases, arrests remaining and the reasons, and where negligence is being committed; the officers with the most pending cases are proceeded against. A compliance report is sent by the 2nd of each month, the Range DIG reviews these points during his tours and reports negligence to the police chief, and the status of cases in which charge sheets remain to be filed is reviewed as a campaign.
steps.deadline: Every month; compliance report by the 2nd of the month
steps.responsible: District SSP/SP; Circle Officers; Range DIG
steps.triage_why: Administrative duty of the district police chief regarding general management, not a case-specific investigative step.

steps.title: Monitor case diaries and record reasoned supervisory remarks
steps.text: Supervisory officers who receive a copy of the FIR shall read its contents and ensure prompt receipt of the case diaries; as and when diaries are received, note the date and initial them, read them promptly and thoroughly and pass remarks wherever necessary - remarks being more advisory in form than fault-finding unless there are glaring omissions and commissions. Record the gist of the case diaries in your own hand in the crime register or the Special Report file (with approval by an officer senior to you) together with specific, meaningful and reasoned directions that set the direction of the investigation; do not record only general and vague directions as a ritual formality. Supervision must not remain limited to directing quick disposal - it must evaluate the quality and fairness of the investigation - and supervisory officers must use their training, experience and legal knowledge to make effective and meaningful interventions.
legal_basis: Section 158 CrPC (cited in the source as the provision under which the supervisory officer monitors case diaries)
steps.triage_why: Supervisory duty regarding the review of case diaries; does not constitute a statutory duty of the IO to collect evidence.

steps.title: Enforce legal compliance and train Investigating Officers
steps.text: In all cases the IO shall adhere to strict compliance with the provisions of the criminal procedure law, the Police Act and the Regulations relating to investigation, and superior police authorities shall develop an effective monitoring system to ensure that compliance, curing willful and intentional violations at the earliest and taking appropriate action against the erring IO. Organise training programmes regularly to update Investigating Officers on new enactments, amendments and the latest judgments; hold periodical coordination meetings between the investigation, prosecution, forensic and supervisory wings; keep organising workshops of investigators and supervisory officers; and brief Circle Officers, SHOs, IOs and staff in the monthly crime review meeting so that compliance is complete.
steps.triage_why: General mandate for legal compliance and training; not a specific action step for this case.

ticks.do: Adhere, as the IO, to strict compliance with the provisions of the criminal procedure law, the Police Act and the Regulations relating to investigation in all cases.
Develop an effective monitoring system, as superior police authorities, to ensure that compliance.
Cure willful and intentional violations at the earliest and take appropriate action against the erring IO.
Organise training programmes regularly to update Investigating Officers on new enactments, amendments and the latest judgments.
Hold periodical coordination meetings between the investigation, prosecution, forensic and supervisory wings.
Keep organising workshops of investigators and supervisory officers.
Brief Circle Officers, SHOs, IOs and staff in the monthly crime review meeting so that compliance is complete.

details.text: Keep the district surveillance (technical) cell active, through which authenticated evidence against the offender can be gathered and the quality of investigation improved.

steps.title: Issue reasoned observations and enforce compliance by the IO
steps.text: While monitoring case diaries, if the supervisory officer finds any statement or evidence irrelevant, or finds additional statements or evidence necessary in the interest of the investigation, he may record his Observation with reasons in the crime register and send clear directions accordingly to the IO. Consideration of every lawful order of the supervisory officer during the investigation is mandatory for the IO; if the IO does not comply and presents no adequate reason, the supervisory officers have full authority to take action against him, to withhold his integrity certificate and to hand the investigation over to another IO.
steps.triage_why: Supervisory procedure for directing the IO; not a direct investigative action.

ticks.do: Consider recording your Observation with reasons in the crime register where, while monitoring case diaries, you make either of these findings:
sub: Any statement or evidence on record is irrelevant
Additional statements or evidence are necessary in the interest of the investigation
notes: The source leaves this to the supervisory officer: he 'may' record such an Observation.

ticks.do: Send clear directions accordingly to the IO where you record such an Observation.
notes: This too rests with the supervisory officer's discretion.

ticks.do: Give consideration to every lawful order of the supervisory officer during the investigation, which is mandatory for the IO.
Take action against the IO, withhold his integrity certificate and hand the investigation over to another IO where he does not comply and presents no adequate reason.

steps.title: Supervise serious and heinous crime investigations in person
steps.text: In serious and heinous crime: on the occurrence of the incident the supervising officer must in every case promptly inspect the scene and have the available witnesses and exhibits collected, taking the help of the local forensic team as required; hold frequent meetings with the Investigating Officers and issue specific directions for unravelling the crime and for a quality investigation - an entry regarding those specific directions must be made in the case diary; review the action taken at every step of the investigation; and obtain legal and expert-specialist advice as required, ensuring the use of modern scientific evidence (DNA test, photographs, footprints, fingerprints, polygraph, brain mapping, narco-analysis etc.) in appropriate cases.
steps.applies_when: Serious/heinous crime investigations
steps.triage_why: This is a POCSO case involving physical injury; prompt scene inspection and forensic collection are critical to prevent degradation of physical evidence.

ticks.do: Inspect the scene promptly in every case on the occurrence of a serious or heinous incident.
Have the available witnesses and exhibits collected, taking the help of the local forensic team as required.
Hold frequent meetings with the Investigating Officers and issue specific directions for unravelling the crime and for a quality investigation.
Make an entry in the case diary regarding those specific directions.
Review the action taken at every step of the investigation.
Obtain legal and expert-specialist advice as required.
Ensure the use of modern scientific evidence in appropriate cases, such as:
sub: DNA test
Photographs
Footprints
Fingerprints
Polygraph
Brain mapping
Narco-analysis

steps.title: Scrutinise investigations and establish a scrutiny cell
steps.text: Scrutiny of the investigation by the supervisory officer at its different stages, during the course of the investigation, is mandatory; investigations of serious and sensitive crimes must be intensively reviewed and closely supervised by senior officers. Obtain the assistance of the legal expert posted in the office of the state/district police chief for that scrutiny, and establish a scrutiny cell, which may consist of a Deputy Superintendent of Police, Investigating Officers and a legal functionary.
steps.triage_why: Administrative requirement for supervisory scrutiny and legal expert consultation.

Obtain the assistance of the legal expert posted in the office of the state or district police chief for that scrutiny.
Establish a scrutiny cell.
notes: The cell may consist of a Deputy Superintendent of Police, Investigating Officers and a legal functionary.

steps.title: Record further statements without repeated supervisory approvals
steps.text: Where the IO finds during investigation that witness statements or documentary evidence beyond the approved action plan are needed, he prepares a questionnaire for those witnesses and records their statements under s.161 CrPC [now BNSS 180] as necessary; no repeated approvals from the designated officers are required for recording such further statements or collecting such evidence (the earlier requirement of prior approval under ADG Circular 02/2013 point 9(1)(B) having been modified). Supervisory control operates through case-diary monitoring, not through prior approval.
steps.triage_why: Standard practice for expanding the evidence base via witness statements to strengthen the prosecution.

ticks.do: Prepare a questionnaire for the witnesses where witness statements or documentary evidence beyond the approved action plan are found necessary during the investigation.
Record the statements of those witnesses under s.161 CrPC [now BNSS 180] as necessary.
Proceed without repeated approvals from the designated officers for recording such further statements or collecting such evidence.
notes: The earlier requirement of prior approval under ADG Circular 02/2013 point 9(1)(B) has been modified.
Supervisory control operates through case-diary monitoring, not through prior approval.

steps.title: Route the confidential report for the SP's opinion
steps.text: Before concluding the investigation, the investigator prepares on the basis of the available evidence a Confidential report recording his clear recommendation and sends it up the chain (investigator to Circle Officer to Additional SP to the SP in charge of the district); on the basis of those comments and the evidence, the SP records his clear opinion on deleting or adding the name of any accused, reducing or enhancing the offence sections, and on sending a charge sheet or a final report, and the report is returned down the same chain; the Circle Officer ensures the SP's opinion is formally made available to the investigator by letter, and the investigator submits the charge sheet or final report on that basis.
steps.responsible: IO; Circle Officer; Additional SP; district SP
steps.applies_when: Investigations of murder and rape (DG Circular 03/2013)
steps.triage_why: Internal police procedure for recommending charges; while important for administration, the legal basis for prosecution is the evidence collected.

Send that report up the chain in this order:
sub: Investigator
Circle Officer
Additional SP
SP in charge of the district

Reducing or enhancing the offence sections
Sending a charge sheet or a final report

ticks.do: Return the report down the same chain.

steps.title: Examine the successor when the author is unavailable
steps.text: Where a document or report of a public servant, police officer, medical officer or scientific expert is to be used in evidence and its author has been transferred, has retired or has died, cannot be found, is unable to give evidence, or where keeping him present is likely to delay the trial or other proceedings, the deposition is secured from the successor - the officer who at the time of the evidence holds the post the author held - through whose evidence the report is admissible; the successor's evidence may be recorded by audio-video electronic means. In case of any ambiguity about who the successor is, the head of the concerned department or the SHO determines the officer who is to depose under BNSS 336.
steps.stage: Trial stage: evidence of public servants and court liaison
legal_basis: BNSS 336
steps.responsible: Court; head of department / SHO (identifying the successor)
steps.triage_why: Procedural rule for handling evidence when a public servant/expert is unavailable.

ticks.do: Secure the deposition from the successor, the officer who at the time of the evidence holds the post the author held, through whose evidence the report is admissible.
notes: Applies where a document or report of a public servant, police officer, medical officer or scientific expert is to be used in evidence.

ticks.do: Apply this where the author is in any of these situations:
sub: Has been transferred

steps.title: Examine a substitute witness where no successor exists
steps.text: When there is no successor, prove the earlier police officer's document/report under Section 41 BSA 2023 by examining as a witness any police officer who satisfies one of these points: (a) he is acquainted with the handwriting or signature of the person by whom the report was written; (b) he saw the document being written or prepared, such writing or preparation having taken place in his presence; (c) by reason of holding the post of an authority he received the document or report in reply to documents written by him; or (d) it was submitted to him in the routine course by the person who prepared it and he received it in the ordinary course of business.

legal_basis: Section 41 BSA 2023
steps.triage_why: Evidentiary rule under BSA 2023 for proving documents when no successor is available.

steps.title: Submit every report through the appointed superior officer
steps.text: Report how submitted. [BNSS 177]: Every report sent to a Magistrate under section 176 SHALL, if the State Government so directs, be submitted through such superior officer of police as the State Government, by general or special order, appoints in that behalf. The routing requirement is conditional on a State Government direction existing, but is mandatory once that direction exists. Such superior officer MAY give such instructions to the officer in charge of the police station as he thinks fit, and SHALL, after recording such instructions on such report, transmit the same without delay to the Magistrate. The instruction-giving is therefore permissive while the recording-and-transmission is mandatory.
legal_basis: Section 177 BNSS 2023
steps.deadline: The superior officer of police shall transmit the report to the Magistrate "without delay" after recording his instructions on it (sub-s (2)) - a promptness requirement; no numeric period is prescribed.
steps.triage_why: This is a procedural routing requirement for the final report to the Magistrate, conditional on State Government orders; it does not affect the immediate investigation of the crime.

notes: The instruction-giving is permissive.

ticks.do: Record such instructions on such report and transmit the report without delay to the Magistrate.

steps.title: Track what the Magistrate may do next
steps.text: Power to hold investigation or preliminary inquiry. [BNSS 178]: The Magistrate, on receiving a report under section 176, MAY direct an investigation, or, if he thinks fit, MAY at once proceed, or MAY depute any Magistrate subordinate to him to proceed, to hold a preliminary inquiry into, or otherwise to dispose of, the case in the manner provided in the Sanhita. Every limb of the section is permissive - the Magistrate is given options, not obligations - and the whole power is triggered by receipt of the section 176 report. No time limit and no form is prescribed.
legal_basis: Section 178 BNSS 2023
steps.triage_why: This describes the Magistrate's discretionary powers upon receiving a report, not a mandatory investigative step for the officer.

steps.title: Lift and pack physical evidence as directed
steps.text: Lift and pack the physical evidence strictly in accordance with the procedure laid down under the law and as directed by the forensic expert.
legal_basis: s.27 Indian Evidence Act [now the proviso to BSA 23] — recovery pursuant to disclosure
s.65-B Indian Evidence Act [now BSA 63(4)] — certificate for electronic records
s.172 Cr.P.C. [now BNSS 192] — case diary record of scene and recovery proceedings
steps.triage_why: Failure to properly lift and pack physical evidence in a sexual assault/POCSO case leads to contamination or loss of DNA/forensic evidence, which is critical for prosecution.

ticks.do: Lift and pack the physical evidence strictly in accordance with the procedure laid down under the law and as directed by the forensic expert.

steps.title: Requisition the Polygraph Division only after full investigation
steps.text: Requisition the services of the Polygraph Division only after making a thorough investigation and after collecting the relevant documents including physical evidence, mobile call details, PM report, inquest report, injury report and age certificates — in the absence of such details it is extremely difficult for the examiner to formulate proper questions and unreveal inconsistencies in the statements of the subject.
legal_basis: Article 20(3) of the Constitution of India — protection against self-incrimination; written voluntary consent of the subject required

Smt. Selvi and others v. State of Karnataka (Criminal Appeal No 1267 of 2004), full bench of the Hon'ble Supreme Court, order dated 5 May 2010 — no individual should be forcibly subjected to polygraph, narco analysis or brain electrical activation profile tests; voluntary administration permitted with safeguards; results by themselves not admissible as evidence (source: All India Reporter, July 2010, pp. 2060-1)
Indian Evidence Act, 1872 s.27 — information or material subsequently discovered with the help of voluntarily administered test results may be admitted [now the proviso to BSA 23]
National Human Rights Commission Guidelines for administration of Polygraph Test (Lie Detector Tests) on an accused, letter no. 117/8/97-8 dated 11/01/2000
Criminal Procedure Code s.161 — statements of subject(s) recorded by the police, to be attached to the requisition [now BNSS 180]
steps.deadline: Only after making a thorough investigation and after collecting the relevant documents (physical evidence, mobile call details, PM report, inquest report, injury report, age certificates)
steps.applies_when: Where a polygraph (lie-detector) examination of an accused, suspect, witness or victim is being considered or requisitioned in the case.
steps.triage_why: This is a guideline for the effectiveness of a polygraph; missing it makes the test less useful but doesn't legally defeat the prosecution.

ticks.do: Requisition the services of the Polygraph Division only after making a thorough investigation and after collecting the relevant documents.

steps.text: Understand that Lie Detection is a psycho-biological test to check the veracity of statements on computerized equipment known as a lie-detector or polygraph, and that the lie detector measures the following autonomic nervous system activities in the form of graphs — abdominal respiration, thoracic respiration, galvanic skin resistance (GSR), blood pressure/pulse rate, muscular pressure, finger pulse and skin temperature.

steps.title: Never force a polygraph test on anyone
steps.text: Do not forcibly subject any individual to a polygraph test: a full bench of the Hon'ble Supreme Court of India in Smt. Selvi and others versus State of Karnataka (Criminal Appeal No 1267 of 2004), order dated 5 May 2010, held that no individual should be forcibly subjected to any of the techniques in question, whether in context of investigation in criminal cases or otherwise, as doing so would amount to an unwarranted intrusion into personal liberty; room is left for the voluntary administration of the impugned techniques in the context of criminal justice, provided that certain safeguards are in place.
legal_basis: Article 20(3) of the Constitution of India — protection against self-incrimination; written voluntary consent of the subject required

steps.title: Note the evidentiary limits of test results
steps.text: Note the limits of the result: even when the subject has given consent to undergo any of these tests, the results by themselves cannot be admitted as evidence because the subject does not exercise conscious control over the responses during the administration of the test; however, any information or material that is subsequently discovered with the help of voluntary administered test results can be admitted in accordance with Section 27 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872 [now the proviso to BSA 23].

steps.title: Digitise the charge sheet for online crimes
steps.text: In crimes involving digital data, especially online crimes, prepare the charge sheet digitally as well, and document the data and evidence in digital format simultaneously.
legal_basis: Section 111 BNS — human trafficking as an organized crime. NOTE ON PROVENANCE: this framing is NOT printed in pp.101-130; it is the book's premise stated at PDF pp.5, 13 and 40 ('Since human trafficking is an organized crime, u/s 111 BNS…'; 'Section 111 BNS defines the constituents of organized crime, which includes "human trafficking for prostitution"'; 'The trafficker is liable under 143 BNS / 111 BNS'). Section 143 BNS (370 IPC) is the definition of trafficking; 144 BNS (370A IPC) is exploitation of a trafficked person
S.7 ITPA and S.18(2) ITPA — action to be moved through the prosecutor once the court decides on the offence (printed 'u/s.7 ITPA, 18(2) ITPA etc.', p.102)
S.19 ITPA — application to the Magistrate for a protective home / corrective institution / supervision; S.17(4) ITPA — such order may also be made suo moto by the Magistrate (p.103)
section 366 BNSS / 327(2) of the CrPC — mandates in-camera trials in all rape cases (printed exactly thus, p.103)
S.160 CrPC (179 BNSS) — female victim not to be called to the police station after evening (p.105)
S.157 of the CrPC (176 BNSS) and S.24 of the POCSO Act — rape victims and child victims of sexual abuse to be interviewed at a place of her choice (p.105)
S 398 BNSS — witness protection section; Witness Protection Scheme, 2018 legally mandatory for the union, all States and UTs (Mahender Chawla Vs Union of India, p.107)

Section 357A CrPC (introduced 2009) — victim compensation; the source itself states 'Under BNSS, Section 396 deals with the subject' (p.107); section 357A(5) of the CrPC [now s.396(5) BNSS] — DLSA enquiry to be completed within two months (p.108)
POCSO Act S.33(8) read with Rule 7 of the POCSO Rules — compensation ordered by the Special Court hearing the POCSO case (p.109)
section 192 BNSS [= 172 CrPC] — Case Diary, operational part (pp.127-128)
Sections 180 and 183 BNSS [= 161 and 164 CrPC] — statements of victim/witness (p.127; the recording protocol is carried in the companion entry 'trafficking-interrogation-skills')
Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2015 — trafficked child is a 'child in need of care and protection', not a 'child in conflict with the law' (p.106)
steps.applies_when: Crimes involving digital data, especially online crimes
steps.triage_why: Best practice for digital crimes to ensure data integrity, but the physical charge-sheet remains the primary legal record.

ticks.do: Prepare the charge sheet digitally as well in crimes involving digital data, especially online crimes.
Document the data and evidence in digital format simultaneously.

steps.title: Consult the prosecutor on complex charge-sheets
steps.text: In important cases of a complex nature involving questions of law and fact, prepare the charge-sheet in consultation with the Assistant Public Prosecutor and with the Public Prosecutor wherever necessary; send the case diary file along with the charge-sheet and give the prosecutor sufficient time to scrutinise it.
steps.triage_why: Sound practice for complex cases to ensure legal viability, but not a statutory requirement for the IO.

details.text: Consultation is required in: (1) cases exclusively triable by the Court of Sessions; (2) cases under Section 120B IPC; (3) grave crimes; (4) case-and-counter-case situations where it must be decided whether both or only one is to be charge-sheeted; (5) cases involving complicated questions of law or fact; (6) any other case where the IO, SDPO, DCP or SP desires it; (7) any case where the Prosecutor, Director or Deputy Director of Prosecution considers it necessary.

details.text: Consult the APP or PP if necessary even at the investigation stage, so that the investigation is conducted on proper lines and the evidence the law requires is collected.
