steps.title: Keep the trial moving when an accused absconds
steps.text: Where despite all efforts the presence of one of the accused cannot be secured, set the absconder procedure in motion and split the charge-sheet so the trial of the accused who are present is not delayed; the court can then record regular evidence against the accused present and order evidence to be recorded under Section 299 Cr.P.C. against the absconding accused.

legal_basis: Section 299 CrPC
steps.applies_when: One or more co-accused cannot be produced despite efforts
steps.triage_why: This is a procedural rule for handling absconders during the trial phase, not a primary investigative step for the IO's immediate checklist.

steps.title: Charge three same-kind offences together
steps.text: Three offences of the same kind committed within a year may be charged together (Section 219 Cr.P.C.). Offences are of the same kind when punishable with the same amount of punishment under the same section of the IPC or of any special or local law; an offence under Section 379 IPC is deemed of the same kind as one under Section 380 IPC, and an offence is deemed of the same kind as an attempt to commit it where the attempt is itself an offence.
steps.stage: Joinder of charges and split charge-sheets
legal_basis: Section 219 CrPC
steps.triage_why: This is a legal definition/rule regarding the joinder of charges for the court's benefit.

ticks.do: Join in one charge three offences of the same kind committed within a year, as Section 219 Cr.P.C. permits.
Treat offences as of the same kind when punishable with the same amount of punishment under the same section of the IPC or of any special or local law.

details.text: Distinguish 'same kind' from 'same offence' (Lalu Prasad Yadav, AIR 2017 SC 3389, 'Fodder Scam'): defalcations in different treasuries were distinct offences, though of the same kind, by different sets of accused, requiring separate charges and separate trials; defalcation across different treasuries, years, amounts, allotment letters, supply orders and suppliers is not the same transaction.

details.text: There may be a larger conspiracy and a smaller one developing in successive stages involving different accused; where defalcations are made in various years by combinations of different accused there can be separate trials (Ram Lal Narang v. steps.title: Group connected offences into one trial
steps.text: Apply Section 220 Cr.P.C. when deciding what may be tried at one trial: (i) more offences than one committed by the same person in one series of acts so connected as to form the same transaction; (ii) criminal breach of trust or dishonest misappropriation together with falsification of accounts committed to facilitate or conceal it; (iii) acts constituting an offence falling within two or more separate definitions of any law; (iv) several acts which, one or more being an offence in themselves, when combined constitute a different offence; and (v) nothing in Section 220 affects Section 71 IPC.

steps.title: Resist an accused's demand for joint trial
steps.text: Treat the joint-trial provisions as enabling only: an accused cannot insist, with ulterior motive or otherwise, on being tried as a co-accused with accused in a different case; it is a discretionary power the court may allow if the interest of justice so demands, to prevent a miscarriage of justice (Essar Tele holdings, 2015 KHC 4648).

steps.title: Move for a proclamation and publish it widely
steps.text: If the warrant cannot be executed within a reasonable time, move the court for a proclamation under Section 82 Cr.P.C. [now BNSS 84], placing before it all details of the efforts made so as to convince it that the warrantee is evading arrest, has gone into hiding, and that the warrant could not be executed. Once proclamation orders are issued, promulgate them immediately and ensure the proclamation is widely published in the manner provided in that section.

steps.title: Attach the proclaimed person's property without delay
steps.text: Orders of attachment under Section 83 Cr.P.C. [now BNSS 85] can be issued simultaneously with the proclamation: the court may at any time order attachment of any property, movable or immovable or both, of the proclaimed person. Carry out the attachment promptly after proper issue of the proclamation, seizing the property before the proclaimed person has time to transfer, alienate, mortgage or conceal it.

steps.title: Watch the harbourers of an absconding warrantee
steps.text: To facilitate the arrest of an absconding warrantee or proclaimed offender, maintain an effective watch over his harbourers. Persons who wilfully or knowingly harbour such offenders can be prosecuted under Section 216 IPC, so give the widest publicity to the proclamation so that knowledge of it can be conclusively proved against the harbourer; in appropriate cases the officer in charge may approach the Judicial Officer who issued the proclamation to invoke Section 174-A IPC.

steps.title: Preserve witness evidence against an unarrested accused
steps.text: If there is no immediate prospect of arresting the accused even after action under Sections 82 and 83 Cr.P.C. [now BNSS 84 and 85], the court may, in the absence of the accused, examine the prosecution witnesses and record their depositions under Section 299 Cr.P.C.; the Magistrate then enters the case in a separate register of long pending cases. If the accused is later apprehended or appears, the case against him is treated as a new case and dealt with according to law.

steps.applies_when: No immediate prospect of arresting the proclaimed accused

steps.title: Draft the final report to standard
steps.text: When preparing a final report: type it in double space with a dark ink impression and number the paragraphs; make the enquiry thorough and complete with information adequate on all points; keep allegations, facts, available evidence, opinions and comments separate and succinct; avoid repetition, list the allegations in proper order in clear and definite form and discuss each separately in detail; keep the analysis of facts separate from the opinion, with a clear conclusion on each allegation and each accused, naming each accused and his accused number in the final recommendation; state clearly with reasons any necessary witness who could not be examined or document that could not be obtained; and incorporate the expert's opinion, or at least the relevant portion, in the report.
steps.triage_why: These are formatting and quality guidelines for report writing to ensure clarity; while helpful, failure to double-space does not defeat the prosecution.

steps.title: Follow up the Magistrate's order on the final report
steps.text: Anticipate the Magistrate's response to a final report: he may accept it and issue proceedings, or decline it and send it back directing further investigation, in which case investigate further and send a report. If the further investigation does not improve the position, send the report again with your findings. The Magistrate cannot direct the officer to file a charge-sheet, but may take cognizance suo motu on the report.
steps.responsible: Officer in charge of the police station
steps.triage_why: Describes the Magistrate's potential legal responses and the IO's subsequent obligations; it is a procedural guide to court dynamics.

conflicts.description: kerala_police_sop_2020 (kerala-final-report, p.234) records, on Rama Chaudhury v. State of Bihar (AIR 2009 SC 2308), that the law does not mandate prior permission of the Magistrate for further investigation, though it is good to inform the Court; bnss_2023 (BNSS 193) requires the court's permission for further investigation during trial and caps it at ninety days, extendable by the court.
conflicts.resolution: The BNSS requirement governs, being the law layer and highest authority: obtain the court's permission and complete the further investigation within ninety days unless the court extends it. The Kerala position states the pre-2023 law under Section 173(8) CrPC and is retained in details[] only as the historical rule; its practice of informing the court is subsumed by the BNSS permission requirement.

steps.title: Execute court summonses and warrants
steps.text: When the case is posted for appearance and the court issues summons, serve it promptly and return served summonses to the court at least a day before the date of hearing; where a summons could not be served, inform the court of the non-service and specify the reasons. steps.title: Depose in Court with discipline and order
steps.text: Go to the witness box ready with the case diaries and witness statements and hand the case diaries over immediately if the Court calls for them, since delay may draw an adverse inference on the IO's conduct. Appear in uniform even if working in a Special Unit, salute the Court on entering and leaving the Court and the witness box, and keep the decorum of the Court. After taking the oath, narrate the statement chronologically - from receipt of information and registration of the case, through the steps adopted and evidence collected, up to filing of the charge sheet - and mention witnesses, exhibits and material objects in the chronological order marked in Court (PW, Exhibit P, MO). Give short answers in simple language, never answer hastily without understanding the question and do not delay unduly, since lengthy answers open fresh rounds of questions. An officer who investigated only part of the case should depose about his own role and its handover alone, and not about investigation done by other officers unless verified by him.
steps.stage: The investigating officer in the witness box
steps.triage_why: The IO must produce case diaries if called by the Court; failure to do so or delay can lead to adverse inferences regarding the integrity of the investigation.

steps.title: Hold your ground under cross-examination
steps.text: Remain calm and do not argue with the defence counsel, while still ensuring your points reach the Court. Understand the question patiently and answer only after it is completed; answer looking at the Judge, and if the question is unclear bring it to the Court's notice. Never turn towards the prosecution counsel when questioned by the adverse party, as it suggests reliance on the prosecutor for the reply. Do not take offence at the nature of the questions, and if a question is unnecessarily vexatious represent the matter to the Court and seek its protection. Be vigilant against questions framed so that only 'Yes' or 'No' can be answered - give a suitable explanation instead, and if counsel insists, seek the Court's permission to suffix an explanation.

steps.triage_why: These are guidelines on courtroom etiquette and demeanor, not procedural steps.

steps.title: Report case progress through Court Diaries
steps.text: Report the progress of cases in Courts, including appeals and revisions, regularly through Court Diaries in the prescribed form, in duplicate - one copy to the Public Prosecutor and one to the District Police Chief. The Court Diary forwarded by the District Police Chief must invariably contain: (i) names of prosecution or defence witnesses summoned or examined; (ii) how the witnesses fared and a gist of their evidence, and where a witness turns hostile, that fact with the District Police Chief's comment on how the damage will be remedied; (iii) how the case proceeded; (iv) what proceedings are due on the next hearing date; (v) reasons for any adjournment, indicating whether granted at the request of prosecution or defence or because the Court could not take up the case; and (vi) where adjournment was occasioned by non-production of witnesses, the reasons for it.
steps.responsible: Prosecuting Officers in charge of the cases; District Police Chief on forwarding
steps.triage_why: Reporting progress via Court Diaries is an administrative requirement for police supervision, not a requirement for the legal validity of the prosecution.

steps.title: File revisions within limitation and with restraint
steps.text: File a revision petition within ninety days of the date of the order. steps.title: Drive the appeal against acquittal to time
steps.text: Drive the appeal process against an acquittal to time. In a Sessions case the Public Prosecutor reports to the Collector and the Superintendent of Police soon after the judgment with his recommendation; where he considers an appeal or revision should be filed he obtains certified copies of the necessary records and forwards them with his report direct to the Advocate General, sending a copy to the District Collector, who promptly addresses the Home Department for instructions to the Advocate General. In Magistrate court acquittals the Assistant Public Prosecutor sends the proposal to the District Collector through the Superintendent of Police, obtaining certified copies of depositions and other records promptly. The District Collector, after consulting the Public Prosecutor if necessary, sends a report to the Government in the Home Department with a copy to the Director General of Prosecutions; his report must reach the Government within 45 days of the judgment, and if he decides no appeal is needed he immediately informs the Superintendent of Police. Where the District Police Chief is of the view that grounds exist, he sends a report to the State Police Chief through proper channel to move the Government.

steps.title: Weigh the judgment before recommending an appeal
steps.text: Never recommend an appeal or revision mechanically without analysis of the judgment. While examining a case for appeal against acquittal or discharge, keep in mind the decisions of the High Courts and the Supreme Court on the scope of the Appellate Court's power to interfere under Section 378 Cr.P.C., and weigh: (i) the trial court's views on the credibility of witnesses; (ii) the appellate court's reluctance to disturb findings of fact recorded by the court which saw and heard the witnesses; (iii) the accused's right to the benefit of doubt; and (iv) any other factor the Public Prosecutor considers relevant.

steps.triage_why: This concerns post-trial appellate strategy and analysis of judgments, not the current investigation phase.

steps.title: Distinguish appeal from revision correctly
steps.text: Do not use 'appeal' and 'revision' loosely or interchangeably. Sections 372 to 394 Cr.P.C. deal with appeals and Sections 395 to 405 Cr.P.C. with revisions. An appeal is a legal right by which the appellant approaches a higher Court for review or reversal of the verdict below on legal and/or factual grounds, and lies both against conviction and against acquittal (Section 378(2) Cr.P.C.). A revision invokes the supervisory jurisdiction of a higher Court to examine the correctness, legality or propriety of any finding, sentence or order of an inferior Court; under Section 397 Cr.P.C. the High Court cannot re-appreciate evidence in revision and interferes only in exceptional cases of real and substantial injustice.

steps.title: Abandon review once the judgment is signed
steps.text: Do not seek review or modification of a judgment once it has been signed. Under Section 362 Cr.P.C. the criminal court becomes functus officio the moment the disposal order is signed, and the order cannot be altered except to correct a clerical or arithmetical error. The prohibition is absolute - even the High Court, exercising its inherent power under Section 482 Cr.P.C., has no authority or jurisdiction to alter the judgment (Hari Singh Mann v. Harbhajan Singh Bajwa & Ors, AIR 2001 SC 43; Chhanni v. State of U.P., AIR 2006 SC 3051).

steps.triage_why: Standard operating procedure for specimen collection to prevent contamination/fraud, but not a statutory mandate that defeats prosecution if slightly deviated from.

Take the specimen or impression on the next sheet only thereafter.

steps.title: Seize thirty-six specimens in six marked sets
steps.text: The IO shall seize the specimen samples/impressions desirably in 6 sets of 6 specimens each — a total of 36 specimens — and a separate clear mark shall be given to each set.
steps.stage: S.O.P. for taking specimen signature, handwriting, voice sample, etc. (Section 349 BNSS)
steps.triage_why: Best practice for forensic quantity, but the specific number of sets (36) is a guideline rather than a legal requirement for admissibility.

ticks.do: Seize the specimen samples or impressions desirably in 6 sets of 6 specimens each, a total of 36 specimens.

steps.title: Restrict the F.S.L. despatch to the original
steps.text: Only the disputed original document shall be sent to the F.S.L. for examination; under no circumstances is a copy of the original document to be sent.
steps.stage: S.O.P. for taking specimen signature, handwriting, voice sample, etc. (Section 349 BNSS)
steps.triage_why: Forensic labs generally cannot authenticate copies; sending a copy instead of the original can lead to the evidence being rejected or deemed inadmissible.

ticks.do: Send only the disputed original document to the F.S.L. for examination.

steps.text: After collection, the IO shall properly pack and seal in the proper manner all the specimens seized — the disputed as well as the genuine specimens — and send them at the earliest to the forensic laboratory for examination.

steps.title: Check the form of every court summons
steps.text: Ensure every summons issued by a Court under the Sanhita is in writing, in two copies, signed by the presiding officer of the Court (or such other officer as the High Court may by rule direct), and bears the seal of the Court (Section 63).

steps.text: Serve every summons through a police officer, or, subject to rules made by the State Government, through an officer of the Court issuing it or another public servant.

steps.text: If, despite due diligence, the person summoned cannot be found, serve by delivering his copy of the summons to some adult member of his family residing with him; that person must invariably sign an acknowledgement of receipt on the reverse side of the second copy (Section 66).

steps.text: If, despite due diligence, service cannot be effected under Section 64, 65 or 66, affix one copy of the summons to some conspicuous part of the house or homestead in which the person summoned ordinarily resides; the Court, after such inquiry as it thinks fit, may then declare the summons duly served or order fresh service in such manner as it considers proper (Section 67).

steps.text: The copy of the summons on which the person served (or the person with whom it was left) purported to make an endorsement in the manner of Section 62 or Section 64 is admissible in evidence, and the statements therein are deemed true unless the contrary is proved (Section 70).

steps.title: Record and route the rape distress call
steps.text: When a call or information of rape or sexual assault is received in the police control room, the operator handling the call will try to record every relevant detail given by the caller (caller's name, address and profession; the victim's name, address and age; the exact place of occurrence; the accused's name, address and age if known), and must immediately bring it to the notice of the supervisory officer of the control room, inform the concerned police van and the district control room, and disclose it to no one unconnected with the matter; where the information reaches the police station by wireless message or telephone, the Duty Officer shall record it accurately in the Daily Diary.
steps.responsible: Police control room operator; police station Duty Officer
steps.triage_why: This describes the duty of the Police Control Room (PCR) operator, not the Investigating Officer.

conflicts.description: The sources differ on how far the prohibition reaches. The national sources are child-specific: bprd_rape_sop (p.5) bars detaining any child at night under Section 24(4) POCSO, and child_guidelines (p.5) bars keeping a child victim in the police station overnight 'on any pretext whatsoever, including medical examination'. Among the same-layer state advisories, up-handbook-rape (p.14) states an unqualified prohibition — 'In no circumstance shall the victim be kept at the police station' — with no night qualifier, whereas up-handbook-women-crimes (p.15) limits it to 'at night' and delhi-sexual-offence-response (p.4) to 'overnight'.
conflicts.resolution: Because the divergence is between sources of the same layer, it is resolved by adopting the formulation common to the national child-specific sources and to the majority of the state advisories, namely the night/overnight prohibition. UP's broader unqualified prohibition is preserved verbatim as a detail rather than blended into the operative wording, and the extension of the rule from child victims to every victim is attributed in the text to the state guidance that alone carries it.

steps.title: Keep victim and accused apart during medical examination
steps.text: Under no circumstances take the victim and the accused in the same vehicle for the medical examination, and ensure in every manner that the victim and the accused do not come face to face during the medical examination.

steps.triage_why: Essential to prevent witness intimidation, trauma, or claims of coercion/collusion during medical evidence collection.

steps.triage_why: Statutory prohibition against disclosing the identity of a POCSO victim; violation is a criminal offence and breaches legal mandates.

steps.title: Engage Legal Services Authority for Rape Victim
steps.text: The SHO shall inform the Legal Services Authority immediately of the commission of the rape so that it deputes a social worker/para-legal worker to contact the victim and her family within a week; the IO and SHO shall then assist the Authority in processing rehabilitation and compensation by supplying all requisite information and maintaining constant liaison.

steps.text: Obtain consent before the medical examination and record it explicitly in the report — nothing makes an examination without consent lawful. conflicts.description: Gujarat SOP 6 (pp.23-24) sets the self-consent threshold at 12 years, while BPR&D (p.10) and the Tripura rape SOP (p.11) set it at 18 years — a victim above 18 consenting for herself and a victim below 18 requiring written parental consent under Section 27 POCSO. Delhi SO 303/2019 (p.7) also works with a 12-year line. BNSS 184 itself prescribes no age threshold, requiring only the consent of the woman or of a person competent to consent on her behalf, and the UP handbook (p.13) likewise refers only to 'her own consent or the consent of her guardian'.
conflicts.resolution: The binding Gujarat circular governs the canonical text, so the 12-year threshold is stated. The 18-year threshold of the national BPR&D SOP and the Tripura rape SOP is recorded here unaltered and is not blended with the Gujarat figure; neither threshold is averaged, and no combined rule is stated.

conflicts.description: The sources split on whether the female examiner is absolute. Gujarat SOP 6 (p.23, on Section 51(2) BNSS), BPR&D (p.10) and the Tripura POCSO SOP (p.4, girl child) state it absolutely; the Tripura rape SOP (p.11) says 'as far as possible ... only by a lady doctor', and Delhi SO 303/2019 (p.6) and the Delhi compendium (p.9) say the examination of a girl child victim shall be conducted 'preferably by a female doctor'. Note that the two divergent formulations sit in different sections of the same Tripura bundle.
conflicts.resolution: Gujarat SOP 6 (p.23), the binding source, states the requirement absolutely on the basis of Section 51(2) BNSS — only a registered female medical practitioner or only under her supervision — and that wording governs; the national BPR&D SOP and the Tripura POCSO SOP agree. The weaker 'as far as possible'/'preferably' formulations of the Tripura rape SOP and the two Delhi documents do not dilute the binding requirement.

steps.text: Seize the victim's clothes without delay and, after properly drying them if necessary, seal them and send them immediately to the FSL for examination so that the seized biological evidence does not deteriorate.

steps.title: Enforce the ban on the two-finger test
steps.text: Ensure the prohibition on the use of the two-finger test to establish rape is observed — Lillu Vs State of Haryana, (2013) 14 SCC 643.
legal_basis: Section 111 BNS — human trafficking as an organized crime. NOTE ON PROVENANCE: this framing is NOT printed in pp.101-130; it is the book's premise stated at PDF pp.5, 13 and 40 ('Since human trafficking is an organized crime, u/s 111 BNS…'; 'Section 111 BNS defines the constituents of organized crime, which includes "human trafficking for prostitution"'; 'The trafficker is liable under 143 BNS / 111 BNS'). Section 143 BNS (370 IPC) is the definition of trafficking; 144 BNS (370A IPC) is exploitation of a trafficked person
S.7 ITPA and S.18(2) ITPA — action to be moved through the prosecutor once the court decides on the offence (printed 'u/s.7 ITPA, 18(2) ITPA etc.', p.102)
S.19 ITPA — application to the Magistrate for a protective home / corrective institution / supervision; S.17(4) ITPA — such order may also be made suo moto by the Magistrate (p.103)
section 366 BNSS / 327(2) of the CrPC — mandates in-camera trials in all rape cases (printed exactly thus, p.103)
S.160 CrPC (179 BNSS) — female victim not to be called to the police station after evening (p.105)
S.157 of the CrPC (176 BNSS) and S.24 of the POCSO Act — rape victims and child victims of sexual abuse to be interviewed at a place of her choice (p.105)
S 398 BNSS — witness protection section; Witness Protection Scheme, 2018 legally mandatory for the union, all States and UTs (Mahender Chawla Vs Union of India, p.107)

Section 357A CrPC (introduced 2009) — victim compensation; the source itself states 'Under BNSS, Section 396 deals with the subject' (p.107); section 357A(5) of the CrPC [now s.396(5) BNSS] — DLSA enquiry to be completed within two months (p.108)
POCSO Act S.33(8) read with Rule 7 of the POCSO Rules — compensation ordered by the Special Court hearing the POCSO case (p.109)

steps.title: Check for Infection and Examine Bite Marks
steps.text: Ask the doctor to check both the victim and the accused for any sexually transmitted disease or infection so that the allegations can be corroborated, the appropriate sections of law invoked and the victim given necessary treatment at the earliest; where teeth or bite marks are found, have them properly examined, measured and photographed for comparison with the accused's denture by a forensic odontologist and take the accused to a dental expert.
steps.triage_why: While corroborative and helpful for treatment, the absence of an STD test does not typically defeat a rape/POCSO prosecution if other evidence exists.

steps.title: Requisition Swabs, Injury Record and Potency Test
steps.text: Give a written requisition to the medical officer to collect, during the medical examination, the vaginal swab and foreign hair of the victim and the penile swab of the accused (if arrested immediately), and seize these accordingly; ensure that any marks of injury on the victim or the accused are recorded by the medical officer in his report, and request a potency test of the accused.
steps.triage_why: Swabs and potency tests are primary forensic evidence for sexual offences; failure to collect these promptly results in the permanent loss of biological proof of penetration/contact.

foreign hair of the victim
penile swab of the accused (if arrested immediately)

Ensure that any marks of injury on the victim or the accused are recorded by the medical officer in his report.
Request a potency test of the accused.

steps.title: Collect Proof of Age in Prescribed Order
steps.text: In all POCSO cases where the age of the victim is material, collect proof of age relying in this order (Section 34 POCSO Act read with the Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act): first, the date-of-birth certificate from the school or the matriculation or equivalent certificate from the concerned examination Board, if available; in its absence, the birth certificate given by a corporation, municipal authority or Panchayat; and only in the absence of both, determine age by an ossification test or any other medically proven and improved age-determination test.

Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act (printed in the operative sources as the 2000 Act; the Act in force, cited elsewhere in the same source set, is the JJ Act, 2015)

steps.title: Examine the Issuer and Seize the Age Register
steps.text: Prove the age document, do not merely seize it: where a school certificate is relied on, examine the headmaster or teacher who issued it under Section 161 CrPC [now BNSS 180] and put his name in the list of witnesses, and seize as per procedure the register on which the certificate was based, since that register is necessary to prove the content of the certificate; follow the same procedure as far as practicable for a birth certificate, and in no circumstance release the certificate or the register on bail from police custody.

steps.applies_when: Age of the victim is material (POCSO case)
steps.triage_why: Mere seizure of a document is insufficient for admissibility in court; the source register and issuing authority must be proved to establish the document's authenticity.

conflicts.description: For the statement recorded by the police, the BPRD SOP (national advisory, bprd-rape-investigation p.7) makes videography of an interpreter-assisted statement permissive — the statement 'may be videographed'. The Tripura POCSO SOP (state advisory, tripura-pocso p.4) makes it mandatory ('ensure that the statement of the child is also recorded by audio-video means'), and the Delhi Police guidelines (state advisory, delhi-sexual-offence-response p.8) require it 'wherever possible' under Section 26(4) POCSO Act.
conflicts.resolution: The higher-authority national advisory governs the canonical text, which keeps videography permissive at this stage; the mandatory state-advisory formulations are preserved as details and should be followed in POCSO cases, where Section 26(4) POCSO is the stated basis. This permissive rule is confined to the police statement — at the Magistrate stage under Section 183 BNSS audio-video recording of a disabled maker's statement is mandatory (see module-sexual-offences-183-disabled-maker).

steps.title: Pack, Seal and Rush Exhibits to FSL
steps.text: Properly pack, preserve and seal the collected and lifted exhibits and send them to the FSL for chemical analysis as quickly as possible.
steps.deadline: Deposit exhibits and documents with the FSL as early as possible, preferably within 7 days from the date of collection (delhi-sexual-offence-response p.11); biological samples such as blood and semen, which putrefy or degenerate rapidly, on the same day or the next day of collection (delhi-sexual-offence-response pp.11-12). The Gujarat SOP requires the victim's clothes and the biological evidence they carry to be sealed and sent to the FSL immediately (guj_cid_29_sops_2024 SOP 6 p.24) — see conflicts.
steps.triage_why: Biological evidence (semen, DNA) degrades rapidly; failure to seal and send promptly results in loss of primary forensic proof.

conflicts.description: On how quickly biological exhibits must reach the laboratory, the Gujarat CID SOP (binding, guj_cid_29_sops_2024 SOP 6 p.24) directs that the victim's clothes be seized without delay and, after drying if necessary, sealed and sent to the FSL immediately so that the seized biological evidence does not deteriorate. The Delhi Police guidelines (state advisory, delhi-sexual-offence-response pp.11-12) set a general outer limit of preferably 07 days from collection for exhibits and documents, with blood, semen and similar rapidly degrading samples going on the same day or the next day of collection.
conflicts.resolution: The binding Gujarat SOP prevails for the victim's clothing and the biological material it carries, which must go immediately; the Delhi 7-day outer limit is retained only as the fallback for exhibits and documents that are not biological, and the same-day/next-day rule as the outer limit for other biological samples. The Delhi periods must never be read as licence to hold biological exhibits that the Gujarat SOP requires to be dispatched at once.

steps.title: Seize Hard Disks and Certify Electronic Evidence
steps.text: Collect all available electronic evidence, such as CCTV footage and phone call details, and collect all CCTV footage whenever available; focus on primary evidence by collecting the hard disk and the relevant memory disks and not the footage alone (Section 58 BSA, earlier Section 63 of the Indian Evidence Act, on primary and secondary evidence), and prove the electronic evidence in the manner prescribed under Section 63 BSA (earlier Section 65-B of the Indian Evidence Act).

steps.triage_why: The case relies on Instagram messages and call recordings; failure to follow BSA (formerly IEA) primary evidence rules makes electronic evidence inadmissible.

steps.text: Draw the site plan / spot map of the place of occurrence properly, indicating the distances between the items found at the spot and showing the position of witnesses, if any.
steps.triage_why: Strengthens the case by visualizing the crime scene, but omission does not typically defeat a prosecution based on victim testimony and DNA.

details.text: The site plan shall be drawn correctly by indicating the directions from where the accused person came and left; it should also include the surrounding areas of the scene of crime, where the incident took place, from where the exhibits were lifted, and the source of light during night. steps.text: Fill the FSL forwarding form with due care and put only specific, evidence-oriented queries so that the exhibits can be linked to the victim and to the accused without any plausible doubt; where more than one accused is alleged, apply your mind carefully while sending exhibits; and request the FSL to deal with the case on priority and make its report available at the earliest.
steps.triage_why: Administrative precision in FSL forms ensures clarity, but the core requirement is the submission of the evidence itself.

steps.title: Investigate and document allegations

steps.triage_why: Analytical work to strengthen the case narrative, but the individual pieces of evidence are the statutory requirements.

steps.title: Send Arrested Accused for Medical Examination
steps.text: Send the arrested accused for medical examination under Section 52 BNSS [earlier Section 53-A CrPC] under a properly filled-in medical examination sheet and along with an injury sheet detailing the injuries, scratches, bruises and nail marks found on his body, and get him medically examined to prove his physical capacity for committing the alleged crime.
steps.stage: Tracing, arrest and examination of the accused
legal_basis: BNSS 52 (earlier Section 53-A CrPC) — medical examination of the accused
Section 173(5)(E) CrPC [now the Section 193 BNSS charge-sheet documents] — forwarding the accused's medical examination report to the Magistrate
steps.applies_when: Accused arrested
steps.triage_why: Statutory duty under BNSS to examine the accused for biological evidence (DNA/semen) and signs of struggle (scratches).

ticks.do: Send the arrested accused for medical examination under Section 52 BNSS [earlier Section 53-A CrPC] under a properly filled-in medical examination sheet.

details.text: Under no circumstances take the victim and the accused in the same vehicle for the medical examination, and ensure in every manner that the victim and the accused do not come face to face during the medical examination.

details.text: After the arrest of the accused his medical examination by a government doctor must be conducted to obtain evidence of rape so that its commission by him can be confirmed and a sufficient basis of his involvement established, and his semen test shall also be conducted.

details.text: The doctor conducting the examination shall note the name and address of the accused and of the police officer producing him, then immediately conduct the examination, and shall record the factors bearing on rape-related conclusions — the accused's age, the marks of injuries found on his body, and the details of the material collected from his body for DNA profiling.

details.text: Under Section 53(2) CrPC the government doctor shall, using modern scientific methods, examine blood, blood stains, semen, swabs of the cotton used, the accused's semen found on the victim's genitals and the victim's blood and secreted fluid present on the accused's genitals, marks of catching hold with fingernails, DNA profiling and other necessary tests, and shall preserve the material for examination.
details.citation: UP Police - Handbook for the Investigation of Major Crimes (Mukhya Aparadhon ki Vivechna hetu Hast-Pustika), O.P. Singh, DGP UP (~2018) - TRANSLATED FROM HINDI

details.text: The IO shall send the accused's medical examination report to the concerned Magistrate in compliance with Section 173(5)(E) CrPC [now the Section 193 BNSS charge-sheet documents].

conflicts.description: The sources ground the arrested accused's medical examination in three different provisions: BPR&D (p.13) applies Section 52 BNSS (earlier Section 53-A CrPC); the Delhi compendium 2024 (Scenario 1, p.14) directs that the accused shall be medically examined as per Section 53 of the BNSS, 2023; and the UP Handbook (p.13) invokes Sections 53 and 53(A)(1) CrPC, adding Section 53(2) CrPC (p.14) for the scientific examination.
conflicts.resolution: The national advisory outranks both state advisories, so the canonical text is stated on BPR&D's Section 52 BNSS (earlier Section 53-A CrPC). The Delhi compendium's Section 53 BNSS and the UP Handbook's Sections 53/53(A)(1) and 53(2) CrPC are recorded here and their substantive content is preserved in details[]; the provisions are not blended and no single section is presented as agreed.

steps.title: Examine Witnesses Who Reached the Spot First
steps.text: Examine all relevant and material witnesses promptly — especially any witness who reached the spot on hearing the shouts of the victim; where the victim is indisposed, unable to narrate the incident, a minor who cannot comprehend, or in shock, and the next of kin or another person registered the FIR on her behalf or assisted her in registering it, examine that person as an independent witness; and investigate the next of kin and suitably make them prosecution witnesses if they have observed something of evidentiary value.
steps.triage_why: Prompt examination of witnesses is required to prevent memory fade and ensure the case is built on contemporaneous accounts.

ticks.do: Examine all relevant and material witnesses promptly, especially any witness who reached the spot on hearing the shouts of the victim.

notes: Applies where the victim is indisposed, unable to narrate the incident, a minor who cannot comprehend, or in shock.

steps.title: Shield the Victim and Family From Threats
steps.text: Take care in all cases that the victim and her family, or any person in whom she is interested, is not threatened or tempted in any manner by the accused or any other person.
steps.triage_why: Failure to protect the victim from witness tampering or threats by the accused can lead to the victim retracting her statement, defeating the prosecution.

ticks.do: Take care in all cases that the victim and her family, or any person in whom she is interested, is not threatened or tempted in any manner by the accused or any other person.

details.text: Under the applicable witness protection scheme the State Legal Services Authority is the Competent Authority to ensure protection of the victim, her family members and the prosecution witnesses; any order or direction to the police received from the Authority in this regard shall be complied with meticulously.

steps.title: Keep Every Address for the Victim on File
steps.text: Keep the victim's permanent address and any other address in the case file in addition to her present address, along with any information that may help find her during trial if she leaves the reported address, and advise her during the investigation itself to inform the police of any future change of address.
steps.triage_why: Good practice for trial management, but missing a secondary address does not inherently invalidate the legal case.

conflicts.description: The sources specify the supervising rank differently. bprd-rape-investigation p.14 (national_advisory, operative) names only 'an officer of the rank of Dy.SP'. tripura-rape-women p.14 names 'the SsP/DySP'. delhi-sexual-offence-response p.13 (state_advisory) instead requires that 'Inspector (Investigation), SHO and ACP shall personally monitor such cases' and that 'investigation should be closely supervised by the SHO/ACP right from inception'. All three state the duty permissively ('should'), not as 'must'.
conflicts.resolution: Resolved by the authority ladder: the national advisory (BPR&D) governs the canonical wording, so the canonical text states Dy.SP-rank supervision in the source's own 'should' modality. The ACP formulation is retained as the commissionerate equivalent at its own (state_advisory) level through the existing delhi-sexual-offence-response p.13 detail, and is not blended into the national-advisory sentence. In commissionerate systems where there is no Dy.SP post, the ACP is the corresponding rank.

conflicts.description: The sources disagree on the Initial Special Report clock and on who issues it. BPR&D (p.4), the Tripura rape SOP (p.9) and the Delhi compendium (Scenario 1, p.10) fix it at 72 hours of the occurrence (BPR&D and Tripura: through a gazetted officer; the compendium: prepared by the IO and dispatched to senior officers), whereas the Delhi Standing Order (p.8) requires the ISR to be issued by the ACP within 24 hours of registration and to reach the district office the same evening. The clocks also run from different events — occurrence versus registration.
conflicts.resolution: The higher-authority national advisory's 72-hours-from-occurrence limit, issued through a gazetted officer, is stated in the canonical text; the Delhi Standing Order's stricter 24-hours-from-registration requirement and its ACP-level issuer are preserved as a detail so that a state or district that has adopted the tighter clock is not misled. The figures are not averaged and the two starting events are not merged.

conflicts.description: BPR&D (p.3) treats only rape cases as Grave/Special Report Cases; the Delhi Standing Order (p.8) extends the same treatment to cases registered under the POCSO Act.
conflicts.resolution: The canonical text states the scope carried by the higher-authority national advisory (rape cases). The Delhi extension to POCSO cases is a state-advisory addition and is recorded in details[] rather than folded into the canonical scope, so that a POCSO-only case is not represented as being under a national-advisory special-reporting mandate.

conflicts.description: The sources give three different outer limits for completing a sexual-offence investigation. 60 days / two months: BPR&D (p.14) on Section 193 BNSS; the Delhi Standing Order (p.13) on the Criminal Law (Amendment) Act 2018; and the Tripura rape SOP (p.14) on Section 173(1A) CrPC. 90 days: the Guidelines for Police Officials Dealing with Children (p.6), stated as 'preferably within ninety days' of registration. Three months: the Tripura POCSO SOP (p.5), and the UP Handbook (p.14) for rape cases involving children. The clash is sharpest between the Tripura rape SOP and the UP Handbook, which cite the same provision — Section 173(1A) CrPC — for two months and three months respectively.
conflicts.resolution: BPR&D's 60-day limit governs the canonical text. The children guidelines are national advisory too, so authority alone does not separate them: BPR&D prevails because it is the only source written on the current statute (Section 193 BNSS) and states a hard limit, whereas the children guidelines state a preference ('preferably') in an instrument that predates both POCSO and the BNSS (it cites the JJ Act 2000 with the 2006 amendment and 2007 Rules, and Section 164A CrPC). Between the two state advisories citing Section 173(1A) CrPC, neither can outrank the other, so both figures are recorded here rather than reconciled, and neither displaces the 60-day canonical limit. No figure is averaged. Where the accused is in custody the separate statutory custody clock (Section 167 CrPC / Section 187 BNSS) runs independently and is recorded in details[].

steps.title: Flag uncovered points and track further investigation
steps.text: Where all points could not be covered in the main charge sheet, say so clearly in it and state that a further report will be filed under Section 193(9) BNSS [earlier Section 173(8) CrPC]; seek the court's permission before filing the supplementary charge sheet during trial and complete the further investigation within 90 days, extendable by the court. Enter every action required after the main charge sheet — arrest of co-accused, proclaimed-offender proceedings, deposit of exhibits, age estimation, filing of the FSL report — in the Follow-up Action/Supplementary Charge Sheet Register so that follow-up survives the transfer of the IO or SHO, and keep such rape/POCSO cases on the Pending Investigation list to be reviewed in crime review meetings until the investigation concludes in all respects.
steps.stage: Charge sheet and completion of investigation
legal_basis: BNSS 193(9) (earlier Section 173(8) CrPC)
steps.deadline: Further investigation after permission for a supplementary charge sheet to be completed within 90 days, extendable by the court — Section 193(9) BNSS
steps.triage_why: This is a procedural guide on how to handle supplementary reports if the main charge sheet is incomplete.

Complete the further investigation within 90 days, extendable by the court.
notes: Deadline under Section 193(9) BNSS.

details.text: Where despite best efforts all points have not been covered in the main charge sheet, the IO should clearly specify this and mention that a further report (supplementary charge sheet) under Section 173(8) CrPC [now Section 193(9) BNSS] will be filed in due course; the supplementary charge sheet shall be filed as soon as possible after completion of investigation, and second or subsequent supplementary charge sheets can be filed as required.

details.text: Pending further-investigation actions must be mentioned in the last paragraph of Column No. 16 (Brief Facts of the Case) of the Final Report, and a red-ink entry made in the index of the relevant FIR book by the record keeper at the time of issuing the Road Certificate, duly attested by the SHO or Inspector (Investigation).

details.text: Such cases shall be handled as 'Pending Investigation Cases' and reflected and discussed in the crime review meetings held by the district and range heads until the investigation is concluded in all respects.

steps.title: Put Draft Charge Sheet to Prosecutor Promptly
steps.text: Prepare the draft charge sheet in a sexual-assault case within 45 days without fail and put it up to the Public Prosecutor on the next working day rather than keeping it with yourself; the Inspector (Investigation), SHO and sub-divisional officer shall personally monitor these cases and ensure the draft is put up to them by the IO within the stipulated period, and if the charge sheet is not filed within 30 days the case shall be brought to the notice of the range head.
steps.stage: Charge sheet and completion of investigation
steps.deadline: Draft charge sheet within 45 days; put up to the Public Prosecutor on the next working day; escalation to the range head if not filed within 30 days
steps.responsible: Investigating Officer; Inspector (Investigation), SHO and sub-divisional officer (monitoring)
steps.triage_why: Internal deadlines for drafting are sound practice to ensure the 60-day statutory limit is met, but the draft date itself is not the statutory deadline.

Bring the case to the notice of the range head if the charge sheet is not filed within 30 days.

conflicts.description: The Delhi Standing Order (p.13) sets the 45-day draft-charge-sheet clock without naming its starting point, while the Delhi compendium (Scenario 1, p.12) runs the same 45 days from the date of arrest where the accused is in judicial custody remand.
conflicts.resolution: Both formulations are state advisory and neither outranks the other, so the canonical text uses the Standing Order's unanchored 45-day internal deadline as the general rule and preserves the compendium's arrest-anchored variant as a detail. Neither the law nor the Gujarat SOPs fix an internal draft deadline, so no higher source resolves the anchor.

steps.title: Build the charge sheet from collected evidence
steps.text: The charge sheet must not be a mere reproduction of the complaint or the FIR: it must be a bundle of the evidence collected from the first information to the date of preparation, commenting on each allegation with the evidence supporting it — the initial complaint/statement, the history alleged in the MLC, the statement recorded by the Magistrate, expert opinion on the exhibits, CDRs, the witness statements, other documentary evidence, the previous involvement of the accused, and the chances of his not joining trial if released on bail. Where more than one accused is involved, state specifically the role played by each, and state the permanent addresses of the victim, the accused and the prosecution witnesses to ensure service of summons and presence in court.
steps.stage: Charge sheet and completion of investigation
steps.triage_why: A charge sheet that is a mere reproduction of the FIR without supporting evidence (MLC, statements, CDRs) will fail to sustain a conviction during trial.

ticks.do: Avoid making the charge sheet a mere reproduction of the complaint or the FIR.
Compile it as a bundle of the evidence collected from the first information to the date of preparation.
Comment on each allegation with the evidence supporting it, covering:
sub: the initial complaint/statement
the history alleged in the MLC
the statement recorded by the Magistrate
expert opinion on the exhibits
CDRs
the witness statements
other documentary evidence
the previous involvement of the accused
the chances of his not joining trial if released on bail

ticks.do: State specifically the role played by each accused where more than one accused is involved.
State the permanent addresses of the victim, the accused and the prosecution witnesses to ensure service of summons and presence in court.

details.text: The IO/SHO shall ensure that all material documents — medical examination reports, FSL reports, Test Identification and the relevant daily diary/Roznamcha entries — are included with the charge sheet.

details.text: File with the charge sheet: the FIR along with the written complaint; the victim's statement recorded by the Magistrate; the seizure lists and the State FSL report; the medical examination reports of the victim and of the accused; the age proof of the victim; the hand sketch map of the place of occurrence; the statements of the relevant witnesses; and any other evidence collected by the IO.

details.text: Before the charge sheet, submit a summary report to the supervising officer to obtain permission to file it, stating the ingredients of the FIR, the action taken during investigation, the evidence collected, the articles seized, the particulars of witnesses, the evidence derived from expert reports, the particulars and status of arrested and absconding accused, and the sections of law under which the charge sheet will be submitted.

steps.title: Quote both POCSO and BNS penal sections
steps.text: File the report in final form quoting the penal sections both under the POCSO Act and under the IPC [now BNS], because Section 42 of the POCSO Act provides alternate punishment and the offender is liable to the punishment which is greater in degree.
steps.stage: Charge sheet and completion of investigation
legal_basis: POCSO Act s.42 (alternate punishment)
steps.applies_when: POCSO case
steps.triage_why: Failure to quote both BNS and POCSO sections may result in the accused not being charged with the more severe penalty provided by law.

ticks.do: File the report in final form quoting the penal sections both under the POCSO Act and under the IPC [now BNS].
notes: Section 42 of the POCSO Act provides alternate punishment and the offender is liable to the punishment which is greater in degree.

steps.title: Seek a Special Public Prosecutor and in-camera trial
steps.text: In sensational or gruesome rape and sexual assault cases, a Special Public Prosecutor may be got appointed for the proper conduct (pairvi) of the case, and an in-camera trial under Section 327(2) CrPC [now BNSS 366(2)] [now BNSS 366(2)] should be requested.

legal_basis: Section 327(2) CrPC [now BNSS 366(2)] as printed [now BNSS 366(2)] — in-camera trial of rape and sexual offences
steps.applies_when: Sensational or gruesome rape/sexual assault cases
steps.triage_why: This is a request for court procedure (in-camera trial) and appointment of prosecutors, not an investigative step.

steps.title: Appoint a Holding IO to monitor the trial
steps.text: Appoint an officer not below the rank of Sub-Inspector — ideally the IO of the case — as Holding IO to monitor the progress of the trial and submit a progress report on each date of trial to the supervisory officers including the SP; ensure the timely production of prosecution witnesses for briefing by the PP/APP and the physical availability of all relevant records and material objects at the time of trial, and monitor the service of summons to ensure the presence of witnesses, issuing summons also in e-format wherever possible.
steps.responsible: Holding IO (not below Sub-Inspector rank); Investigating Officer; court follow-up (pairvi) officer; malkhana in-charge
steps.triage_why: Monitoring the trial is sound practice for witness production, but the IO's primary duty is the investigation leading to the charge sheet.

steps.title: Oppose bail and inform the victim
steps.text: Oppose the bail application with relevant grounds through the prosecution, and where a bail application is presented by or on behalf of the accused, inform the victim about it within appropriate time so as to give her an opportunity to oppose it if she so desires.
steps.triage_why: Opposing bail is a prosecutorial function; while important, the omission of this step does not defeat the underlying prosecution of the crime.

ticks.do: Oppose the bail application with relevant grounds through the prosecution.
Inform the victim within appropriate time where a bail application is presented by or on behalf of the accused, so as to give her an opportunity to oppose it if she so desires.

details.text: Inform the complainant or victim through any possible means of communication about the listing of bail applications so they can put their version before the court if they desire.

details.text: Every bail matter should be attended by the IO and/or the Inspector (Investigation) with a detailed brief for the Court and the Public Prosecutor, and copies of the bail application, the replies and the court's order should be part of the police file; the IO should also keep in mind Section 40 of the POCSO Act and Rule 4 of the POCSO Rules on the child's right to legal counsel.
details.citation: Delhi Police Standing Order No. 303 of 2019 (23-05-2019) - Guidelines for Police Response and Investigation in Cases of Sexual Offence

details.text: Information of bail matters of rape accused, whenever listed, must be forwarded to the rape crisis cell of the State Women's Commission through its notified helpline, mobile number, fax, e-mail or address.

steps.title: Atomize the case and investigate every violation
steps.text: Treat the case as a 'basket of crimes' and conduct investigation into each of these violations: sensitive questioning and listening to the victim, to the untold story, is an art which a professional investigator should possess, and the story as it unfolds unravels a long list of offences perpetrated by various offenders on the victim; atomizing a typical case of sex trafficking of a girl child would reveal that human trafficking is an organised crime with several crimes in itself (Box 3).
legal_basis: Article 23, Constitution of India — express prohibition of human trafficking of every kind
Section 111 BNS — organised crime, expressly includes 'human trafficking for prostitution'
Section 143 BNS (370 IPC) — definition of trafficking (Action + Modus Operandi + Intention); Explanation 2 makes victim's consent immaterial
Section 143(4) BNS / 370(4) IPC — trafficking of a minor (person of any gender who has not attained 18), rigorous punishment and fine
Section 144 BNS / 370A IPC — knowingly engaging a trafficked person for sexual exploitation; higher punishment where the trafficked person is a minor

Sexual exploitation heads as printed at para 1.3: 'BNS 64, 65(1), 65(2), 67, 68, 70(1), 70(2) / 376 IPC, 377 IPC (excluded under BNS)', POCSO Act 2012 and the sexual offences under the Information Technology Act, 2000
Box 3 kidnapping/abduction heads: 'Sections 137(1)(b), 138, 137(2), 87 BNS / 361, 362, 365, 366 IPC'

Box 3 child-specific heads: 63 BNS (rape of a minor); 70 BNS (gangrape of any child); 77 BNS (disrobing and voyeurism); 139 BNS (maiming a child for child labour); 95 BNS (hiring a child for criminal activities)
Box 3 procurement/sale chain: 96 BNS / 366A IPC; 98 BNS / 372 IPC; 99 BNS / 373 IPC; 141 BNS / 366B IPC
Box 3 rape and technology heads: '63, 68, 69, 70 BNS / 375 IPC, 3, 5 of the POCSO Act'; '13 POCSO Act, 67B Information Technology Act, 2000'; '377 IPC – excluded under BNS'

Sections 88 to 94 BNS / 312 to 318 IPC — causing miscarriage; 146 BNS / 374 IPC — unlawful compulsory labour; 356(1) BNS / 499 IPC — defamation; 60 BNS / 120B IPC — criminal conspiracy; 54 BNS / 114 IPC — abetment; 222 BNS / 187 IPC — refusal to assist public servant
steps.triage_why: Encourages thoroughness to find additional crimes, but the primary charges are already identified in the FIR.

ticks.do: Treat the case as a 'basket of crimes' and conduct investigation into each of these violations.
Question the victim sensitively and listen to the untold story, an art which a professional investigator should possess.
notes: The story as it unfolds unravels a long list of offences perpetrated by various offenders on the victim.

ticks.do: Atomize the typical case of sex trafficking of a girl child, which would reveal that human trafficking is an organised crime with several crimes in itself (Box 3).

steps.title: Investigate consequential harms and add their offences
steps.text: Investigate the consequential harms and add the offences they attract: oftentimes victims become pregnant as they are subjected to non-protective sex, and if the victim has been subjected to miscarriage the offender becomes liable under Sections 88 to 94 BNS / 312 to 318 IPC; and if the exploitation becomes fatal, wherein the victim succumbs to the direct effects of the harm or to the consequential problems arising thereof, the offence of homicide/murder is attracted.

steps.title: Base the FIR on the Complainant's Statement
steps.text: The content: the FIR has to be on the statement (FIS – First Information Statement) of the complainant, and that statement cannot be altered or amended by the police. If the complainant is the victim herself she may be traumatised and unable to recall the events which constitute specific offences; the police officer can help her to recall such events.
steps.stage: Registering the crime (FIR) at the police station (4.2)
legal_basis: s.176(3) BNSS – mandatory visit of a forensic expert to the scene of crime, with videography of the process on a mobile phone or other electronic device (printed at PDF pp.65 and 88)

s.180 BNSS – statement of witnesses/victim to police. The handbook prints it BOTH ways: para 4.2 (PDF p.64) prints 'u/s 180, BNSS (Section 161, CrPC)', while the heading of para 4.10 (PDF p.82) prints 'Recording Statement u/s. 180 BNSS (160 CrPC)'. Both printed forms are retained verbatim; s.180 BNSS in fact corresponds to s.161 CrPC
s.183 BNSS [CrPC 164] – statement recorded before a Magistrate (printed at PDF pp.64, 79, 84)
s.187 BNSS [CrPC 167] – 60/90-day charge-sheet limit and default bail (PDF p.91)
s.192 BNSS [CrPC 172] – case diary; the '192 portion' (PDF pp.84, 86)
s.18(8) BNSS [proviso to CrPC 24(8)] – private lawyer permitted to assist the prosecutor and extend legal counselling to the victim (PDF p.75)
ss.115–122 BNSS [ss.105–110 CrPC] – provisions put to use for confiscating the illicit (PDF p.95)
s.143 BNS [IPC 370] and s.144 BNS [IPC 370A] – trafficking of persons and of a child; both cognizable (PDF p.92)

BNS sections 98, 99, 63, 96, 141, 143, 144 – the sections whose application the handbook says turns on the age of the rescued person (printed as a list at PDF p.76, with the rider '(Also see BNSS provisions)'). [BNS 63 = IPC 375 rape; BNS 96 = IPC 366A; BNS 98 = IPC 366B; BNS 99 = IPC 373; BNS 141 = IPC 372]
ss.3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8 and 9 ITPA – the cognizable offences under the Immoral Traffic (Prevention) Act, 1956 (PDF p.92)
s.5(3) ITPA – jurisdiction of courts at source, transit and destination (PDF p.64)
s.13(2A) ITPA – notification of a retired woman police officer as Special Police Officer where WPOs are short (PDF p.66)
steps.triage_why: The integrity of the FIS is a statutory requirement; unauthorized alteration of the complainant's statement can lead to the case being thrown out.

ticks.do: Base the FIR on the statement (FIS - First Information Statement) of the complainant.
Leave that statement unaltered, as it cannot be altered or amended by the police.
Note that the police officer can help the victim complainant to recall the events which constitute specific offences, where she is traumatised and unable to recall them.

steps.title: Do Not Hold Up FIR Registration for Detail
steps.text: Do not hold up registration for want of detail. The statement of the victim recorded in due course u/s 180 BNSS (printed in the source as 'Section 161, CrPC') or u/s 183 BNSS (164 CrPC) should bring in all details, including those missed out in the FIR. There need not be any anxiety to fill up the FIR with every detail, though all efforts should be made to make it as comprehensive as possible; even a cryptic hand-written note which makes out a cognizable offence is adequate to get the FIR registered.

steps.title: Consolidate Multiple FIRs on the Same Issue
steps.text: If two or more FIRs are lodged at different police stations on the same issue, the police officials can eventually consult each other and transfer the evidence and case documents to one of the police stations, which can follow it up thereafter. This is no reason to deny an FIR or not to commence investigation.

steps.title: Keep the FIR Free of Distortion
steps.text: No distortion: the FIR is the first document initiating the process of justice delivery and the steps that follow are mostly dependent on it. A distorted FIR where the victim has been shown as accused entails further violations and harm to the victim. Therefore the victim must be projected as a victim and never as an accomplice.

In respect of child victims under the age of 12 years, the consent may be taken from the parent or guardian if they are not part of the problem. steps.title: Provide Trained Mental Health Care to the Victim
steps.text: Box 15 – Psychological care of victims: mental health care is an area often neglected by the police and other after-care agencies despite its crucial role in victim care and rehabilitation. The Mental Healthcare Act, 2017 provides for mental healthcare and services in a rights-based manner and lays down procedural requirements. Do associate appropriate governmental/non-governmental agencies; an untrained counsellor can cause further damage and trauma to the victim, so try and provide a trained and qualified expert from the very beginning. Trauma counselling should be ensured even at the home/lodging house and should be a continuous process, as the victim will take time to get over the trauma. Further, the counsellor/psychiatrist can be an important witness in the court of law if cited as an expert witness in the charge sheet filed against the accused. The focus should be to empower the victim, and all steps and initiatives must be rights-based and in the best interest of the victim.

steps.title: Record every injury, illness and psychological harm
steps.text: Map and document the entire harm and damage done to the victims — a significant aspect usually neglected in the investigation process. Box 18 lists the essential features: injuries of physical assault (beating, cigarette burning, etc.); injuries of rape and other sexual assaults; injuries consequential to the various acts of exploitation (e.g. abortion or sexually transmitted infections due to denial of safe sex methods); injuries consequential to the denial of medical care and attention (e.g. UTI which arises due to lack of timely treatment of minor injuries) or lack of hygiene; the psychological harm (mental torture, trauma, anxiety, PTSD, stress and tension levels) arising not only from exploitation, intimidation and denial of privacy and dignity but also from neglect of oneself, of one's children, and abuse of the children; and physical and mental harm to the dependent children of the victim, especially those staying with her.

steps.title: Dissect the offence into elements and marshal evidence
steps.text: Dissect the law and list out the elements of the offence, then check out the contents of each of these elements. Develop a POA for investigation into each element so that none is missed out, and marshal evidence element-wise so that the presentation is cogent and convincing. The elements vary with the offence alleged, though there are certain common points in all the offences. A ready reckoner on the major elements of the penal sections of ITPA and 370 IPC [now s.143 BNS], along with the nature and type of evidence which can be adduced, is given in the Checklist at Appendix-I of the handbook.

steps.title: Build corroboration for every point in the statement
steps.text: While interviewing the victim and recording the 180 statement, develop all the points that need corroboration with documents, materials and exhibits, which may be even electronic. For example, if the victim was trafficked by train from Katihar to Patna, the train tickets and the CCTV footage at Katihar and Patna railway stations will be relevant. Such evidence will clinch the offence against the trafficker even if the victim fumbles under intimidation, will put less strain on the victim and will also ensure the victim's rights.

steps.title: Follow POCSO safeguards when interviewing a child

steps.title: Secure the 183 BNSS statement before a Magistrate
steps.text: Get the statement recorded u/s 183 BNSS [s.164 CrPC] as a safety measure, mainly for two reasons. Firstly, admission before a police officer is not admissible under Indian law ('25 Ev Act' — s.25 Indian Evidence Act, 1872, now s.23 BSA 2023), but a statement recorded before a Magistrate becomes admissible as evidence, and it forms important corroboratory evidence in the prosecution of offenders. Secondly, even if the victim/witness whose statement has been recorded eventually turns hostile, the 183 BNSS statement can be used to confront the person. The statement u/s 183 BNSS is mandatory in all sexual offence cases and is to be recorded as soon as the commission of the offence is brought to the notice of the police.

steps.text: Use the s.192 BNSS portion of the case diary properly — an important aspect usually neglected. This portion of the CD is not available to the defence, but the court can have access to it. steps.title: Extend the scene of crime beyond the brothel
steps.text: What is the SOC: investigation is a professional art which is in the exclusive domain of the investigators and a prerogative of the police; investigation at the SOC has to be comprehensive and holistic and should not be perfunctory or superficial. Usually, as seen in the case diaries of several crimes, the SOC is perceived to be a room in a brothel — this is incorrect. The scene of crime extends to the place from where the person was trafficked, the places where she was taken to, all the transit places and all the destinations where she was exploited. Therefore the SOC should include: the source point (e.g. the place of recruitment); the trafficking routes (including the mode of transport); the transit points (e.g. halting places enroute); the destination point; the points of exploitation (e.g. the brothel); the places where the 'products' of exploitation were transferred to (e.g. in a case where the CSE was to produce pornography, the places where the pornographic materials were edited, value added, published, copied, stored, sent to, transported, and the places where they were sold or purchased); the electronic sites where messages and pictures were exchanged, stored or utilised; the call records of all relevant communications; and the money trails of all transactions including cash, hawala, non-banking channels, crypto and mule accounts.

steps.title: Bring a forensic expert to every scene
steps.text: Forensic evidence: s.176(3) BNSS mandates a forensic expert to visit the scene of crime to collect evidence and cause videography of the process on a mobile phone or any other electronic device. The different materials that are relevant in a SOC of rape ipso facto apply to a sex-trafficking SOC too. The IO/rescuing official should carry out a thorough search of all the scenes of crime, collect, preserve and document all relevant materials and get them examined by forensic experts.

steps.title: Time the Arrest to Protect the Charge-Sheet Clock
steps.text: Arrest of offenders should be done only at the appropriate time and only when it is warranted based on the evidence. There is no point in rushing to arrest, as it will delimit the time available for filing a charge sheet: as per s.187 BNSS [s.167 CrPC], if the charge sheet is not filed within 60 days (90 days in cases of graver offences) of arrest, the arrestee will be bailed out. If the evidence could be adequately built up and marshalled before arrest, it would be useful for opposing his bail in the court of law.

ticks.do: Put these forensic queries to the laboratory in cases of cyber-enabled trafficking and the production, storage or sale of pornographic material:
sub: Ask what data can be recovered from the seized cell phones, computers, pen drives and electronic recorders, including deleted messages, chats, e-mails, images and videos
Ask which device was used to capture, edit, value-add, copy, store, transmit or sell the pornographic material
Ask whether the call records and message logs establish contact between the traffickers, agents, customers and the victim, and over what period
Ask whether the seized devices contain transaction records evidencing transfer of funds through bank channels, hawala, crypto or mule accounts
Ask whether the electronic trail can be reconstructed where messages were erased or the computer was formatted

steps.title: Act in Emergency as Officer-in-Charge of the Station
steps.text: In cases of emergency, even when an SI-rank official is not available, any official whosoever is in charge of the police station must act, since the CrPC [now BNSS] empowers the officer-in-charge of the police station to take all steps to prevent crimes. He must record the reasons in the General Diary and act swiftly; when the senior official arrives he can take over the investigation. (Step spans PDF pp.65–66.)
legal_basis: s.13(1) ITPA – State Government may notify one or more police officers not below the rank of Inspector of Police as Special Police Officer (PDF p.50)
s.13(2A) ITPA – District Magistrate may notify a retired police officer (not below Inspector at retirement) or a retired military officer (Commissioned Officer at retirement) as SPO (PDF pp.51, 66)
s.13(3)(a) ITPA – SPO to be assisted by an adequate number of subordinate police officers including women police officers, wherever practicable (PDF p.51)
s.13(3)(b) ITPA – State Government may notify a non-official advisory body of leading social workers, up to five persons, including women social workers (PDF p.53)
s.13(3)(4) ITPA – Government of India may notify Anti-Trafficking Police Officers (ATPO) with powers throughout India (PDF p.51)
s.15 ITPA – search of premises without warrant by the Special Police Officer, and rescue (PDF p.65)

s.15(2) ITPA and its proviso – two or more respectable persons of the locality to attend and witness the search, one of whom shall be a woman; the male witness from the locality, the female witness may be from anywhere (PDF pp.54, 66)
s.15(3) ITPA – refusal or neglect, without reasonable cause, to attend and witness a search on an order in writing is deemed an offence u/s 222 BNS / 187 IPC (PDF p.55)
s.15(5A) ITPA – Magistrate to order medical examination for (a) age determination, (b) injuries, (c) sexual assault, (d) presence of STD (PDF p.68)

s.15(6) ITPA – the authorised police officer, the witnesses and the NGOs who take part in, attend or witness a search shall not be liable to any civil or criminal litigation for bona fide work connected with a search u/s 15 ITPA (PDF p.57)

s.15(6A) ITPA – any female person rescued or removed during a search (including victims, suspects and accused) may be interviewed only by a female police officer, or by a male police officer in the presence of a female police officer, or of a female member of an NGO where no female police officer is available (PDF pp.54, 66)

s.16 ITPA – rescue of any person, irrespective of age, made to carry on prostitution in a brothel, on the order of a Judicial Magistrate (MM or JM) or an Executive Magistrate (DM or SDM), directed to any police officer not below the rank of SI; rescued persons to be produced forthwith (PDF pp.44, 45, 65–67)
steps.triage_why: This is a rule regarding administrative authority and emergency protocols, not a specific investigative step for this case.

steps.title: Report Suspected POCSO Offences to the Police
steps.text: Where any person suspects that an offence under the POCSO Act — which includes sexual exploitation in the context of trafficking — has taken place or may take place, that person is legally obligated to report such information to the police under s.19(1) POCSO Act. Failure to report is punishable under s.21 POCSO Act with imprisonment up to six months or fine or both.

steps.title: Move the court for in-camera trial
steps.text: In-camera trial: move the court for allowing in-camera trial; the Supreme Court of India in 'Sakshi vs. Union of India' has directed that in-camera trial should be extended to all cases of sexual assault on children.
steps.stage: Victim care and protection during trial (Ch. 6.3)
legal_basis: Section 111 BNS — human trafficking as an organized crime. NOTE ON PROVENANCE: this framing is NOT printed in pp.101-130; it is the book's premise stated at PDF pp.5, 13 and 40 ('Since human trafficking is an organized crime, u/s 111 BNS…'; 'Section 111 BNS defines the constituents of organized crime, which includes "human trafficking for prostitution"'; 'The trafficker is liable under 143 BNS / 111 BNS'). Section 143 BNS (370 IPC) is the definition of trafficking; 144 BNS (370A IPC) is exploitation of a trafficked person
S.7 ITPA and S.18(2) ITPA — action to be moved through the prosecutor once the court decides on the offence (printed 'u/s.7 ITPA, 18(2) ITPA etc.', p.102)
S.19 ITPA — application to the Magistrate for a protective home / corrective institution / supervision; S.17(4) ITPA — such order may also be made suo moto by the Magistrate (p.103)
section 366 BNSS / 327(2) of the CrPC — mandates in-camera trials in all rape cases (printed exactly thus, p.103)
S.160 CrPC (179 BNSS) — female victim not to be called to the police station after evening (p.105)
S.157 of the CrPC (176 BNSS) and S.24 of the POCSO Act — rape victims and child victims of sexual abuse to be interviewed at a place of her choice (p.105)
S 398 BNSS — witness protection section; Witness Protection Scheme, 2018 legally mandatory for the union, all States and UTs (Mahender Chawla Vs Union of India, p.107)

Section 357A CrPC (introduced 2009) — victim compensation; the source itself states 'Under BNSS, Section 396 deals with the subject' (p.107); section 357A(5) of the CrPC [now s.396(5) BNSS] — DLSA enquiry to be completed within two months (p.108)
POCSO Act S.33(8) read with Rule 7 of the POCSO Rules — compensation ordered by the Special Court hearing the POCSO case (p.109)
section 192 BNSS [= 172 CrPC] — Case Diary, operational part (pp.127-128)
Sections 180 and 183 BNSS [= 161 and 164 CrPC] — statements of victim/witness (p.127; the recording protocol is carried in the companion entry 'trafficking-interrogation-skills')
Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2015 — trafficked child is a 'child in need of care and protection', not a 'child in conflict with the law' (p.106)
steps.triage_why: Statutory and judicial mandate for POCSO/sexual assault cases to protect the child victim; failure to move the court can violate the victim's rights and legal procedure.

ticks.do: Move the court for allowing in-camera trial.
notes: The Supreme Court of India in 'Sakshi vs. Union of India' has directed that in-camera trial should be extended to all cases of sexual assault on children.

steps.title: Weigh the prosecutrix's evidence as an injured witness
steps.text: Rely on the principle that a prosecutrix of a sex-offence cannot be put on par with an accomplice and is a victim of the crime — her evidence must receive the same weight as is attached to an injured in cases of physical violence, and the same degree of care and caution must attach in the evaluation of her evidence as in the case of an injured complainant or witness and no more — State of Maharashtra Vs Chandra Prakash Kewal Chand Jain, AIR 1990 SC 658.
