steps.title: Gather Crime Scene, Suspect and Trail Details
steps.text: Interview (c) to gather information about the scene(s) of crime, witnesses, sequence of events, name and details of the suspects / accused, evidence against them, money trail and communication trail.
steps.stage: Purpose and planning of the victim / witness interview (Ch. 7.3)
legal_basis: Sections 180 and 183 BNSS [= 161 and 164 CrPC] — statements of victim/witness, printed by the source as 'statements u/s 180 and 183 BNSS' (p.117) and 'The 180 and 183 statements' (p.127), to be recorded as per the procedure in the ITPA and POCSO Acts

ITPA — the 180 statement of a rescued woman, irrespective of age, shall be recorded by a female police officer; if a female is not available, by a male police officer in the presence of a female social worker (p.127)

POCSO Act — mandatory to have a female official interview and record statements of children, both male and female; if a female police officer is not available, a female government official, and if that is not possible, a woman from an NGO (p.127); the law does not exclude male police officers from interviewing, it only requires that the statement be recorded by a female person

section 192 BNSS [= 172 CrPC] — operational part of the Case Diary, in which the interview challenges, emotional outbursts, trauma and related responses of the victim are to be captured without editing (p.120)

Indian Evidence Act — admission of the accused before a police officer is not admissible unless it leads to discovery or recovery (p.124) [the source cites the IEA as such; under the new era s.25 IEA is now s.23(1) BSA 2023, s.26 IEA is now s.23(2) BSA, and the discovery/recovery exception in s.27 IEA is now the proviso to s.23(2) BSA]

Provision in law for turning a co-accused into an 'approver' and treating that person as a witness (the source refers to the provision without citing a section, p.125) — the admission must be inculpatory and not exculpatory, the role must be of a minor nature and not that of the mastermind, and the prosecutor must agree and place it before the court and the court must finally agree
Rights-based interrogation: torture and 'third degree' are not permitted at all and shall be shunned completely; even fear and threat constitute torture (p.123)
steps.triage_why: Essential for identifying the crime scene and establishing the communication trail (Instagram/calls) which is the primary evidence in this case.

witnesses

communication trail

steps.title: Decode the Child Victim's Own Vocabulary
steps.text: Decode the child victim's own vocabulary rather than the adult's: the mind of the IO should be agile and alert to analyse the events, situations, statements and materials — in the source's paedophilic exploitation case the child, whose father had been sodomising her for long, kept saying that the 'father feeds me, he feeds with feeding bottle, it stinks', 'bottle' being the child's own word taught by the father; by careful listening the IO could make out what the child meant, and by associating child psychologists the offence of sodomy was proved in the court.
steps.triage_why: Provides an illustrative example of decoding child vocabulary.

steps.title: Route a confession through the Magistrate
steps.text: In case the accused wants to make a confession, ensure that the accused is sent to judicial custody and is summoned by the court for recording of the confession. The confession is recorded by a Magistrate under section 183 BNSS, who must first explain that making it is not compulsory and that it may be used as evidence against him, satisfy himself that it is being made voluntarily, follow the section 316 procedure with the prescribed memorandum, and — if the person declines to confess — may not authorise police custody; audio-video recording of the confession in the presence of the accused's advocate is permitted, and no police officer on whom magisterial powers have been conferred may record a confession. If during investigation it is found that there is more than one accused and one or more of them wants to become an APPROVER, the same procedure shall be adopted.
steps.stage: S. Court proceedings: TIP, remand, scientific tests and confessions
legal_basis: BNSS 183
steps.applies_when: Accused offers to confess or to turn approver
steps.triage_why: This is a procedural rule that applies only if the accused chooses to confess; it is not a mandatory step for the IO to initiate.

steps.title: Map the facts to sections, not generic charges
steps.text: Map the established facts to sections using the offence-to-section table rather than charging generically. Data owned in electronic form stolen - Sec 66 IT Act (up to 3 years or fine up to Rs 5 lakh or both). Password stolen and used fraudulently - Sec 66C and 66D IT Act (up to 3 years and fine up to Rs 1 lakh each) with Sec 419 IPC / 319(2) BNS. Capturing/publishing/transmitting the image of a private area without consent - Sec 66E IT Act; Sec 292 IPC / 294 BNS; Sec 354C IPC / 77 BNS (where the victim is female and the perpetrator male); Sec 14 and 15 POCSO where a child is involved. Publishing or transmitting obscene material electronically - Sec 67 IT Act with Sec 292 IPC / 294 BNS. Material depicting children in a sexually explicit act - Sec 67B IT Act with Sec 14 and 15 POCSO. Insulting the modesty of a woman - Sec 509 IPC / 79 BNS. Criminal intimidation online - Sec 506 IPC / 351 BNS, and by anonymous communication Sec 507 IPC / 351(4) BNS. Sending offensive messages - Sec 500 IPC / 356(2)(3)(4) BNS with Sec 12 POCSO.
legal_basis: Sec 12, 13, 14, 15 POCSO Act
Sec 75 Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2015
steps.triage_why: This is a guidance tool for mapping facts to sections, not a procedural step of the investigation itself.

ticks.do: Charge Section 66 IT Act where data owned in electronic form is stolen.
notes: Punishable up to 3 years or fine up to Rs 5 lakh or both.

ticks.do: Charge Sections 66C and 66D IT Act with Section 419 IPC / Section 319(2) BNS where a password was stolen and used fraudulently.
notes: Sections 66C and 66D are punishable up to 3 years and fine up to Rs 1 lakh each.

ticks.do: Charge Section 66E IT Act, Section 292 IPC / Section 294 BNS and Section 354C IPC / Section 77 BNS for capturing, publishing or transmitting the image of a private area without consent.
notes: Section 354C IPC / Section 77 BNS applies where the victim is female and the perpetrator male.
Add Sections 14 and 15 POCSO where a child is involved.

ticks.do: Charge Section 67 IT Act with Section 292 IPC / Section 294 BNS for publishing or transmitting obscene material electronically.
Charge Section 67B IT Act with Sections 14 and 15 POCSO for material depicting children in a sexually explicit act.
Charge Section 509 IPC / Section 79 BNS for insulting the modesty of a woman.
Charge Section 506 IPC / Section 351 BNS for criminal intimidation online, and Section 507 IPC / Section 351(4) BNS where it is by anonymous communication.
Charge Section 500 IPC / Section 356(2)(3)(4) BNS with Section 12 POCSO for sending offensive messages.
notes: The step's cited legal basis also lists Section 67A IT Act, 2000; Sections 153, 153A, 153B, 295A, 354A, 354D, 420, 465, 469, 501, 502, 505 IPC; Sections 75, 78, 192, 196, 197, 299, 336(2), 353 BNS; Section 13 POCSO; and Section 75 of the Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2015.

details.text: Obscenity cases - probable sections: Sec 66E, 67, 67A, 67B IT Act; Sec 354C and 509 IPC (Sec 77 and 79 BNS); Sec 13, 14 POCSO and Sec 75 JJ Act where the victim is a minor.

steps.title: Enforce the IT Act
steps.text: Where the case is registered under the IT Act, respect the Act's jurisdictional reach and rank requirements: the IT Act applies to an offence or contravention committed outside India by any person irrespective of nationality if the act involves a computer, computer system or computer network located in India (Sec 75); it has effect notwithstanding anything inconsistent in any other law in force (Sec 81); investigation must be by a police officer not below the rank of Inspector (Sec 78); and search and seizure in an IT Act case must be conducted by an officer of and above the rank of Police Inspector.
legal_basis: Sec 75 IT Act, 2000
Sec 78 IT Act, 2000
Sec 80 IT Act, 2000
Sec 81 IT Act, 2000
steps.triage_why: This provides legal context on jurisdiction for IT Act cases; the case is already registered at a specific station.

ticks.do: Apply the IT Act to an offence or contravention committed outside India by any person irrespective of nationality (Sec 75) if the act involves:
sub: a computer
computer system
computer network located in India

ticks.do: Give the IT Act effect notwithstanding anything inconsistent in any other law in force (Sec 81).
Ensure the investigation is by a police officer not below the rank of Inspector (Sec 78).
Conduct search and seizure in an IT Act case through an officer of and above the rank of Police Inspector.
notes: The step's cited legal basis is Sec 75, 78, 80 and 81 of the IT Act, 2000.

details.text: The legal provisions empowering the IO to conduct search and seizure of digital evidence are Section 165 CrPC [now BNSS 185] and Section 80 of the IT Act 2008; obtain search warrants complying with the legal process to avoid later issues.
details.citation: Karnataka - Standard Operating Procedures and Guidelines for Investigating Cyber Offences

details.text: Sec 80 (Chapter 13) IT Act: notwithstanding anything in the CrPC 1973 (2 of 1974), any police officer not below the rank of Inspector may enter any public place, search it, and arrest without warrant any person found there reasonably suspected of having committed, of committing, or of being about to commit any offence under that Act; Chapter 11 of the IT Act describes the offences.

steps.title: Classify the cyber offence against the standard typology
steps.text: Classify the cyber offence disclosed in the FIR against the standard typology. Cybercrime is any criminal activity involving computers: the computer may be the tool (e.g. hacking), the target (e.g. data breaches), or both (e.g. ransomware). The recognised classes are (a) online harassment - cyber bullying/stalking (use of ICT to stalk, harass, threaten or intimidate), cyber defamation, sextortion (extorting money or sexual favours by threatening to publish sexually explicit material), catfishing (fake identity built from the victim's own image/information), doxing (publishing sensitive personal data), cyber trolling, revenge porn, online grooming of a child; (b) social media fraud - dating app fraud, account/page takeover by stolen credentials, fake/deepfake/AI impersonating profiles, fake news and misinformation, online pornography including CSEAM, metaverse/virtual-reality crimes, matrimonial fraud; (c) email frauds - email hacking, email spoofing (forged header), spamming.
steps.applies_when: any cyber offence; used to select the offence-specific SOP track
steps.triage_why: This is a definitional guide to cybercrime typology for classification purposes.

ticks.do: Determine whether the computer was the tool (e.g. hacking), the target (e.g. data breaches), or both (e.g. ransomware), cybercrime being any criminal activity involving computers.
Check the case against recognised class (a), online harassment.
sub: Check for cyber bullying/stalking (use of ICT to stalk, harass, threaten or intimidate).
Check for cyber defamation.
Check for sextortion (extorting money or sexual favours by threatening to publish sexually explicit material).
Check for catfishing (fake identity built from the victim's own image/information).
Check for doxing (publishing sensitive personal data).
Check for cyber trolling.
Check for revenge porn.
Check for online grooming of a child.

ticks.do: Check the case against recognised class (b), social media fraud.
sub: Check for dating app fraud.
Check for account/page takeover by stolen credentials.
Check for fake/deepfake/AI impersonating profiles.
Check for fake news and misinformation.
Check for online pornography including CSEAM.
Check for metaverse/virtual-reality crimes.
Check for matrimonial fraud.

ticks.do: Check the case against recognised class (c), email frauds.
sub: Check for email hacking.
Check for email spoofing (forged header).
Check for spamming.

steps.title: Keep digital evidence lawful, auditable and unaltered
steps.text: Apply the cardinal principles of digital forensics to every act in the case: obtain digital evidence in a legally accepted manner; prove its relevance to the case; keep procedures auditable, repeatable and reproducible; acquire enough evidence for a complete and proper investigation; keep all actions justifiable; use a method that satisfies accuracy and reliability of the copy against the original; never work on the original evidence; and document chain of custody at every step. There must be no unlawful collection violating citizens' rights and liberties and no unnecessary collection; handling of the original must be minimised by working on a forensic copy or image; any accidental or unavoidable change to the original must be documented; and no officer may experiment with his learnings on seized original digital evidence.
steps.stage: Digital forensics and electronic evidence fundamentals (reference)
steps.triage_why: Digital evidence (photos/recordings) is volatile; failure to follow forensic principles leads to the evidence being thrown out as tampered with.

ticks.do: Obtain digital evidence in a legally accepted manner and prove its relevance to the case.
Keep procedures auditable, repeatable and reproducible, and keep all actions justifiable.
Acquire enough evidence for a complete and proper investigation.
Use a method that satisfies accuracy and reliability of the copy against the original, and never work on the original evidence.
Document chain of custody at every step.
Avoid any unlawful collection violating citizens' rights and liberties, and any unnecessary collection.
Minimise handling of the original by working on a forensic copy or image, and document any accidental or unavoidable change to the original.
Never experiment with your learnings on seized original digital evidence.

details.text: Four-part test to apply before collecting forensic evidence: is it authentic (comes from where it is said to come from), reliable (consistent story, no reason to doubt the computer was working correctly), complete (shows the whole picture), and free from interference and contamination?
details.citation: Karnataka - Standard Operating Procedures and Guidelines for Investigating Cyber Offences

details.text: General criteria for admissibility: Authenticity (indisputable and representative of its original state), Completeness (tells the whole story, not tailored to a favourable perspective), Reliability (nothing in collection or handling casts doubt), Convincing/Persuasive (true to the facts), and Proportionality (fair methods - prejudice caused must not outweigh probative value).
details.citation: Karnataka - Standard Operating Procedures and Guidelines for Investigating Cyber Offences

details.text: Three-pronged approach: identification of potential digital evidence; extraction and examination (recovering and meticulously analysing data); and presentation of findings in a clear, legally admissible format for court. Digital evidence sources crucial to investigations include computer network logs, mobile phones, CCTV footage, emails, documents and images.
details.citation: Karnataka - Standard Operating Procedures and Guidelines for Investigating Cyber Offences

details.text: Unlike conventional crimes, cybercrime investigation involves intangible electronic evidence which, if not seized or preserved properly, may become unavailable or inadmissible in court.

steps.title: Know the forensic branches and what they deliver
steps.text: Know the sub-branches of digital forensics and what a forensic examination can deliver. Sub-branches: Disk Forensics (hard disks, USB, CD/DVD, flash drives); Network Forensics (volatile, dynamic traffic); Database Forensics; Malware Forensics (viruses, trojans, worms, key loggers); Mobile Device Forensics; Memory Forensics (registers, cache, RAM raw dumps); IoT Forensics; Cloud Forensics; Drone Forensics; Vehicle Forensics. Digital forensics can protect the subject system from alteration, damage, corruption or virus introduction during examination; discover all files (active, deleted-but-remaining, hidden, password-protected, encrypted); recover deleted files; reveal hidden, temporary and swap file contents; access protected or encrypted files where legally appropriate; analyse special inaccessible disk areas; and provide expert consultation or testimony. Analysis outcomes include data recovery from unallocated and slack space, string and keyword searching, volatile evidence analysis, timeline analysis, system file analysis, malware analysis, smartphone analysis and network analysis. The globally practised process is Preparation, Identification, Collection, Preservation, Examination, Analysis, Presentation.
steps.stage: Digital forensics and electronic evidence fundamentals (reference)
steps.triage_why: This is background knowledge about forensic branches, not an action step.

ticks.do: Identify the sub-branch of digital forensics the case requires.
sub: Consider Disk Forensics (hard disks, USB, CD/DVD, flash drives).
Consider Network Forensics (volatile, dynamic traffic).
Consider Database Forensics.
Consider Malware Forensics (viruses, trojans, worms, key loggers).
Consider Mobile Device Forensics.
Consider Memory Forensics (registers, cache, RAM raw dumps).
Consider IoT Forensics.
Consider Cloud Forensics.
Consider Drone Forensics.
Consider Vehicle Forensics.

ticks.do: Require the examination to protect the subject system from alteration, damage, corruption or virus introduction during examination.
Ask for discovery of all files - active, deleted-but-remaining, hidden, password-protected and encrypted - and for recovery of deleted files.
Ask for the contents of hidden, temporary and swap files to be revealed and for access to protected or encrypted files where legally appropriate.
Ask for analysis of special inaccessible disk areas and for expert consultation or testimony.
Expect the analysis outcomes the laboratory can deliver.
sub: Expect data recovery from unallocated and slack space.
Expect string and keyword searching.
Expect volatile evidence analysis.
Expect timeline analysis.
Expect system file analysis.
Expect malware analysis.
Expect smartphone analysis.
Expect network analysis.

ticks.do: Follow the globally practised process in its order.
sub: Preparation
Identification
Collection
Preservation
Examination
Analysis
Presentation

steps.title: Identify potential evidence device by device
steps.text: Identify the potential evidence each class of device can yield, using the device-wise map. Desktop/laptop: browser usage, external device/USB usage, file and folder opening, account usage, file download and execution, deleted files, network activity, physical location. RAM: processes and threads, malware, network sockets, URLs, IP addresses. Smartphones/tablets: open files, user-generated content (passwords, caches, clipboards), encryption keys, hardware/software configuration, registry keys and event logs, photographs with EXIF metadata, video/audio, maps, MMS, GPS waypoints, stored voicemail, online accounts and purchased media (often discoverable in embedded metadata), email IDs, internet and social networking information, alternate messaging systems, chat logs, spoofing apps, anonymizers, malware applications. Server: event logs, Active Directory settings, mailboxes, backups. NAS, memory cards, flash drives, external hard drives and optical discs: files/folders, multimedia, applications, date and time stamps. Digital cameras: images, videos, sound recordings, GPS details, timestamps. GPS navigation: travel logs, home location, previous destinations, waypoints. Dash cameras: GPS data, vehicular speed, licence plate data, temporal data. Smartwatches: contacts, SMS, health and sports data. Smart TVs: connected devices, browsing history, installed applications. Drones: diagnostic logs, paired devices, multimedia, flight/telematics logs, map artefacts. Vehicles: VIN/serial/part/build numbers, connected phones and media, tracklogs and saved routes, device IDs, calls, contacts, SMS, media, door/light events, Bluetooth/Wi-Fi/USB connections, GPS time syncs, odometer and telematics.
steps.stage: Digital forensics and electronic evidence fundamentals (reference)
steps.triage_why: This is a reference map to help the IO identify what to look for on devices.

ticks.do: Examine a desktop or laptop for the evidence it yields.
sub: Look for browser usage and external device or USB usage.
Look for file and folder opening and account usage.
Look for file download and execution and deleted files.
Look for network activity and physical location.

ticks.do: Capture RAM for the evidence it yields.
sub: Look for processes and threads and malware.
Look for network sockets, URLs and IP addresses.

ticks.do: Examine smartphones and tablets for the evidence they yield.
sub: Recover open files, user-generated content (passwords, caches, clipboards) and encryption keys.
Record the hardware and software configuration, registry keys and event logs.
Extract photographs with EXIF metadata, video and audio, maps, MMS, GPS waypoints and stored voicemail.
Extract online accounts and purchased media, often discoverable in embedded metadata, and email IDs.
Extract internet and social networking information, alternate messaging systems and chat logs.
Look for spoofing apps, anonymizers and malware applications.

ticks.do: Examine a server for event logs, Active Directory settings, mailboxes and backups.
Examine NAS, memory cards, flash drives, external hard drives and optical discs for files and folders, multimedia, applications and date and time stamps.
Examine cameras and navigation devices for the evidence they yield.
sub: Take from digital cameras the images, videos, sound recordings, GPS details and timestamps.
Take from GPS navigation the travel logs, home location, previous destinations and waypoints.
Take from dash cameras the GPS data, vehicular speed, licence plate data and temporal data.

ticks.do: Examine wearables and smart TVs for the evidence they yield.
sub: Take from smartwatches the contacts, SMS and health and sports data.
Take from smart TVs the connected devices, browsing history and installed applications.

ticks.do: Examine drones and vehicles for the evidence they yield.
sub: Take from drones the diagnostic logs, paired devices, multimedia, flight and telematics logs and map artefacts.
Take from vehicles the VIN, serial, part and build numbers, connected phones and media, tracklogs and saved routes and device IDs.
Take from vehicles the calls, contacts, SMS and media, door and light events, Bluetooth, Wi-Fi and USB connections, GPS time syncs, odometer and telematics.

steps.title: Register the FIR and decide on preliminary enquiry
steps.text: Register the FIR on information disclosing a cognizable offence. The information may be given orally or by electronic communication and must be recorded irrespective of the area in which the offence was committed (zero FIR); oral information is written down, read over to the informant and signed, while information given electronically must be signed by the informant within three days of being taken on record. A free copy of the FIR goes to the informant or victim forthwith. A preliminary enquiry to decide whether a prima facie case exists is available only where the offence is punishable with three years or more but less than seven years, only with the prior permission of an officer not below the rank of Deputy Superintendent of Police, and must be completed within fourteen days; otherwise the officer proceeds straight to investigation. Refusal to register may be escalated by the informant to the Superintendent of Police and then by application to the Magistrate.
steps.stage: Complaint receipt, registration and first response
legal_basis: BNSS 173
BNSS 175
BNSS 176
steps.deadline: Electronic FIR to be signed by the informant within 3 days; preliminary enquiry (3 to under 7 years offences only) within 14 days; FIR copy to informant/victim forthwith
steps.triage_why: The FIR is already registered (as per the case description), making the registration process a past event/reference.

ticks.do: Register the FIR on information disclosing a cognizable offence, the information being capable of being given orally or by electronic communication.
notes: Legal basis: BNSS 173, 175 and 176.
Refusal to register may be escalated by the informant to the Superintendent of Police and then by application to the Magistrate.

ticks.do: Record the information irrespective of the area in which the offence was committed (zero FIR).
Write down oral information, read it over to the informant and have it signed.
Get information given electronically signed by the informant within three days of being taken on record.
Give a free copy of the FIR to the informant or victim forthwith.
Hold a preliminary enquiry to decide whether a prima facie case exists only within its stated limits.
sub: Hold it only where the offence is punishable with three years or more but less than seven years.
Take the prior permission of an officer not below the rank of Deputy Superintendent of Police.
Complete the enquiry within fourteen days.

ticks.do: Proceed straight to investigation otherwise.

details.text: Karnataka workflow: on receipt of a complaint conduct a pre-investigation assessment and determine whether a criminal offence is made out; if yes register the FIR, if no issue an endorsement to the complainant (matter of civil nature / outside legal jurisdiction). After FIR registration, collect information and documents from the complainant and from intermediaries, banks and others, then analyse what is received.

steps.title: Get the offending content removed and preserved
steps.text: Move in parallel to have the offending content removed and preserved. Capture the URL where the content is found; guide the victim to report it to the concerned service provider; and communicate the collected information to the nodal officer of the social media intermediary from the official email ID or the designated law-enforcement portal, seeking both removal and preservation, clearly stating the reasons for removal by explaining the nature and impact of the content, and attaching an appropriate order of the investigating officer under Section 79(3)(b) IT Act and the IT (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021. Without delay also apply to the competent court for an order addressed to the intermediary for removal of the content and preservation of relevant evidence, and immediately serve that order on the intermediary; intermediaries may in certain cases insist on a court order. On any delay in compliance with the court's order, contact the platform's law-enforcement nodal officer directly.
steps.stage: Evidence preservation notices and content takedown
legal_basis: Sec 79 and 79(3)(b) IT Act, 2000
IT (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021
steps.deadline: Court application to be made without delay; the court order to be served immediately on receipt; intermediaries to act well within the time stipulated in the court order
steps.triage_why: Electronic evidence (photos/recordings) is volatile and can be deleted by the accused; prompt preservation is critical.

steps.title: Lock down records with preservation notices
steps.text: Serve a preservation notice on the intermediaries, platforms, website administrators and service providers holding relevant records at the preliminary stage of the investigation, to prevent destruction of evidence. The preliminary-stage notice under Section 7 of the IT Act 2000 directs the recipient to retain electronic records (a) in the format in which they were originally generated, sent or received, (b) accessible for subsequent reference during investigation or court proceedings, and (c) with the identifying features about origin, destination and date/time stamp retained. Where the recipient has already submitted records in secondary form, serve the subsequent-stage notice directing preservation of the original source in its original format, accessible at subsequent stages, with metadata retained. Where digital evidence cannot feasibly be seized, the preservation notice is the substitute and information/document collection continues.

legal_basis: Sec 7 IT Act, 2000
steps.triage_why: Prevents the destruction of evidence by intermediaries; essential for the integrity of the digital trail.

conflicts.description: Within the same document the Karnataka SOP places the preservation notice at three different points in the workflow: Annexure 4 is headed 'preservation notice at preliminary stage' (karnataka-cyber-annexures-tools, p.50); the search-and-seizure preparation checklist lists issuing a preservation notice among the steps taken while preparing for seizure (karnataka-cyber-evidence-handling, p.21); and the investigation flowchart places it only on the 'No' branch of the seizure-feasibility decision, i.e. after that decision has been taken (karnataka-cyber-investigation, p.28).
conflicts.resolution: All three placements sit in the same source document at the same authority layer (state_advisory), so the ladder does not separate them. The canonical text adopts the earliest and most evidence-protective placement - the preliminary stage per Annexure 4 - and records the flowchart placement as a detail. The flowchart position is not read as barring an earlier notice, and the earlier draft wording 'before any seizure decision' has been removed because the flowchart contradicts it.

steps.title: Write, copy and hand over the case diary
steps.text: Maintain the case diary as the primary record of investigative action. Record each day's investigative action taken for working out the case and for progress in the investigation; the current and permanent addresses and mobile numbers of all witnesses must mandatorily be recorded. Entries must be made only in the pre-printed numbered proforma and in that same serial order, in legible handwriting, because the court may use the diary not as evidence but as an aid to the trial. Supervisory directions and prosecution officers' legal opinions on the file must not be reproduced in the diary - only the action taken in pursuance of them. Keep a carbon copy of the case diary (and, in enquiry cases, of the report sent to the Superintendent of Police); on transfer of the investigation hand the carbon copy to the successor officer against acknowledgment, and on conclusion deposit it in the record room. Where co-investigators are appointed, each maintains a Supplementary Case Diary which must be sent to the chief investigator without delay, summarised in his main diary and attached to the diary sent to the Superintendent of Police. Both copies must carry all annexures such as copies of witness statements and seizure memos, but not the daily correspondence with organisations and individuals.

legal_basis: Section 172 CrPC [now BNSS 192]
steps.triage_why: Statutory requirement for police officers to maintain a case diary; failure can jeopardize the admissibility of the investigation in court.

steps.title: Compel production of records by written order
steps.text: Compel production of records by written order. The officer in charge of a police station may issue a written order, in physical or electronic form, requiring any person believed to have possession or power over a document, electronic communication (including a communication device likely to contain digital evidence) or other thing necessary or desirable for the investigation, to attend and produce it or simply to produce it at the stated time and place; production through another person satisfies the requisition. The order cannot override the privileges under Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam sections 129-130 or the Bankers' Books Evidence Act, 1891, and does not reach items in postal custody.
steps.stage: Collection of information from intermediaries, telecom and banks
legal_basis: BNSS 94
Section 91 CrPC [now BNSS 94]
steps.deadline: Production must be at the time and place stated in the order; the law fixes no statutory period. The sample notice template at Annexure 2 of the Karnataka SOP allows seven days from receipt of the notice.
steps.responsible: Officer in charge of the police station (Courts issue summons)
steps.triage_why: A tool for evidence collection, but not a mandatory duty for every single case unless specific records are refused.

Require the person to attend and produce it, or simply to produce it, at the stated time and place.
Accept production through another person as satisfying the requisition.

steps.title: Identify every intermediary and frame its request
steps.text: Identify every intermediary holding relevant records and frame the request to each using the platform-specific matrix, supplying the identifiers the platform needs and asking for the data it holds. Social media (Facebook, Instagram, Twitter) - supply the profile URL; request account registration details, registration device name, registered email ID, mobile number, registration and access IP logs, recovery email/phone, and location details (especially Instagram). Instant messaging (WhatsApp) - supply the mobile number; request registration device details, registration date and time, current or last access IP, linked contact numbers, and desktop/web session system details. Email providers (Gmail, Yahoo, Hotmail, Outlook, Rediff) - supply the email ID, secondary email ID and IMEI; request registration details, registration and access device IDs, secondary/recovery email and phone, date of creation, two-step verification details, and access details with date/time and time zone, activity or event type and IP addresses. Domain hosting providers (GoDaddy, Bigrock) - supply the domain URL; request user registration details, registration date/time, date and time of hosting, login IP and MAC ID at hosting, website-owner information, correspondence address, synchronised activity log from hosting to date, payment details (registrant's account number, credit card, payment gateway) and linked mobile and email. UPI providers (Google Pay, Paytm, PhonePe) - supply the UPI ID, amount and transaction ID with date and time; request beneficiary account details, beneficiary mobile numbers, UPI-linked bank accounts and transaction details. Payment gateways (PayPal, Citrix, Billdesk, CC Avenue, Razorpay) - supply mobile number, email and KYC details; request transaction details, beneficiary account details, merchant registration and KYC. Cryptocurrency exchanges (Binance, WazirX, Unocoin) - supply TXID/wallet ID/email/user ID/phone number, amount, date and time; request customer information (user ID, email, mobile, registration date, KYC), account balance, order/deposit/withdrawal history, P2P logs, access logs with IPs, approved devices, card list, OTC trading, gift card transfers, loan orders and exchange trades.
steps.stage: Collection of information from intermediaries, telecom and banks
legal_basis: Sec 2(1)(w) IT Act, 2008 (definition of intermediary)
Section 91 CrPC [now BNSS 94]
steps.triage_why: Necessary to link the Instagram account to the accused; without specific identifiers, the evidence cannot be retrieved.

The IO must work out what information relevant to the investigation is available with third-party companies and providers.

steps.title: Resolve every IP address to a subscriber
steps.text: Resolve every IP address to a subscriber. Collect the IP logs from the service provider under a written production order; identify the IP address with its date and time and convert the time zone to Indian Standard Time using an online time-zone converter; identify the internet service provider using an IP lookup service such as apnic.net or myip.ms; then requisition from the ISP the IPDR and end-user details - the landline (broadband) or mobile number behind the data connection, the physical address with supporting documents such as the Customer Application Form, and other subscriber information. Take CDR, IPDR and IMEI details wherever necessary, obtain identification details of the device, and collect documents proving ownership or use of the device. Verify the persons in whose possession the IP-resolved mobile number or internet connection is actually found.

legal_basis: Section 91 CrPC [now BNSS 94]
steps.triage_why: Crucial to prove the accused was the one using the device/account; without IP resolution, the link to the suspect is circumstantial.

steps.title: Establish legal authority before entering the premises
steps.text: Establish the legal authority for the search before entering. Where the place is a private place, obtain a search warrant complying with the legal process. Where the investigating officer searches without a warrant within his own station limits, he must have reasonable grounds to believe the thing cannot otherwise be obtained without undue delay, must first record those grounds of belief in the case diary and specify the thing sought, must conduct the search in person if practicable, and must have the search recorded through audio-video electronic means, preferably by mobile phone. Delegation to a subordinate requires a written order recording the reasons, the place and the thing sought. The general search provisions of Section 103 apply. Copies of the search records must reach the nearest empowered Magistrate forthwith and not later than forty-eight hours, and the owner or occupier is entitled to a free copy on application.
steps.stage: Search and seizure of digital evidence - planning and legal authority
legal_basis: Section 185 BNSS 2023
Section 165 CrPC [now BNSS 185]
Sec 80 IT Act, 2008
steps.deadline: Copies of the search records to the nearest empowered Magistrate forthwith and not later than 48 hours
steps.triage_why: Constitutional and statutory requirement for search and seizure; illegal searches can lead to evidence being thrown out.

steps.title: Anchor the seizure with independent panch witnesses
steps.text: Conduct the seizure with independent panch/mahzar witnesses. A search made by a police officer under Section 185 BNSS attracts the general search provisions of Section 103, which require independent witnesses and a search list. Two independent witnesses must invariably be kept during the seizure proceedings at the scene, so that in addition to the electronic evidence their testimony assists the prosecution and no difficulty arises when evidence is given in court. As best practice, summon a government official with subject knowledge to act as a mahazar witness.

legal_basis: Section 185 BNSS 2023 (attracting the Section 103 general search provisions - independent witnesses, search list)
steps.triage_why: Statutory requirement under BNSS for independent witnesses during seizure to prevent allegations of planting evidence.

steps.title: Draw a documented plan of action for the search
steps.text: Draw a documented plan of action for the search, assessing each case individually because no single procedure fits all. The plan must document the questions needed to understand the type of case and its scope, a thorough interview of the complainant, witness and suspect, and the purpose of conducting the search; the type of digital evidence expected, its location and the associated challenges; the specific hardware and software tools required; and the full seizure team with each member's competencies and role. Do not take assistance from unauthorised individuals or companies. Carry personal safety requirements such as hand gloves to avoid static electricity. Before commencing, confirm the action plan is complete and accurate. Consider the ISO 27037 points: which collection or acquisition methods apply; what equipment is needed on site; the volatility level of the data; whether remote access to any device is possible and threatens evidential integrity; what happens if data or equipment is damaged; whether data could already have been compromised; and whether any device could be configured to destroy, spoil or obfuscate data - for instance a logic bomb - if switched off or accessed in an uncontrolled way. Decide in advance where the hardware or data will be kept so that after seizure it can be sent securely to the computer forensic laboratory.
steps.stage: Search and seizure of digital evidence - planning and legal authority
steps.triage_why: Good planning strengthens the case, but the lack of a written 'plan of action' document does not defeat the prosecution.

steps.title: Carry the digital search-and-seizure kit to the scene
steps.text: Carry the digital search-and-seizure kit to the scene: storage devices such as USB drives, hard disks and pen drives for preparing images of files; labelling material for writing on cables and on the computer's sockets so that it is known which cable was connected to which port; screwdrivers and other tools for separating the computer's parts; gloves, since searching and seizing must be carried out only while wearing gloves; packing materials - rubber bands, tape, boxes, bubble wrap, anti-static plastic bubble wrap and a Faraday bag, with a paper envelope as a substitute if anti-static bubble wrap is unavailable; aluminium foil; plain paper; a camera for video recording and photographs; chain-of-custody report sheets and the other forms necessary for taking case property into custody; a volatile data collection kit and, if available, a portable computer forensic kit; an electronic evidence container; and a scale, measuring tape, note pad, sketch pad, pen, pencil and permanent marker. Only material connected with the crime shall be taken into police custody.

steps.triage_why: Technical best practice for forensics, but failure to use a specific kit does not automatically invalidate the evidence.

steps.title: Requisition expert help for digital evidence collection
steps.text: Where the team lacks digital evidence expertise, seek assistance before acting. If the IO is not competent or trained enough to complete the evidence collection himself, he may requisition the services of Scene of Crime Officers or Inspectors in charge of designated cyber crime police stations, and this requisition must be duly recorded in the mahazar. Where a computer system is connected to any physical network - LAN, fibre optic, cables, telephones, Wi-Fi or Wi-Max, even a mobile phone with a wireless communication port - the IO must be extremely cautious and obtain guidance from a computer expert; if the expert is not available on the spot he may be contacted by telephone for guidance. If a network or mainframe is connected with the crime, do not disconnect the computer; further action must be taken only with the help of a computer forensic expert.
steps.stage: Search and seizure of digital evidence - planning and legal authority
steps.triage_why: Prudent to avoid spoiling evidence, but the IO has the legal authority to act; seeking help is a quality measure.

BNSS 185

steps.title: Take control of the scene and isolate the suspect
steps.text: On reaching the scene, reveal your identity and communicate the purpose of the search to the person present on the premises, then secure and take control of the scene both physically, by limiting the access of all persons, and electronically, by limiting new entries through disabling connectivity. Do not permit the suspect or accused to use any part of the computer used in the crime in any manner: with a single key press or one mouse click he can destroy or tamper with the entire data, and computer data can very easily be destroyed wirelessly over the network. Remove the suspect from the computer immediately and allow no unauthorised person to operate it. Ensure that no one can tamper with the devices or equipment. Where the computer is connected to a network or mainframe, do not disconnect it; in that situation further action must be taken only with the help of a computer forensic expert.
steps.stage: Crime scene handling and seizure execution
steps.triage_why: Standard operating procedure for searches to prevent evidence destruction, but not a statutory duty that defeats prosecution if a specific step (like disabling Wi-Fi) is missed.

conflicts.description: The Tripura SOP (tripura-cyber, p.6) directs the officer to secure the devices by 'removing devices from the network, unplugging them'. The Karnataka SOP forbids simply pulling the plug on a live system (karnataka-cyber-evidence-handling, p.24). The UP handbook cuts against BOTH of them for one class of machine: where a network or mainframe is connected with the crime, 'do not disconnect the computer' and take further action only with a computer forensic expert (up-handbook-cyber, p.18 and p.22).
conflicts.resolution: The canonical text adopts the Karnataka position as the general rule - isolate the scene electronically by disabling connectivity rather than by unplugging - because Karnataka is the operative advisory backbone for this bucket and its rule is the one that preserves volatile evidence. Tripura's 'unplug' instruction is not carried into the canonical text; physical disconnection is permitted only after the live-system and switched-off rules have been applied. UP's networked-computer carve-out is not merely corroborative of Karnataka: it is a narrower prohibition that overrides even the disable-connectivity instruction where a LAN or mainframe is involved, and it is therefore carried explicitly into the canonical text as its final sentence.

steps.title: Identify and seize every relevant digital device
steps.text: Identify all relevant parties and equipment on the scene to determine every device needing seizure. If the person at the scene cannot say whether a device is relevant, seize it anyway - increased workload is preferable to missing relevant evidence. Take into custody every digital device from the standpoint of necessary evidence: PDAs, mobile phones, MP3 players, cameras, flash cards, print-outs, software and data disks, other missing parts and storage devices, together with all computer-related manuals at the scene, all devices attached to the computer, and chiefly the software, operating system and other related material. Seize the original media wherever possible. Lift fingerprints from the keyboard and mouse. Check any printer present: a print command may have been given and, for want of paper, the print may not have emerged while the printer's indicator light is on - in that case load paper in the printer and take the print-out, taking care not to operate the computer or laptop while doing so.
steps.stage: Crime scene handling and seizure execution
steps.triage_why: The case relies on electronic evidence (photos/recordings). Failure to identify and seize the specific devices containing this evidence results in the loss of the primary corpus delicti.

conflicts.description: UNRECORDED IN THE DRAFT. The UP handbook states a preference for acquiring the data on the spot rather than carrying away hardware: 'seizing the data on the spot is preferable because it avoids carrying unnecessary hardware', with a Computer Forensic Expert taking the download and preserving the data on the spot, and only 'if a Computer Forensic Expert is not available on the spot' should the IO seize all the related material (up-handbook-cyber, p.18 and again p.21). The Karnataka SOP states the opposite default: 'seize original media wherever possible' (karnataka-cyber-offence-wise-sops, p.40), seize the entire device where the hard drive cannot be removed (karnataka-cyber-evidence-handling, p.23), and plan on-site forensic imaging 'only if the IO has the necessary equipment and expertise or technical support; otherwise plan a simple seizure of the equipment' (karnataka-cyber-evidence-handling, p.22).
conflicts.resolution: Both sources sit at the same rung of the ladder (state_advisory), so the tie is broken the same way as elsewhere in this bucket: Karnataka is the operative advisory backbone and is the BSA-aware source, and its rule is the evidentially safer one because the original media is primary evidence and needs no Section 63 BSA / 65B IEA certificate. The canonical text therefore adopts seizure of the original media as the default. UP's on-spot acquisition is not discarded but is confined to the condition UP itself attaches to it and which Karnataka independently requires - a competent, trained person with the necessary equipment and expertise present at the scene; absent that, UP itself directs the IO to seize all the related material, which is the canonical rule.

steps.title: Seize the DVR and certify the CCTV footage
steps.text: For CCTV evidence the priority is to seize the original hard disk along with the DVR system; if seizure of the original storage device is not feasible, obtain a copy of the relevant video or take a forensic copy of it. Obtain the certificate under Section 65B IEA (Section 63 BSA) from the person who owns or has lawful control of the CCTV system, mentioning the technical details - the manufacturer of the DVR system, the hard disk used, the serial and product numbers of the DVR and hard disk, and the date and time shown in the DVR system. Because DVRs store information in a proprietary format, create the copy on DVD or USB both in the original proprietary format and in a converted format such as MP4, and summon the person or agency that commissioned the DVR system to help in the seizure and to supply the relevant software drivers or playback software. CCTV clippings obtained during investigation can be submitted directly to court along with the certificate provided by the owner or in-charge of the system; the FSL is not authorised to provide a 65B certificate for CCTV evidence, since there is lawful control. Send the DVR or CCTV system to the FSL where recovery of deleted footage, image enhancement, gait pattern analysis, identification of tampering or face comparison is essential.
steps.stage: Crime scene handling and seizure execution
legal_basis: Sec 65B Indian Evidence Act, 1872 / Sec 63 Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023
steps.triage_why: CCTV is secondary evidence here; the primary evidence is the accused's phone/Instagram. Section 63 BSA/65 IEA compliance is necessary for admissibility, but not the central pillar of this specific cas

steps.title: Acquire volatile data from a live system
steps.text: For a system found switched on, do not simply pull the plug - dealing with a live system requires special skill. The live computer may hold running processes, logged-in users, open network connections, encryption keys or decrypted applications, and running malware. Acquire the volatile data using software tools, and take a RAM dump where the system is on. Where the accused computer is on and the disk is suspected to be encrypted, image the complete system in live condition; take expert advice before proceeding, and ensure the person performing the live acquisition is competent and trained. Run the imaging process from an external storage device and store the output on a sterile digital storage medium such as USB storage, then follow the remaining switched-off machine procedure.
steps.stage: Crime scene handling and seizure execution
steps.responsible: Investigating Officer, assisted by a computer forensic expert
steps.triage_why: Volatile data (RAM) is useful but not essential for proving the existence of stored photos and call recordings.

conflicts.description: The UP handbook directs that if a laptop or computer is found in the on state at the scene, its battery should be removed and it should be switched off (up-handbook-cyber, p.18 and p.21). The Karnataka SOP forbids pulling the plug on a live system and requires volatile data acquisition, and live imaging where the disk is suspected to be encrypted (karnataka-cyber-evidence-handling, p.24-25).
conflicts.resolution: The canonical text follows Karnataka, the operative advisory backbone for this bucket and the more recent, BSA-aware source; powering down a live machine destroys RAM contents and encryption keys. The UP handbook is internally inconsistent on this point - at p.20 it itself requires that where the computer is on, the help of a computer forensic expert must definitely be obtained for volatile data collection - and that consistent instruction is retained as corroboration.

conflicts.description: The Karnataka SOP allows creation of a forensic image copy on site at the time of seizure (karnataka-cyber-evidence-handling, p.24) while elsewhere requiring court permission before forensic imaging and before any access to seized electronic evidence (karnataka-cyber-evidence-handling p.27 flowchart; karnataka-cyber-offence-wise-sops p.34 and p.40).
conflicts.resolution: Read together as the source intends: on-site acquisition at the moment of seizure (RAM dump, live imaging of an encrypted disk) is part of the seizure itself and is done in the presence of the panch witnesses; court permission is required before off-site forensic imaging and before any post-seizure access to the seized media. Both requirements are carried into the canonical steps for live-system handling and for forensic imaging respectively.

steps.title: Seize a switched-off computer without powering it on
steps.text: For a computer found switched off, never switch it on at this stage under any circumstances - a hacker may have configured the system to destroy the related data on power-up, and switching on would in any event change the computer's logs and affect the integrity of the evidence; the electronic evidence must be seized in that very off state. First verify that the computer is really off, because screen savers can give the appearance of being off while the hard drive and monitor are active. Be aware that some laptops power on when the lid is opened, so remove the laptop battery wherever possible. For all-in-one computers whose hard drives are embedded in the monitor and cannot be removed, seize the entire device. Unplug the power cable and the other devices from their sockets. Carefully open the outer casing of the CPU or laptop, identify the hard disk, detach it from the motherboard by disconnecting the data transfer and power cables, and record its unique identifiers - make, model and serial number - noting these identifiers even where the entire CPU is seized. Obtain the signature of the accused and the witnesses on the hard disk using a permanent marker pen, and ensure every item is signed and carries a complete exhibit label. Prepare detailed notes giving the when, where, what, why and who, and the overall actions taken in relation to the computer equipment.
steps.stage: Crime scene handling and seizure execution
steps.triage_why: Switching on a device can overwrite logs or trigger data wipes, potentially destroying the only copies of the incriminating photos/recordings.

ticks.do: Never switch on a computer found switched off at this stage under any circumstances; seize the electronic evidence in that very off state.
notes: A hacker may have configured the system to destroy the related data on power-up, and switching on would in any event change the computer's logs and affect the integrity of the evidence.
Responsible: Investigating Officer.

steps.title: Draw the seizure mahazar with full particulars
steps.text: Draw the seizure mahazar (panchanama) recording: the crime number and the sections of law; the full details of the witnesses; the exact place of the mahazar with its latitude and longitude and the schedule of its north, south, east and west boundaries; the date and the start and end times; the introduction of the IO and the team to the panch witnesses; the accused's introduction and his production of the device; and the complete device identifiers - device, product and model names, serial number, IMEI for each slot, phone numbers and other unique identifiers. The item name, make, model and serial number of all equipment and the time of seizure must invariably be recorded. Where the alleged content is found readily available on the device during seizure, document the file path in the mahazar and capture the metadata of that content in the source device. Fill the details of all seized devices in the digital evidence collection form. Document the whole seizure by photography and videography, and obtain the signatures of the accused, both panch witnesses, the typist, the photographer or videographer, the technical assistance, the IO's assistant and the investigating officer.
steps.stage: Crime scene handling and seizure execution
steps.triage_why: The mahazar/panchanama is a statutory requirement for the legality of the seizure; failure to document witnesses and location can lead to the evidence being thrown out.

steps.title: Pack, seal and transport the seized parts
steps.text: Complete the separation of all parts of the crime-related computer at the scene and then pack them very carefully in anti-static plastic bubble wrap for despatch to the forensic laboratory, so that no part is damaged in transport; as far as possible, use anti-static packaging bubble wrap for seizing any type of storage device, and where anti-static bubble wrap is not available a paper envelope may be used. Keep all parts belonging to a computer with that same computer so that it can easily be reconstructed. Do not carry seized computer equipment in boxes or vehicles into which dust is likely to enter; keep it in a secure, cool and dry place and away from generators, because the electromagnetic signals emitted by generators can destroy the computer's data. Keep the acquired data in sealed condition and protect the integrity of the evidence throughout the investigation life cycle, storing it in an environment free from heat, cold and fire.

steps.triage_why: Proper packaging prevents physical damage, but is a matter of best practice rather than a statutory duty.

steps.title: Handle a seized mobile device to preserve keys
steps.text: For a mobile device found switched on and without a passcode, enable flight mode and disable all network connections including Wi-Fi and Bluetooth; if flight mode cannot be turned on, place the device in a Faraday bag while ensuring sufficient power from a battery pack or external source to prevent battery drain. Enable USB debugging, keep the device awake and disable the screen-lock time-out, and identify applications having a passcode and either disable them or obtain the passcode from the user. Remember that a mobile phone cannot be write-blocked. For a device found switched off, check for physical damage and try to remove the battery if possible. It is critical to identify at the time of seizure whether the phone is After First Unlock (AFU) or Before First Unlock (BFU): File Based Encryption is now the default on Android, so physical extraction is of no use and Full File System extraction is what matters, and after first unlock the key is still present in RAM, so keep the device in a hot (powered) state for key recovery. Collect all device identifiers - the FCC ID and the equipment identifiers IMEI, MEID and ESN.
steps.stage: Crime scene handling and seizure execution
steps.triage_why: Crucial to prevent remote wiping of the device (via Find My Device/Instagram) which would permanently destroy the evidence.

conflicts.description: The UP handbook directs that before seizing a mobile phone the battery should be removed if possible, and only if it cannot be removed should a Faraday bag, four to five layers of aluminium foil, or flight mode be used (up-handbook-cyber, p.21). The Karnataka SOP requires a powered-on device to be kept powered - flight mode or a Faraday bag with a power source - because after first unlock the decryption key resides in RAM (karnataka-cyber-evidence-handling, p.25).
conflicts.resolution: The canonical text follows Karnataka for a device found switched on: isolate it from the network but keep it powered, and identify AFU/BFU state at seizure. UP's battery removal is retained only for a device already found switched off, where Karnataka gives the same instruction. UP's aluminium-foil wrapping is preserved as a field substitute where no Faraday bag is available.

steps.title: Seize the cloud account and secure its credentials
steps.text: For data stored in the cloud, contact an expert to acquire it using appropriate tools. The IO may obtain the user's login credentials and must document that fact in the mahazar proceedings, but must never disclose passwords in the mahazar document - the password is written on a piece of paper kept by the IO alone. Where the cloud service requires two-factor authentication by OTP to a phone or email, the IO may change the recovery mobile number or email ID to an official one so that the OTP messages come to him for verification. In the mahazar record the cloud storage name, the linked email ID, the drive creation date, each folder name and creation date containing offending material, the number of files, other particulars, and the date and time of access during the mahazar. Back up the relevant cloud content to a sterile USB storage device or DVD, preserve the media in a holder box or jewel case, obtain the signatures of the accused, the panch witnesses and the IO team on the seized article with a CD-marker pen, seal it using kora cloth with a unique impression or stamp affixed on wax, and collect a sample seal. The IO then takes control of the cloud account by changing the password and linking his official mobile number for two-factor authentication, documenting the updated password on a piece of paper enclosed in an envelope marked 'Secret and Confidential', duly sealed with a wax impression and signed by the IO, the accused and the witnesses, who declare that they have not seen the new password.

steps.title: Check the BIOS clock after removing the disk
steps.text: Guard against clock inaccuracy in the seized system. After removing the hard disk from the suspected system - and only after it has been removed, which is the one point at which the machine may be powered up - switch the system on and enter the BIOS/UEFI settings, note the date and time shown in the BIOS, and highlight any deviation against standard time sources in the mahzar (panchnama) proceedings document.

steps.triage_why: Clock drift is a technical detail for timeline precision, but rarely defeats a prosecution in a sexual offence case.

steps.title: Task the FSL with a case-specific questionnaire
steps.text: Send the original device to the FSL and obtain expert opinion, drafting a questionnaire specific and relevant to the case. Chart out the questions to be asked so as to obtain an optimal opinion, send all relevant information about the case and the seized property so that the analysis can be properly directed, and ask for a further opinion if deemed necessary. Provide the path of the alleged content found during investigation. Frame the questionnaire to cover the incident details and the role of the accused whose devices are analysed, the presence of evidence related to the case, and digital artifacts such as URLs, messages, photographs and videos, email IDs and any other user activity. Request opinion establishing the identity of persons, places or things in the content, and opinion ruling out tampering of the evidence where necessary; to filter obscenity-related information, request sharing of the multimedia files containing the exposure.
steps.stage: Forensic imaging, FSL tasking and analysis
steps.triage_why: Expert opinion from FSL is required to authenticate the digital evidence (photos/recordings) to prove they weren't morphed or fabricated.

steps.title: Image the seized media under court permission
steps.text: Never access seized electronic evidence prior to court permission and never work on the original media - always work on the forensic mirror image. Take the court's permission for conducting off-site forensic imaging, carry out the imaging in the presence of the panch witnesses and draw a separate panchanama for the imaging. To create an image copy of a seized hard disk, connect the suspected drive to the investigator's computer through a write blocker device for forensic previewing and copying; dedicated hardware imaging devices and acquisition software may be used, and detailed notes must be made of all actions concerning the computer equipment. Request the FSL to make additional forensic copies, a minimum of three, for further use. Analyse the image copy and identify the evidence in it.
steps.stage: Forensic imaging, FSL tasking and analysis
steps.triage_why: Working on original media alters metadata (last accessed dates), which can be used by the defense to claim the evidence was tampered with by police.

steps.title: Verify every forensic copy by hash value
steps.text: Verify that every forensic copy matches the original using the hash function, and record the hash values on the record. Hashing acts as the fingerprint of an electronic record - any change to the record changes the hash, which proves tampering. Where evidence is downloaded from an online platform, the mahazar must carefully record the hash values of the electronic data. Use SHA1, SHA256 or MD5 or another legally acceptable standard, and enclose the hash report with the certificate.
steps.stage: Forensic imaging, FSL tasking and analysis
steps.triage_why: Hash values are the only way to prove the integrity of electronic evidence in court. Without them, the prosecution cannot prove the copy is an exact duplicate of the original.

ticks.do: Verify that every forensic copy matches the original using the hash function, and record the hash values on the record.
notes: Hashing acts as the fingerprint of an electronic record - any change to the record changes the hash, which proves tampering.
Responsible: Investigating Officer.

steps.title: Capture online content with a forensic capture tool
steps.text: Where the evidence is a web page, a social media post or other online content, capture and archive it with a dedicated internet evidence capture tool that securely records the page - including its dynamic content - as a verifiable record, rather than by an ordinary screenshot or 'save page'. The free open-source tools listed for this purpose are FAW (Forensic Acquisition of Websites) and Magnet Forensics Web Page Saver. Use the tool as part of the mahazar download process conducted in the presence of independent witnesses, so that the captured page is taken with its integrity intact and its hash values are recorded on the mahazar. This is the acquisition method that makes the downloaded online content stand up as electronic evidence, and it is the one category of the eight in the SOP's forensic tool annexure that no other canonical step carries.

steps.responsible: Investigating officer, with technical assistance where the IO is not trained in the tool
steps.applies_when: objectionable social media content, obscenity, impersonation, defamation and any case where the primary evidence is online content that the platform may remove or alter
steps.triage_why: While professional tools are best practice for authenticity, screenshots are often accepted if corroborated, though less robust.

steps.title: Certify secondary electronic evidence under Section 63 BSA
steps.text: Obtain the certificate under Section 63 BSA (Section 65B IEA) for every item of secondary electronic evidence. Information in an electronic record printed on paper, or stored, recorded or copied in optical or magnetic media or semiconductor memory produced by a computer or communication device ('computer output') is deemed a document and is admissible without further proof or production of the original if the statutory conditions are met: the output was produced during the period the device was regularly used by the person having lawful control; information of that kind was regularly fed in the ordinary course of activities; the device was operating properly throughout, or any malfunction did not affect the record or its accuracy; and the information reproduces or is derived from information fed in the ordinary course of activities. The storing or processing function may have been performed by a combination of computers or by different computers in succession. The certificate must record the device details, the type and nature of the electronic evidence, the provisions relied on, optionally the security details such as password or firewall, a declaration that the content is a true reproduction of the original, and the issuing person's designation and declaration; use the two-part form with Part A completed by the party (device or source type, make, model, serial number, IMEI/UIN/UID/MAC/Cloud ID, declaration of lawful control and proper working, and hash values with the hash report enclosed) and Part B completed by the expert with the same device and hash particulars, name, designation and signature. The certificate may be issued during investigation, along with the charge sheet, or during trial; its production is mandatory and it may be filed at any stage during the trial.
legal_basis: Sec 63 Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023
Sec 65B Indian Evidence Act, 1872
steps.triage_why: Under the BSA/IEA, secondary electronic evidence is inadmissible without the mandatory certificate; missing this defeats the prosecution of digital evidence.

conflicts.description: The UP handbook states that while collecting electronic evidence the IO must obtain the proforma certificate under Sections 65A and 65B of the Indian Evidence Act from the concerned Administrator and produce it in court, 'because without the above proforma certificate the evidence collected by you will not be admissible' (up-handbook-cyber, p.22). The Karnataka SOP, citing Arjun Panditrao Khotkar vs Kailash Kushanrao Gorantyal (2020 INSC 453) and State of Karnataka Lokayukta vs M R Hiremath (AIR 2019 SC 2377), states that failure to produce the certificate at the time the charge sheet is filed is not fatal and that it can be filed at any stage during the trial.
conflicts.resolution: Both sources sit on the same state_advisory rung, so the ladder does not decide between them; the tie is broken by the binding Supreme Court authority that Karnataka cites and UP does not. The canonical text therefore follows Karnataka on timing: production of the certificate is mandatory but a case is not lost merely because the certificate was not filed with the charge sheet, and it may be filed at any stage during the trial. UP's operational instruction - obtain the certificate from the system administrator at the time of collection and produce it in court - is retained as a detail, since pursuing the certificate from the moment of collection is the safe practice both sources support.

steps.title: Decide between primary and secondary electronic evidence
steps.text: Decide at the outset whether the electronic material is going in as primary or secondary evidence. Primary evidence under Section 62 IEA (Section 57 BSA) is the original document or electronic record and any computer output produced during its regular use; secondary evidence under Section 63 IEA (Section 58 BSA) is a copy or a reproduction or derivative of the original meeting the specified conditions, and Section 63 BSA (Sections 65A and 65B IEA) specifies the procedure for admitting secondary evidence in electronic form. As a best-evidence rule, endeavour to collect the original content from the source; where that is impossible, present secondary electronic evidence with the reasons recorded, along with due certification. No certificate is needed if the original device itself is produced, or for an original recording; a certificate is required for a copy of the original recording.
legal_basis: Sec 57, 58, 60, 63 Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023
Sec 62, 63, 65, 65A, 65B Indian Evidence Act, 1872
steps.triage_why: This is a legal classification step to ensure the correct evidentiary path is followed.

ticks.do: Decide at the outset whether the electronic material is going in as primary or secondary evidence.
notes: Legal basis: Sec 57, 58, 60, 63 Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023; Sec 62, 63, 65, 65A, 65B Indian Evidence Act, 1872.

steps.title: Pursue the remedies when no certificate is forthcoming
steps.text: Where the certificate cannot be obtained, use the available remedies rather than abandoning the evidence. Where a party with control over the electronic evidence withholds the essential certificate despite reasonable attempts to obtain it, the court has discretion to issue a directive compelling its production. Where the person in charge of the evidence has been transferred or has retired, the certificate is based on designation and on management of the activity, not on the specific individual, so the prosecution officer can apply under Sections 91 and 311 CrPC (Sections 94 and 348 BNSS) for a certificate from the current lawful custodian. The law likewise allows the successor officer holding the post to depose on a report whose author has been transferred, retired, died, cannot be found, is incapable of deposing, or whose presence would delay the proceedings, and such deposition may be taken through audio-video electronic means. Where jurisdictional or similar limitations make a certificate for secondary electronic evidence difficult to obtain, courts have allowed later submission during trial.
legal_basis: Sections 91 and 311 CrPC (Sections 94 and 348 BNSS)
BNSS 336
steps.triage_why: This provides a contingency plan if the primary requirement (the certificate) cannot be met.

steps.title: Seek the certificate only from a lawful custodian
steps.text: Seek the certificate only from the person entitled to give it - the person with lawful control over the computer or device at the relevant time, or the person managing the related activities. A certificate cannot be given by: the accused, who cannot be compelled to submit it; a person who downloaded content from the public domain without lawful control over the source; an FSL scientific officer, in respect of data not in his lawful control; or a police station or entity that merely provided technical aid in creating a forensic image, which should not be compelled to produce one. Foreign service providers may not comply with Indian certification requirements. Providing a certificate 'as a service' is not allowed - only an individual or company with lawful control over the system can provide it. Where an outsider's services are used for video recording of investigation proceedings, the certificate must be given by the person having lawful control over the storage device. Evidence extracted from seized articles with technical support from specialised police stations is not admissible, since such units are not notified as experts under the Indian Evidence Act and the IT Act. A photograph of a conversation on a phone can be treated only as information and may not have evidentiary value unless supported by other evidence.
steps.triage_why: Ensures the certificate is legally valid; an invalid certificate may be challenged in court.

steps.title: Build the charge accused by accused
steps.text: Take the advice of a legal advisor while preparing the final report, and build the charge accused by accused. Segregate all collected documents, statements, reports and material objects; interlink the collected evidence and the expert opinion with each accused; frame a separate charge for each accused showing the role he played with the applicable sections; and include all the interlinking documents that prove the offence - being party to the conspiracy, common intention, identity theft, impersonation, unauthorised access. Prepare a memo of evidence indicating the role of each witness who will depose. Attach the certificates required wherever applicable - the Section 63 BSA (65B IEA) certificates, the certificate under Section 79A ITAA 2008 and the Bankers' Books Evidence Act certificates - together with the FSL reports, and cross-verify the digital evidence with respect to date and time.

steps.title: File sensitive and electronic annexures separately
steps.text: Handle sensitive and electronic annexures separately when filing. Avoid attaching hard copies of obscene pictures - attach a password-protected soft copy, or use sealed covers bearing a special note such as 'This cover contains sexually explicit content' or 'This envelope contains CSAM (Child Sexual Abuse Material) content'. Keep the electronic evidence - CD, DVD, pen drive, memory card or SD card - separately and securely while submitting the charge sheet documents. Verify that all photocopy annexures are duly attested so as to facilitate marking. Check that sufficient mirror images or copies are available to supply to the accused, and where the victim is a minor, make a special mention in the charge sheet requesting the court to review any request by the accused or the defence counsel for supply of a mirror image of the digital media containing the alleged material under Section 207 CrPC (Section 230 BNSS).
legal_basis: Section 207 CrPC (Section 230 BNSS)
steps.applies_when: obscenity, CSEAM and offences against women and children
steps.triage_why: This is a matter of administrative propriety and sensitivity regarding obscene material, not a requirement for conviction.

steps.text: Establish the method of search based on investigative theory, size of area to be searched and other factors: zonal method (area divided into squares/sectors with an officer assigned to each zone), spiral or circle method (effective in a small area, beginning from the centre or the perimeter and moving in a circular path), wheel method (searchers gather at the centre and move radially outwards, with the drawback of spoiling evidence at the centre and ever increasing distance between searchers), grid method (best procedure for a large area, searchers moving parallel to one another and covering the same area twice), or cross-hatch method (two dimensional — the scene is covered length wise and then width wise).

steps.title: Document Sequence of Transactional Facts
steps.text: The IO should record the whole surrounding episode, not just the act charged: what the accused, the victim and the bystanders said and did at the incident or so shortly before or after it that it belongs to the same transaction, as illustration (a) shows. Do not drop connected events from the case diary or charge-sheet merely because they happened at a different time or a different place, and in multi-act or multi-location offences collect each component act since it can be proved as part of the general transaction even where the accused was not present at all of them.
steps.stage: Evidence law: Relevancy of facts forming part of same transaction
legal_basis: BSA 4
steps.triage_why: The prosecution may fail to link the digital coercion to the physical crime, allowing the defense to argue the events are disconnected incidents.
