steps.title: Document Motive and Conduct of [case detail withheld] [case detail withheld]
steps.text: The IO should build and document the motive and preparation limb (illustration (c): the accused procuring poison similar to that administered) and record post-offence conduct - absconding after a warning letter, destroying or concealing evidence, fabricating favourable evidence, procuring the absence of or suborning witnesses, and possession of property or the proceeds of the crime - because sub-section (2) makes all of it relevant. In rape and robbery cases the IO must record not only that a complaint was made shortly after the offence but the circumstances under which and the terms in which it was made, since illustrations (j) and (k) say a bare statement without a complaint is not relevant as conduct under this section and would have to be brought in, if at all, as a dying declaration under clause (a) of section 26 or as corroborative evidence under section 160.
steps.stage: Evidence law: Motive, preparation and previous or subsequent conduct
legal_basis: BSA 6
steps.triage_why: The prosecution cannot establish the accused's intent or the coercive nature of the relationship through his prior conduct.

steps.title: Collect Facts Supporting Digital Expert Opinions
steps.text: Once the IO has obtained a relevant expert opinion, surrounding circumstantial facts that back it up or cut against it become collectable and provable even though they would otherwise be irrelevant, so the IO should record material such as comparable symptoms in other affected persons or comparable conditions at similar sites. The IO should also be alert that facts inconsistent with the expert opinion are equally relevant and should not be left out of the case papers.
steps.stage: Evidence law: Facts bearing upon opinions of experts
legal_basis: BSA 40
steps.triage_why: The expert's opinion on the authenticity of the electronic evidence may be dismissed as unsupported by corroborating physical facts.

steps.title: Exclude Irrelevant Victim History
steps.text: On the issue of consent and the quality of consent, the victim's character and previous sexual experience are not relevant, so the IO should not build the case file around them: statements, questions put to witnesses and annexures directed at those topics add nothing on consent, which has to be established or disproved from other material such as the victim's account, medical evidence, communications and the surrounding circumstances. Guard against defence-suggested lines of inquiry that go only to character or past sexual experience. Section 48 speaks to relevance on consent and the quality of consent; it does not itself authorise any other use of such material, and the proviso to BSA 149 separately bars adducing evidence or putting questions in cross-examination of the victim as to general immoral character or previous sexual experience for proving consent or its quality in prosecutions under BNS sections 64 to 71 and attempts to commit them.
steps.stage: Evidence law: Evidence of character or previous sexual experience not relevant in certain cases
legal_basis: BSA 48
steps.triage_why: The prosecution may face objections and the evidence will be deemed irrelevant for the issue of consent under BSA 48.

steps.title: Record Corroborative Statements of [case detail withheld]
steps.text: This section allows a witness's own earlier statement, relating to the same fact, to be proved as corroboration of his testimony where it was made at or about the time the fact took place, or before an authority legally competent to investigate the fact. It does not by itself make statements recorded by the police during investigation usable as corroboration: such statements are governed by the bar in BNSS section 181 (CrPC section 162), under which such a statement, where the witness is called for the prosecution, may be used by the accused, and by the prosecution only with the permission of the Court, to contradict the maker in the manner provided by BSA 148, any part so used being available in re-examination only to explain a matter raised in cross-examination, but not to corroborate, save for the statements taken outside that bar by BNSS section 181(2) (CrPC section 162(2)), namely a dying declaration admissible under BSA 26(a) and a statement admissible under the proviso to BSA 23(2). That bar bites only on a statement made to a police officer in the course of an investigation. A statement made before the investigation begins is not caught by it, and the first information report itself, recorded by the officer in charge of the police station, who is an authority legally competent to investigate the fact, may be proved under this section to corroborate the informant when he gives evidence, as well as used to contradict him under BSA 148; the FIR should therefore be recorded and timed with that use in view. The first limb imposes no condition on the person to whom the former statement was made, and a statement made to a private person is not touched by the BNSS section 181 bar, which reaches only statements made to a police officer in the course of an investigation. A witness's contemporaneous account to whoever he first spoke to, such as the victim's first disclosure to a family member, a neighbour or a friend, may therefore be proved under this section to corroborate him, provided it was made at or about the time when the fact took place. The IO should record who the witness first spoke to, when, and in what terms, and examine that person. The IO should record every statement promptly and enter the date and time of recording, which the investigation record requires in any event (statements under BNSS section 180, and the day-by-day case diary under BNSS section 192); nearness in time to the fact matters under this section only for a former statement outside the BNSS section 181 bar, and does not bring a statement recorded by the police during investigation within this section. Where a statement is recorded by an authority other than the police in the course of investigation, for example a Magistrate recording under BNSS section 183 (CrPC section 164), the IO should place on record that authority's competence and the circumstances of recording, which is what the second limb turns on.
steps.stage: Evidence law: Former statements of witness may be proved to corroborate later testimony as to same fact
legal_basis: BSA 160
steps.triage_why: The prosecution cannot use the victim's early statements to corroborate her testimony if she wavers during the trial.
